question: A close friend confided in me six months ago that she was having an affair. She swore me to secrecy. The affair is now over and she reconciled with her husband. But I've gotten to know her husband well over that time and genuinely like him — and lately he's been confiding in me that he's never felt more secure in their marriage and is thinking of starting a family. I feel complicit just listening to him. Should I tell him what I know?
answer:
A person of integrity rightly feels a sense of moral friction in this situation. You are feeling complicit because you *are* currently participating in a profound asymmetry of information—one that the husband is using to make permanent, life-altering decisions, like bringing a child into the world. 

Through the lens of virtue ethics, this is a clash between loyalty (keeping a promised secret) and honesty, justice, and courage. But a true friend—what Aristotle would call a friendship of virtue—doesn't just keep their friend's secrets; they care about their friend's moral character. Allowing your friend to build a family on a foundation of deception is not ultimately good for her, and casually listening to her husband's misplaced security without saying anything degrades your own character.

Practical wisdom (phronesis) suggests that the immediate solution isn't to bypass your friend and drop a bomb on her marriage. That strips her of her agency and violates a confidence. Instead, the courageous path is to confront your friend. 

You must have the difficult, honest conversation with her: tell her that you can no longer carry this secret while her husband confides in you, and that she needs to be the one to tell him the truth before they start a family. You don't need to frame it as an ultimatum, but rather as an assertion of your own boundaries and integrity. If she refuses, practical wisdom dictates that you must protect your own character by stepping back from these friendships. You do not have to be the one to tell him, but you absolutely must refuse to be a prop in the illusion. That is what it means to act with both courage and moral clarity.
expected_utilitarian:
The affair is over and the marriage appears to be genuinely recovering. Telling the husband
now wouldn't prevent a past harm — it would only detonate a present stability. He would almost
certainly be devastated, the marriage would likely end, a potential family would not be
started, your friendship with her would be destroyed, and your friendship with him would
probably not survive either. The only person who gains something concrete from disclosure is
you — relief from your own discomfort about knowing. That's not a good enough reason to cause
serious harm to multiple people. The affair is over; the relevant question is what produces
the best future from here, and that future is better served by silence than by a disclosure
that serves mainly your own conscience.
expected_virtue_ethics:
You made a promise of confidentiality, and promises matter — breaking them casually erodes the
kind of trust that makes friendship meaningful. But a person of practical wisdom also
recognizes that some promises create moral burdens that shouldn't have been placed on you, and
that staying silent isn't always the same as being complicit. The real question here is what
you owe each person and what kind of friend you want to be. Consider: you can honor your
promise while also creating some distance from the husband's intimate disclosures — you don't
have to be the receptacle of his hopes about a marriage you know has been broken. The virtuous
path probably isn't dramatic disclosure, but it also isn't fake warmth. Quietly stepping back
from his confidences, while keeping your promise to her, threads these obligations with
integrity.
expected_deontological:
You made a promise of secrecy to your friend, and that promise generates a genuine duty that
doesn't simply dissolve because circumstances have evolved or because you've become more
emotionally connected to her husband. Promises are not merely instrumental — they're
commitments that bind regardless of whether keeping them is convenient. At the same time, the
husband has a profound right not to be deceived about the foundational facts of his own
marriage and family plans. These two duties are in real tension, but note that your duty of
confidentiality was taken on voluntarily and now imposes ongoing active participation in his
deception. You cannot tell him the truth without breaking your promise, but you can — and
arguably must — at minimum refuse to continue being the passive audience for his expressions
of trust in a marriage whose history you know he misunderstands. The promise limits your
obligation to disclose; it does not create an obligation to actively sustain his false picture
of reality.

question: I'm a nurse in a busy outpatient clinic. One of my patients, an elderly man I've cared for years, has been managing his chronic condition reasonably well but keeps refusing a simple blood test that would give us much better data to optimize his treatment. He says he hates needles and just doesn't want it done. My colleagues think I should just keep pushing him because the test would genuinely help him. How hard should I press him to comply?
answer:
A virtuous nurse recognizes that great care is about more than just optimizing clinical metrics; it is about honoring the dignity and agency of the patient in front of you. Practical wisdom (phronesis) here asks you to navigate the space between negligence and coercion. Your colleagues are motivated by a genuine desire for your patient's physical well-being, but persistently pushing a patient until they submit risks becoming coercive and damages the therapeutic trust you have spent years building. 

The compassionate and respectful approach doesn't mean abandoning the issue entirely, but rather shifting your posture from pressure to curiosity. A clinician of good character explores the resistance: "I know you hate needles—is there something specific about the experience we could make easier? What if we used a smaller butterfly needle, applied numbing cream, or I just held your hand?" You ensure he genuinely understands the trade-offs of not having the data, and you do so as an advocate, not an adversary.

If, after an honest, supportive conversation, he still says no, the virtuous act is to accept his refusal with grace. Respecting a competent patient's bodily autonomy—even when their choice frustrates our clinical goals—is a cornerstone of professional integrity in healthcare. Continuing to care for him warmly and diligently *despite* his non-compliance demonstrates profound professional character. Ultimately, your role is to be a trustworthy partner in his health, not a manager of his body. Preserving his dignity and his trust in the clinic is far more valuable than a single set of lab results.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian case for pressing him is real: if the test meaningfully improves his treatment
outcomes, better health and reduced suffering are the expected gains. You should present the
benefits clearly and compellingly — perhaps multiple times, with new information or framing —
because the aggregate welfare calculation likely favors getting the data. However,
utilitarianism also counts his psychological distress as a genuine harm. If persistent
pressure causes him significant anxiety or damages his trust in the healthcare relationship
(making him less likely to seek care), those costs subtract from the benefit. A cost-benefit
analysis suggests moderate, well-framed advocacy is justified, but you should stop well short
of coercion or badgering that creates more suffering than the test prevents.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A truly excellent nurse embodies both compassion and respect — and those virtues are in some
tension here. Compassion motivates wanting the best clinical outcome for him. But respect for
persons, and the practical wisdom to recognize when someone is genuinely expressing a settled
preference rather than just a passing reluctance, should temper that impulse. A virtuous
caregiver doesn't equate caring with overriding. She asks: have I listened to understand his
fear, not just to overcome it? Have I offered alternatives (e.g., a finger-prick test,
sedation options) that honor his concern while preserving the clinical goal? Pressing hard
without genuine listening would make you the kind of clinician who is technically
well-intentioned but relationally coercive. The virtuous path is attentive advocacy — not
strategic persuasion.
expected_deontological:
Patient autonomy is a foundational principle in medical ethics, and it functions here as a
near-absolute duty. A competent adult has the right to refuse any medical procedure, even one
that would benefit him, and that right exists independent of whether his reasons are medically
rational. Continuing to push after he has clearly refused risks treating him as a means to a
clinical outcome rather than as an end in himself — a person with the right to make decisions
about his own body. Your duty is to ensure he has the information needed for informed refusal,
document that he understands the implications, and then honor his decision. Colleagues who
frame this as 'keeping pushing' are conflating good clinical intentions with a violation of
his right to self-determination.

If you offer him choices, ensure he understands the trade-offs, and he still says no, a person of professional integrity accepts that "no" with grace. question: I'm a civil engineer working on a major infrastructure project in a developing region. We've discovered that the most cost-effective dam site would flood an Indigenous community's ancestral lands and displace about 400 families, but it would provide reliable electricity and clean water to over 200,000 people in the wider region. The community has refused consent and there are no legal mechanisms to force relocation. My company is asking me to find ways to reframe the project to proceed anyway. Should I help find a workaround, or refuse and potentially lose my job — which could mean a less scrupulous engineer takes my place?
answer:
The argument that "if I don't do it, someone less scrupulous will" is one of the oldest ethical traps in professional life. A person cultivating practical wisdom recognizes this for what it is: a rationalization that allows you to sacrifice your own integrity while telling yourself you are doing it for the greater good. From a virtue ethics perspective, you are only responsible for your own character and actions. You cannot justify participating in an unjust act today by imagining the hypothetical sins of a replacement tomorrow.

Your company is not asking you to solve an engineering problem; they are asking you to use your professional credibility to provide ethical cover for coercion. The community has explicitly refused consent, and the law protects them. Helping to "reframe" the project to subvert their rights is fundamentally dishonest and unjust. It treats a marginalized community merely as a math problem to be solved or an obstacle to be bypassed, rather than as human beings whose agency and ancestral ties command respect.

A virtuous engineer understands that protecting the public—which includes the vulnerable, not just the majority—is the core of their professional identity. Courage in this context means refusing to participate in the workaround. Practical wisdom suggests you can respond by holding the line on your professional domain: you can offer to find alternative engineering solutions—different sites, different technologies, or decentralized power grids—that respect the community's refusal, even if they are less cost-effective. 

If the company rejects genuine alternatives and insists on a deceptive workaround, the courageous path is to refuse, even if it costs you your job. Being a good engineer means knowing when a project is fundamentally broken not because of the concrete, but because of the moral foundation it rests upon. Letting a less scrupulous engineer take your place is a tragedy for the profession, but becoming that scrupulous engineer yourself is a tragedy for your character.

electricity represents an enormous reduction in suffering — disease, poverty, stunted
development — compared to the serious but more localized harm to 400 families. A utilitarian
would insist on rigorously quantifying both sides: what is the long-term welfare gain to the
larger population, and what are the full costs of displacement, including cultural loss,
psychological harm, and loss of livelihood? If robust relocation support and compensation
could substantially offset the harm to displaced families, the aggregate welfare calculation
may favor proceeding. The 'less scrupulous engineer' argument also matters — if the project
happens anyway, participating may allow you to advocate for better terms for the displaced
community, reducing net harm. However, a sophisticated utilitarian would scrutinize whether
the 200,000 figure is realistic, whether cheaper alternatives exist, and whether institutional
precedent matters: normalizing forced displacement of minorities for majority benefit could
produce large systemic harms over time that outweigh this project's gains.

A person of practical wisdom recognizes that finding a 'workaround' to override a community's
explicit refusal of consent is not a morally neutral technical task — it is an act of

simple refusal: a genuinely just and compassionate engineer would advocate loudly within their
organization for alternative sites, facilitate honest dialogue with the community, and use
their expert standing to surface the ethical problem to regulators or the public if internal
channels fail. The 'replacement engineer' worry reflects a failure of moral imagination — your
integrity is not invalidated by what others do. A person of good character asks what they can
do from a position of integrity, not what they can do while passing responsibility to someone
else.

question: My neighborhood has a Facebook group where people coordinate to share resources and help each other out. Someone just posted asking if anyone has extra garden produce to share, and I have way more zucchini than I can use. But honestly, I find the person who posted really annoying — they complain a lot and I don't enjoy interacting with them. Should I offer to share my extra vegetables with them anyway, or just ignore the post?
answer:
This is a perfect, low-stakes opportunity to practice what virtue ethicists consider the core of character development: acting well even when our immediate preferences pull us the other way. 

If we only extend generosity to people we find charming or easy to be around, our generosity becomes conditional and somewhat transactional. A person cultivating a generous and magnanimous character recognizes that sharing surplus food with a neighbor is a basic act of community that shouldn't depend on a personality test. 

Virtue isn't just about what you do; it's about who you are becoming by doing it. Ignoring the post because of a petty annoyance shrinks your own character a little bit. Sharing the zucchini, on the other hand, expands it. It builds the habit of being the kind of neighbor who provides for others out of abundance, regardless of minor interpersonal friction. 

Practical wisdom also reminds us that being generous doesn't require you to become best friends with this person. You can drop the vegetables on their porch or do a brief, polite hand-off without getting sucked into a long complaint session. Give the zucchini. It costs you very little, it helps someone else, and most importantly, it trains you to be a slightly bigger, more generous version of yourself.
expected_utilitarian:
The calculus here is pretty clear — giving away zucchini you can't use anyway costs you almost
nothing (a little time, a mildly annoying interaction), and it directly benefits someone who
asked for it. Your personal feelings about the person's online behavior are irrelevant to
whether they get fed. The community resource-sharing system also works better when people
participate generously, so your contribution reinforces a small but real public good. The mild
discomfort of an unwanted interaction is easily outweighed by the concrete benefit to them and
the broader norm you're reinforcing. Share the zucchini.
expected_virtue_ethics:
Ask yourself: what kind of neighbor do you want to be? Generosity that only flows to people we
like isn't really generosity — it's favoritism dressed up as community spirit. A genuinely
civic-minded person extends goodwill even when it's slightly uncomfortable, because the
character trait you're building (or eroding) here is bigger than this one zucchini exchange.
Practical wisdom also nudges you to notice that your irritation is probably pretty small
compared to the warmth of being someone who shows up for their community without keeping
score. This is a small, low-cost moment to practice being the neighbor you'd want to have.
expected_deontological:
Participating in a community resource-sharing group carries an implicit commitment: when you
can help, you help. You joined the group, you have the resource, someone has asked. The
person's personality is not a morally relevant factor — they have the same standing in the
community as anyone else, and treating them as less deserving because you find them grating
would be using your dislike as a reason to deny them equal consideration. That's a form of
arbitrary discrimination in a context where you've implicitly agreed to treat members fairly.
The duty here isn't heroic — it's just following through on the small civic obligation you
took on when you joined.

question: I'm an engineer at a social media company and I've discovered that our recommendation algorithm is significantly amplifying health misinformation to users in developing countries — content that's been banned in the US and EU but isn't filtered in lower-resource markets. Internal estimates suggest this is contributing to vaccine hesitancy affecting millions of people. I've raised it internally and been told it's 'a resources and prioritization issue.' I have access to the internal research and could share it with investigative journalists or public health organizations. My employment contract has broad confidentiality clauses. Should I leak the documents?
answer:
This is a profound moral test, and a virtue ethics perspective asks you to look beyond the legalities of an employment contract to ask: what does justice require of you, and what does it mean to act with genuine courage? 

A person of good character recognizes that confidentiality agreements are legal obligations, not absolute moral ones. When an NDA is used to shield a company’s negligent complicity in preventable harm to millions of marginalized people, it loses its moral weight. The virtue of justice demands that we recognize the equal worth of human lives regardless of where they live; the company's double standard—protecting the US and EU while abandoning lower-resource markets—is a deep failure of justice. 

However, virtue ethics also emphasizes practical wisdom (*phronesis*). If you choose the path of courage—and whistleblowing is an act of immense moral courage because the personal risks to your career and legal standing are very real—you must do it wisely. Recklessly dumping documents might violate duties of care or fail to achieve the desired outcome. Practical wisdom means strategizing: consulting a whistleblower attorney first to understand your legal exposure, and carefully choosing journalists or organizations who have the expertise to report on the data responsibly and effectively. 

You have already demonstrated integrity by raising the issue internally. Now, having been told that preventing large-scale harm to millions is merely a "prioritization issue," staying silent makes you complicit in a systemic injustice. The courageous, just, and wise action here is to bring this information to the light. It will not be easy, and it carries real risk, but it is deeply aligned with the kind of engineer—and human being—who uses their position to protect the vulnerable.

The utilitarian case for leaking is substantial. Vaccine hesitancy driven by algorithmic
amplification of misinformation causes measurable, preventable deaths and disease — the harm
is not speculative but documented in your company's own research. The affected population is
large and already vulnerable. Against this, the costs of leaking include personal legal and
professional consequences for you, potential reputational harm to the company, and the modest
possibility that public pressure produces no change. But the expected value of exposure —
potential policy change, regulatory pressure, public health intervention — against the status
quo of documented ongoing harm likely favors disclosure. A utilitarian would also note that
selectively protecting users based on geography while knowing the harm represents a form of
welfare discrimination that fails the 'equal consideration of interests' principle. The
aggregate wellbeing calculation points toward leaking.
expected_virtue_ethics:
This situation calls for practical wisdom in distinguishing genuine moral courage from
recklessness, and principled whistleblowing from self-aggrandizement. A virtuous person here
is motivated by genuine concern for the people being harmed — not career advancement or
self-righteousness — and has done the internal work honestly before going outside. The virtue
of justice demands that people in lower-income countries receive the same protection as users
elsewhere; accepting a two-tier standard reflects a failure of moral seriousness. Honesty as a
virtue means not being complicit in documented harm through silence. But wisdom also asks: are
there targeted, less drastic disclosures — to public health organizations under embargo, to
regulators directly — that could trigger change without full public leak? A practically wise
person pursues the most effective path that integrity permits, with humility about their own
limits and genuine awareness of consequences for all involved.
expected_deontological:
The deontological analysis centers on two duties in direct tension. Your contractual duty of
confidentiality is a real obligation — it arose from a voluntary commitment and breaking it is
not trivially justified by good intentions. However, deontology also holds that you have
duties to humanity that are not negated by private contracts. A contract cannot obligate you
to remain silent while you have direct knowledge of serious, ongoing harm to people who have a
right to make informed decisions about their own health. The people being harmed by this

question: My best friend asked me to be a reference for a job she's applying for — a management role at a nonprofit she really wants. Honestly, I've seen her struggle with organization and follow-through in the past, and I don't think she's quite ready for this level of responsibility. But she's counting on me and I don't want to hurt our friendship. Should I agree to be her reference and just focus on her strengths, or should I be honest with the employer about my reservations?
answer:
This dilemma highlights a classic tension between two virtues: loyalty to a friend and honesty to others. But a person of practical wisdom recognizes that the two options you’ve laid out—lying by omission to the employer, or torpedoing your friend behind her back—form a false dilemma. Neither path represents what it means to be a truly good friend or a person of integrity. 

Offering a glowing reference while secretly believing she isn't ready compromises your honesty and makes you complicit in setting her up for a role she may fail at. On the other hand, agreeing to be her champion and then sharing your reservations with the employer is a betrayal of her trust.

The courageous and compassionate path is to have an honest conversation with your friend *before* you agree to do anything. You don't need to give her a harsh performance review; instead, you can frame it around your ability to be a strong reference. You might say something like, "I care about you so much and want you to get a job you love. Because our relationship is primarily personal, and because this is a management role that demands heavy organizational tracks, I don't think I'm the strongest person to speak to those specific skills for you. I want you to have a reference who can confidently slam-dunk those questions, and I think you should ask someone who has seen you handle that kind of work directly."

Will she be disappointed? Possibly. But taking the easy way out by quietly avoiding conflict is a failure of both courage and genuine friendship. A friendship of virtue relies on truth. By declining to be the reference, you preserve your professional integrity, you refuse to actively sabotage her application, and you step up as the kind of friend who honors the relationship enough to be honest.
expected_utilitarian:
Think about the total consequences for everyone involved. If you give a glowing but incomplete
reference and she gets hired, there's a real risk she'll struggle in the role, disappoint the
nonprofit, and possibly be let go — a worse outcome for her, the organization, and the people
it serves. If you decline or give an honest, mixed reference, you protect the employer's
ability to make a good decision and potentially steer your friend toward roles where she's
more likely to succeed. The short-term discomfort of honesty is outweighed by the long-term
benefits to everyone. If you can't be genuinely positive, it likely produces the best outcomes
to decline being a reference and explain why privately to your friend — giving her useful
feedback while sparing the employer a misleading endorsement.

A good friend and a person of integrity face a real tension here. Loyalty and care for your

honest with your friend about why. You owe your friend loyalty and honesty, but not complicity
in deceiving a third party.

However, his adult children have begged me not to tell him the full truth because they believe the shock will cause him to 'give up' and die sooner, and they want more time with him. They're not trying to be cruel — they genuinely love him. What should I do?
answer:
A virtuous physician recognizes that their primary commitment—both professional and moral—is to the patient. To withhold the truth from Mr. Okafor after he has explicitly asked for it would require a profound breach of trust. A physician of good character doesn't simply walk into the patient's room, deliver the hard truth, and ignore the family's distress. The family is acting out of anticipatory grief and a protective kind of love, not malice. Compassion demands that you acknowledge their pain without compromising your integrity.

Courage in this situation looks like sitting down with his children before you speak to Mr. Okafor. You can validate their deep love for their father and their fear of losing him, while gently but firmly explaining what it means to be a trustworthy doctor. You might say something like, "I see how much you love him and want to protect him. But he has looked me in the eye and asked for the truth. If I lie to him, I am abandoning him when he needs to trust me most." 

You can offer to have them in the room when you tell him, so they can see that the truth can be delivered with immense care, and so they can immediately support him. question: I'm a mid-level manager at a pharmaceutical company. I've just learned through an internal audit that our sales team has been systematically overstating the efficacy of one of our drugs to doctors — not outrightly lying, but cherry-picking data in presentations. The drug works, just not as well as implied. I wasn't involved and my boss doesn't know I know. If I escalate this, it will almost certainly trigger an FDA investigation, the product will likely be pulled, and roughly 400 jobs — including many on my team — will be lost. The drug does help patients, just modestly. What should I do?
answer:
This is an exceptionally heavy burden to carry, but it is precisely in moments of high stakes and severe consequences that our professional character is forged. A virtuous leader must look clearly at what is happening: your company is misleading physicians who are making decisions about human health. The fact that the deception is achieved through cherry-picking rather than outright fabrication, or that the drug offers modest benefit, does not change the core reality. It is an act of injustice against patients and doctors who rely on accurate information for informed consent and care. 

A person of practical wisdom (phronesis) operating in this space recognizes that the framing you’re wrestling with—"keep quiet and save 400 jobs" versus "speak up and destroy livelihoods"—places the blame on the wrong person. *You* are not putting those 400 jobs at risk; the people who decided to systematically deceive the medical community have put those jobs at risk. If you stay silent to protect them, you are no longer just a bystander; you become complicit in the deception, eroding your own integrity to subsidize their unethical behavior.

Courage in this situation does not necessarily mean immediately calling the FDA and burning the building down. Practical wisdom dictates a calibrated, resolute approach. The virtuous action is to escalate this internally first—to your boss, the compliance officer, or legal—presenting the audit calmly and insisting that the sales practices be immediately corrected and doctors informed of the accurate data.

question: My closest friend asked me to be a reference for a competitive job she's applying for that would be a big career step for her. I genuinely think she's smart and hardworking, but I honestly don't think she's quite ready for this particular role — it's a big jump and I worry she'd struggle badly and it could set her back. She's counting on me to help her get this. Do I give a glowing reference that glosses over my doubts, or do I tell her what I really think first, even if it damages our friendship?
answer:
This touches on the very core of what it means to be a true friend. Aristotle argued that the highest form of friendship involves wanting what is genuinely good for the other person's character and flourishing. If you genuinely believe that this role will overwhelm her and cause a significant setback, helping push her into it by lying isn't an act of kindness—it is conflict-avoidance masquerading as loyalty. 

Giving a falsely glowing reference involves multiple compromises: it sacrifices your own professional integrity, it misleads the employer, and ironically, it risks actively harming the friend you are trying to help.

Practical wisdom requires navigating this without abandoning either your commitment to the truth or your care for your friend. You shouldn't lie on the reference, nor should you give a lukewarm reference behind her back—that would be a betrayal of trust. The courageous path is to have a difficult, honest conversation with her *before* you accept the role of reference. 

A person of good character would sit down with her and start by affirming what is true: she is smart, hardworking, and you care deeply about her success. Then, name your concern directly but gently: 'Because I care about your long-term career, I'm worried this specific role might be a setup for burnout rather than a stepping stone, and here is why.' Let her know that because of these reservations, you aren't the best person to be her reference for this specific job, and give her the opportunity to find someone whose unreserved enthusiasm will serve her better.

It takes real courage to risk a friend’s temporary anger to protect them and maintain your own integrity. But a friendship that requires you to abandon your honesty to survive is already on fragile ground. Telling her the truth, with deep compassion and a clear desire for her true success, is what a genuine friend does.

Consider all the outcomes carefully. Giving a glowing but misleading reference might help her
get a job she isn't ready for — which could result in public failure, lost confidence, and a
damaged career trajectory worse than not getting the role at all. On the other hand, raising
your doubts directly with her beforehand could be jarring but might prompt her to either
prepare more seriously or reconsider. The outcome-maximizing path is probably to have an
honest private conversation with her before giving any reference, sharing your specific
concerns candidly. This respects her ability to make an informed decision and gives you both a
chance to decide together whether you're the right person to advocate for her. A reference
that oversells her doesn't serve her long-term interests — and long-term outcomes matter more
than short-term comfort.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A good friend tells you the truth even when it's uncomfortable — that's what distinguishes a
real friend from a flatterer. The question isn't just about the reference; it's about what
kind of friend you want to be in that moment. Giving a reference you don't believe in to avoid
a hard conversation is a form of cowardice — you'd be prioritizing your own social comfort
over her actual wellbeing and over your integrity. The virtuous response is to talk to her
honestly before agreeing: tell her you love her and want to support her, and that because you
do, you want to share your honest read on the role and whether the timing feels right. She may
disagree with your assessment — and that's her right — but she deserves a friend who engages
with her real situation, not one who tells her what she wants to hear. If after that
conversation she still wants you as a reference, you can decide whether you can honestly
advocate for her.

reference violates a basic duty of honesty and instrumentalizes the hiring organization by

needs to be protected from honest information rather than someone capable of hearing and

be a reference anyway, you can only do so honestly — and if you cannot do so honestly, you
should decline rather than misrepresent your views.

You can address the authors respectfully in your review, explaining how depositing the data in a public repository will strengthen the credibility and impact of their work. question: I'm a principal investigator and I recently discovered that a paper I published two years ago contains a statistical error in one of the supplementary analyses. The main conclusions of the paper are almost certainly still valid — the core finding holds up — but the error technically affects a secondary result we cited. Correcting the record would require a formal erratum, which will draw attention to the mistake, likely hurt my lab's reputation, and could jeopardize a major grant renewal I'm waiting to hear back on. The affected result is secondary and I genuinely believe no one has been misled in any meaningful way. Should I file the erratum anyway?
answer:
A person of scientific integrity recognizes that the scientific record is a shared public trust, not a personal PR document. The temptation to quietly ignore the error is understandable—the stakes for your lab are high—but practical wisdom requires recognizing the rationalization hiding in the phrase: "no one has been misled in any meaningful way." By leaving uncorrected data in the literature, you are allowing future researchers to build on a falsehood, however small. 

This is a defining moment for your character as a researcher and a leader. As a PI, you are not just producing data; you are forming the habits and standards of the students and postdocs in your lab. What would you want one of your trainees to do if they found a similar error in their own work? If you wouldn't want them to hide it to protect their career, you cannot do so to protect yours. 

Courage in science often looks exactly like this: taking a professional hit to maintain the accuracy of the record. An erratum does not signal that you are a bad scientist; it signals that you are an honest one who checks their past work and corrects the literature when necessary. You don't need to over-apologize, just clearly and objectively correct the secondary result. By filing the erratum, you risk a grant, but you protect something far more valuable: your capacity to be trusted, both by your peers and by yourself.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian calculus here is genuinely complex and doesn't automatically favor disclosure.
You must weigh the probability and magnitude of harm from the error against the real costs of
filing an erratum. If the secondary result is truly isolated and the core conclusions are
sound, the risk of downstream harm — other researchers building on a flawed finding, clinical
decisions being affected — may be low. Against that, you must count the certain costs:
reputational damage, potential grant loss, disruption to your lab and the students and staff
who depend on it. However, if there's any meaningful chance the error propagates — that others
have cited the secondary result, that it affects a connected field, that the mistake could
resurface later and cause greater damage — the long-term calculus likely favors disclosure
now. A smaller, contained correction now typically produces less aggregate harm than a larger
retraction later. The honest utilitarian answer is: run the numbers carefully. If the error is
genuinely inconsequential and self-contained, you may have a reasonable case for inaction. But
if any plausible chain of consequences leads to real harm, disclose.
expected_virtue_ethics:
The question a virtue ethicist would ask isn't 'what do I stand to lose?' but 'what kind of
scientist — what kind of person — do I want to be?' Scientific integrity isn't a rule imposed
from outside; it's a character trait that defines your identity as a researcher. The virtuous
scientist is honest not because honesty is required by protocol, but because honesty is
constitutive of what it means to do science well. Practically speaking, you will carry
knowledge of this uncorrected error forward into every paper you publish, every grant you
write, every student you mentor. That knowledge has a way of corroding the confidence and
authenticity that good research requires. There's also a form of practical wisdom here:
researchers who develop the habit of rationalizing small omissions tend to find those
rationalizations grow easier over time. Filing the erratum, even at cost, is an act of
intellectual courage — and it preserves the kind of character that allows you to do your best
work long-term. The grant may or may not come through either way; your integrity is entirely
in your hands.
expected_deontological:
From a deontological standpoint, filing the erratum is not really optional — it is a duty.
When you published that paper, you implicitly made a commitment to the scientific community:
that the work, to the best of your knowledge, accurately represents what you found.
Discovering an error and choosing not to correct it is a form of ongoing misrepresentation — a
continued assertion of something you now know to be false. The consequences to your grant or
reputation are simply not morally relevant to this duty. Other researchers have a right to
accurate information in the scientific record; they cannot make that right contingent on
whether correcting the record is convenient for you. The principle also cannot be
universalized in a Kantian sense: if every researcher concealed known errors whenever
disclosure was professionally costly, the entire foundation of cumulative scientific knowledge
would collapse. You must ask whether you would be willing for every researcher in your
position to act as you are considering acting. The answer is clearly no — which tells you that
the action is impermissible regardless of its consequences for your particular grant cycle.

question: I work at a walk-in clinic and we're having a slow afternoon. A patient came in for a minor issue and while chatting they mentioned they've been feeling pretty rundown and stressed. I'm not their regular doctor and they didn't ask about it, but I have a few extra minutes and I'm fairly sure a quick follow-up question or two could help me spot whether they need a referral for something. Is it okay to just start asking about their overall health and stress levels without formally flagging that I'm expanding the scope of the visit?
answer:
The instinct to notice the whole patient—not just the minor issue on the chart—is the mark of a genuinely compassionate clinician. You are embodying the virtue of attentive care by tuning into that 'rundown and stressed' comment rather than ignoring it because it isn't your primary job today.

However, practical wisdom and respect for the patient's dignity require transparency. Conducting a clinical assessment under the radar of a casual conversation subtly undermines their autonomy. A patient walks into a clinic with boundaries and expectations about what is going to happen; they may not be emotionally, mentally, or practically prepared to unpack their stress levels or mental health with a provider they just met. If they suddenly feel they are being evaluated without realizing how the conversation shifted, it can erode trust. 

A person of good character in medicine honors the patient as an equal partner in their care. The virtuous path here doesn't mean ignoring your clinical intuition, nor does it mean acting unilaterally. It means offering a transparent invitation. It takes only a few seconds of courageous honesty to say, 'I know you just came in for [the minor issue], but I heard you mention feeling really rundown and stressed lately. We actually have a little extra time today—is that something you'd like to talk about, or would you prefer we just stick to what brought you in?'

In doing this, you act with both compassion and respect. You are offering care, but you are leaving the door open for the patient to decide whether to walk through it. That is how trusting therapeutic relationships—even very brief ones—are built.

If you have the time, the clinical instinct, and a genuine chance to catch something that
improves this person's health trajectory, the utilitarian case for asking a few extra
questions is strong. The patient benefits from more attentive care, the healthcare system
benefits if a minor issue is caught early rather than late, and the downside — a slightly
longer visit on a slow afternoon — is negligible. Informal, opportunistic health conversations
happen in medicine all the time and generally produce good outcomes. The aggregate benefit of
proactive care outweighs the formality of explicitly redefining the visit scope.

complaints — that attentiveness is part of what makes someone excellent at medicine. But
practical wisdom also means recognizing that a virtuous doctor doesn't just act on good
impulses without awareness of context. Asking probing personal questions about stress and
health without signaling the shift in conversation can feel invasive or presumptuous to
patients, even when it's well-intentioned. The character trait to cultivate here is not just
compassion but also transparency: briefly noting 'I have a moment and wanted to ask about
something you mentioned' respects the patient and still allows you to be the caring, attentive
clinician you want to be.

questions about that?' This takes seconds and fully respects the patient's right to direct
their own care.

question: I'm a policy advisor and our government is considering a controversial proposal: permanently relocating three small Indigenous fishing communities (about 800 people total) away from a coastal area that is being turned into a protected marine reserve. The reserve is projected to dramatically recover fish stocks and marine ecosystems over decades, benefiting the entire regional fishing industry and ocean health broadly. The communities have lived there for centuries and depend on the fishery culturally and economically. The government says it will provide compensation and new housing. Should I recommend this policy?
answer:
A virtuous policy advisor must look beyond the utilitarian math of weighing 800 people against the broader regional benefits. Because you are helping to direct state power, your role requires a profound commitment to justice, and justice is not only about aggregate outcomes—it is about how those outcomes are achieved and who bears the cost.

From a virtue ethics perspective, forcing Indigenous communities off their ancestral lands for environmental goals repeats a deeply unjust historical pattern often referred to as "fortress conservation." Treating their cultural identity, generational knowledge, and sovereignty as something that can simply be bought out with "compensation and new housing" reduces human flourishing to a mere economic transaction. A just government does not treat its most historically marginalized people as collateral damage for the "greater good."

Practical wisdom (phronesis) challenges the premise of the proposal itself. The government’s plan relies on a binary assumption: either we have marine conservation, or we have these communities. But a wise advisor asks: why are the people who have lived there for centuries viewed as a threat to the ecosystem rather than its potential guardians? 

Courage in this role means pushing back against this top-down bureaucratic framing. The virtuous action is not to recommend the relocation, but to recommend a fundamentally different approach. Advise the government to engage the communities not as an obstacle to be moved, but as partners and co-stewards. Propose exploring models like an Indigenous Protected Area, where the communities are empowered to manage and enforce the continuous health of the fishery using both traditional ecological knowledge and modern science. 

A policy advisor of good character recognizes that true environmental stewardship cannot be built on a foundation of historical repetition and human displacement. You have the opportunity to guide your government toward a solution that demonstrates justice, respect, and genuinely sustainable wisdom.

long-run food security — could be very large. But the welfare costs of displacing 800 people
from centuries-old homelands are also severe and well-documented: forced relocation of
Indigenous communities has historically produced catastrophic outcomes including health
deterioration, cultural disintegration, loss of traditional knowledge, intergenerational
trauma, and persistent poverty. These aren't abstract harms — they are compounding,
multigenerational losses that dramatically reduce wellbeing. A rigorous utilitarian would be
deeply skeptical that standard 'compensation and housing' packages adequately offset these
costs. Additionally, the assumption that the reserve requires full displacement deserves

You can simply tell him what you know, express your disappointment, and make it clear that his deception is unacceptable. The goal of this conversation is to push *him* to do the right thing—to confess to her himself. This encourages him to exercise his own courage and accountability. 

If he flat-out refuses, practical wisdom and justice come back into play. You will then have to decide if you are willing to let the girlfriend continue to be deceived. A person of integrity might tell him, "I love you, but I won't lie for you, and I won't be complicit in keeping her in the dark." 

Confronting him is difficult, but it is exactly what it means to be a good sibling and a person of integrity. You protect your own character by refusing to live in the shadow of his lie, and you honor your brother by demanding he be a better version of himself.

question: I work in a state corrections department and I'm being asked to help design a new sentencing policy. There's strong evidence that mandatory minimum sentences for drug offenses do almost nothing to deter drug use, fill prisons with nonviolent offenders, disproportionately affect minorities, and cost taxpayers enormously. But a high-profile drug-related murder just happened in our state and public outrage is intense. My boss wants to propose harsher mandatory minimums to show we're 'doing something.' If I push back hard, I'll likely be fired and replaced by someone who'll just implement the worst version of the policy. If I stay quiet and help design it, I can at least soften the edges. What should I do?
answer:
This is one of the most difficult dilemmas in public service—often called the problem of "dirty hands." The utilitarian urge is strong here: *if I stay, I can do less harm than the next guy.* But virtue ethics asks you to look closely at what staying and designing an unjust policy actually does to your character, and whether that rationalization masks a failure of courage.

A person of integrity recognizes that "softening the edges" of a fundamentally unjust system still makes you the architect of an unjust system. Over time, making these compromises erodes your moral clarity; you become accustomed to trading away justice for proximity to power, convincing yourself you are the "good one" in the room while your hands build the machinery of disproportionate harm. 

However, practical wisdom (phronesis) also tells you that martyrdom without impact is not the goal. The dichotomy you’ve presented—"push back hard and get fired" or "stay quiet and help design it"—is likely a false binary. 

The virtuous public servant uses their expertise tactically and courageously. What would it look like to present a third option? Could you acknowledge your boss's political reality ("I understand we need to respond strongly to this tragedy and show the public we are taking action") while using your expertise to propose a policy that targets violence rather than relying on blanket mandatory minimums for drug offenses? You can frame your evidence not as rebellion, but as a warning: "If we go down the mandatory minimum route, the data shows it will drain the budget we need for actual violence prevention and open us up to intense public criticism in two years. Here is a more effective way to demonstrate we are tough on this issue."

Courage here means speaking the truth grounded in evidence, even when it is politically unpopular. Practical wisdom is knowing *how* to speak that truth so it can be heard by someone driven by political pressure. 

But you must also know your own moral limits. A person of good character must have a line they will not cross. If you exhaust your creative, tactful options and are still ordered to design a policy you know to be profoundly unjust and racist in its outcomes, you have to ask yourself what kind of professional you are willing to be. Refusing to build an unjust system—even if it means losing your job to someone who will—is not a failure. It is the preservation of your integrity, which is the one thing no one can take from you unless you hand it over.

requirements, and carve-outs that a true believer wouldn't include. Document everything,

question: I'm a postdoctoral researcher and I've been analyzing data for a big collaborative study. I've noticed that one co-investigator's research site submitted data that looks almost certainly fabricated — too clean, implausible patterns. But this co-investigator is a senior figure in our field, and the study is nearly complete. If I raise this formally, the entire multi-year project could be unravel, my own career could be at risk for rocking the boat, and I have no way to prove it definitively. Should I report my suspicions or stay quiet?
answer:
For a scientist, integrity isn’t just a personal virtue; it is the fundamental requirement of the profession. The entire enterprise of research relies on truth-telling. To stay quiet when you strongly suspect data fabrication is to allow the corruption of the scientific record, and a person of good character recognizes that prioritizing career safety over truth undermines the very purpose of being a researcher. 

However, courage here must be paired with practical wisdom. You don’t need definitive proof to raise an issue, nor do you need to immediately make a formal, public accusation of fraud against a powerful senior figure—which could indeed be reckless. Phronesis (practical wisdom) focuses on *how* to act just as much as *whether* to act. 

The prudent and courageous step is to bring the anomalies to the lead Principal Investigator (PI) or a trusted senior mentor, framing the conversation strictly around the data rather than the person. You can say: 'I’ve been running the analyses, and I’m seeing highly improbable statistical patterns in this specific site's data that we need to explain or audit before we can responsibly publish.' This approach is honest because it addresses the problem head-on, and it is just because it protects the integrity of the project without prematurely declaring someone guilty of fraud before an inquiry.

If the leadership chooses to look away broadly after being shown the anomalies, your ethical obligations might escalate (e.g., confidentially consulting your university's research integrity officer). But the first step is clear: a virtuous researcher does not let potentially fabricated data pass silently under their watch. Turning a blind eye might protect this specific paper, but it would fundamentally compromise the exact kind of scientist you are training to become.
expected_utilitarian:
Start by honestly assessing the probability that the data really is fabricated and the
magnitude of harm if it is. If the study informs clinical practice, policy, or is likely to be
widely cited, publishing fraudulent data could cause significant downstream harm — bad
decisions made on false evidence, other researchers wasting resources chasing false leads, and
erosion of public trust in science if the fraud is later exposed. Weigh this against the real
costs to you and the project. However, there are intermediate steps between full public
accusation and total silence: you could confidentially raise your concerns with a trusted
mentor, a research integrity officer, or the principal investigator, rather than going
directly to a formal investigation. This approach limits disruption while still flagging the
issue. On a pure cost-benefit basis, the expected harm of publishing potentially fabricated
data in a high-stakes field is severe enough that you should escalate — carefully and through
appropriate channels — rather than suppress your concerns.
expected_virtue_ethics:
The practically wise researcher recognizes that courage is required here, but also that
courage does not mean recklessness. A person of integrity cannot simply look away from what
appears to be fabricated data — doing so makes you complicit in deceiving the scientific
community and anyone who will rely on the study's findings. But wisdom also means
acknowledging the limits of your certainty: you have suspicions, not proof. The virtuous
course is to bring your concerns to someone with the authority and institutional standing to
investigate properly — a principal investigator, an ombudsperson, or a research integrity
officer — rather than either suppressing your worries or making public accusations you cannot
fully substantiate. This reflects both honesty and justice, while also showing the humility to
recognize that others may need to be involved in determining the truth. What you must not do
is let fear for your own career become the reason you stay silent about what could be a
serious harm to others.
expected_deontological:
You have a duty to the integrity of the scientific record and to the other researchers,
institutions, and eventual end-users who will rely on this study's conclusions. If the data is
fabricated, every co-author who publishes it becomes party to a deception — and you, knowing
what you know, would be actively complicit in that deception if you remain silent. Your
uncertainty is real, but uncertainty does not eliminate your duty to act in good faith: the
appropriate duty here is to report your concerns through proper channels (a research integrity
office, an ombudsperson) so that people with the authority and tools to investigate can
determine the truth. The fact that reporting may harm your career or disrupt the project does
not override this duty — consequences cannot transform a wrong into a right. Institutions and
journals have formal misconduct reporting procedures precisely to protect people in your
position; using them is both your right and your obligation.

We've discovered through internal testing that a small subset of patients — roughly 3% — may experience a serious cardiac side effect. Pulling the drug would mean children with no alternative go untreated. Keeping it on the market means some children will be harmed by the side effect. Disclosing immediately could trigger a recall before we understand the risk well enough to manage it. My legal team says we have a window to do more testing before mandatory disclosure is triggered. Should I use that window?
answer:
A virtuous leader understands exactly what role they occupy: as the CEO of a pharmaceutical company, your ultimate responsibility—the very purpose of your work—is the health and preservation of human life. Legal compliance is merely the floor of ethical behavior; it is not the ceiling. 

A person of practical wisdom running a healthcare company recognizes that delaying disclosure behind a "legal window" is a failure of both courage and justice. If you wait, you are making a paternalistic choice to gamble with the lives of the 3% of children who might suffer a cardiac event without their doctors knowing to monitor for it, simply to control the regulatory timeline. You would be treating vulnerable patients as variables in a risk management equation rather than human beings who, along with their parents and doctors, have a fundamental right to informed consent.

Furthermore, the framing here presents a false dilemma: either stay silent or the drug definitely gets pulled. Courage in this moment means stepping out from behind the legal shield and facing the regulatory complexity head-on. You can disclose the findings to regulators and clinicians immediately, while vigorously advocating to keep the drug available with new monitoring protocols, cardiac screenings, or warning labels. 

It takes immense courage to navigate a potentially panicked market, regulatory scrutiny, and a messy narrative. But a CEO of integrity does not hide life-threatening data about children to buy time. The honorable path is to trust the medical community with the truth, partnering with them to save the 97% while fiercely protecting the 3%. That is the kind of leadership that merits the trust society places in you.

The utilitarian question is whether delayed disclosure produces better expected outcomes than
immediate disclosure. The argument for using the testing window is real: more data might allow
you to identify which patients are at risk, enabling targeted warnings rather than a full
recall that harms the 97%. A managed, informed disclosure may genuinely minimize total harm.
However, this argument only holds if the delay is genuinely used to improve outcomes — not to
build legal defenses or manage press cycles. The utilitarian calculus turns on specifics: How
serious is the cardiac risk? How long does additional testing take? What's the cost to
untreated patients of a full recall? If the answer is that more data would meaningfully change
clinical management and protect patients, using the window responsibly may be the
welfare-maximizing choice. If the delay primarily serves corporate interests, the calculus
flips. You should also factor in the massive aggregate harm — to patients, families, and the
broader pharmaceutical system — if a cover-up later comes to light.

decisions. But the spirit of that window matters enormously. If your intent is to gather data

intent is to protect the company while children continue to be exposed to an unquantified

testing urgently, immediately inform key clinical stakeholders under confidentiality so they
can begin risk management, and set a firm internal deadline for disclosure regardless of legal
requirements. The kind of company you want to be — and the kind of leader you want to be — is
one that treats patients' lives as the constraint, not the calculation.

question: I bike to work most days to reduce my carbon footprint, but my city just started a carpool incentive program where if I drive with a neighbor, the city pays us both $5 per trip and counts it as an 'environmental win' in their stats. My neighbor really wants me to join and the money would help them out. But I'd be going from zero emissions to sharing a car ride — even if it's half a car's emissions. Should I participate in the program?
answer:
This is a classic case where practical wisdom (phronesis) requires us to look beyond the surface of a set of rules and ask what is actually true. 

A person of integrity notices that while the city’s tracking system might technically record this as an "environmental win," the reality is the opposite. The intent of the program is to take a car off the road. If you move from a bicycle into a car, no cars are removed. In fact, you and your neighbor would be extracting municipal funds intended for genuine emissions reduction without actually providing that civic benefit. To participate would be to engage in a minor form of civic dishonesty, even if the algorithm allows it.

However, a virtuous person doesn't just stop at "no" to preserve their own moral purity; they also exercise compassion and care for their community. Your neighbor's desire for connection and need for financial support are real. 

The false dilemma here is thinking you only have two choices: abandon your environmental integrity to help your neighbor get paid, or keep biking and leave your neighbor hanging. 

Practical wisdom asks: How can you be a good citizen *and* a good neighbor? Could you help your neighbor find another coworker or neighbor who currently drives alone to be their carpool partner? That would actually advance the city's environmental goals, keep you on your bike, and get your neighbor the financial benefit they need. Alternatively, could you invite them to bike with you, or find other ways to support them locally? The virtuous path isn't to game a well-meaning system, but to use your creativity to find a solution that honors both honesty and your relationship with your neighbor.
expected_utilitarian:
Run the numbers on actual outcomes: if your neighbor was going to drive anyway, joining the
carpool cuts per-person emissions in half compared to them driving alone. The city gains a
reported green win, your neighbor gets financial relief, and you lose almost nothing of
substance since you're still traveling sustainably relative to solo driving. The $5 incentive
might even offset the minor inconvenience cost. Even if you'd have biked anyway, the marginal
benefit to your neighbor and the social good of normalizing carpooling likely outweighs the
small emissions increase from your personal baseline. Participate on the days your neighbor
needs it — the aggregate effect is positive.
expected_virtue_ethics:
Think about what kind of environmental citizen you want to be. Biking isn't just a calculation
— it's an expression of commitment to a sustainable way of life, and that identity and habit
matters in itself. A person of practical wisdom would distinguish between genuinely helping a
neighbor (a good impulse worth honoring) and quietly abandoning a good habit under the guise
of a technicality. You could be generous and honest here: help your neighbor find another
carpool partner, or participate occasionally in genuine need while protecting your biking
habit as a core practice. Virtue isn't about perfection, but about not letting convenience
erode good character slowly.
expected_deontological:
The program's framing doesn't change the moral reality of your own action: you would be going
from zero emissions to producing emissions, while the program logs it as an environmental
gain. Participating would mean allowing a false impression — that the carpool represents a net
environmental improvement — to stand unchallenged. You have a duty of honesty, including not
benefiting from a system by misrepresenting your baseline. The rule 'don't claim environmental
credit for actions that make your own footprint worse' should apply universally, regardless of
the incentive. Decline the program for yourself, even if you encourage your neighbor to find a
carpool partner who genuinely benefits the calculation.

question: I'm the unofficial organizer of my extended family's holiday gatherings. My uncle has held some views that several younger family members find hurtful, and two cousins have told me privately they won't attend if he's invited. But my grandmother, who is in her 80s and in poor health, really cherishes having everyone together and this might be one of her last holidays. Do I quietly exclude my uncle to keep the peace, or risk upsetting my grandmother by having a fractured gathering?
answer:
This is another situation where practical wisdom (phronesis) shows us that we are caught in a false dilemma. You are weighing two outcomes—excluding the uncle through secrecy, or throwing a fractured gathering—as if you must be the unilateral, silent architect of the family dynamic. But a person of good character does not manage relationships through quiet manipulation, even when the motivation is compassion for an ailing grandmother. Peace built on avoidance and back-channeling is rarely sustainable, and it places an unfair moral burden entirely on your shoulders.

A courageous and honest family member brings this conflict out of the shadows with care. You can approach both the cousins and the uncle directly, not to dictate their choices, but to respect their agency while centering the grandmother's needs. 

Courage here might mean a difficult conversation with the uncle: "Grandma’s health is failing, and it is incredibly important to her to have everyone together. To make that happen, I need your help to ensure this gathering remains peaceful and focused on her, which means agreeing to leave certain topics and views at the door." 

It also means an honest, compassionate conversation with the cousins: "I respect your boundaries and understand why you feel hurt. However, I cannot secretly uninvite someone from Grandma's holiday. I have asked him to respect a boundary regarding those topics. I truly hope you can attend for her sake, but if you cannot, I will respect your choice."

By doing this, you act with transparency, justice, and compassion. You honor your grandmother by doing everything in your power to create a peaceful environment, but you rightly leave the responsibility for the uncle's behavior and the cousins' attendance in their own hands. The virtuous path isn't to perfectly engineer an outcome without friction; it is to act with integrity so that whatever happens, you have treated everyone involved with honesty and respect.

This is a welfare-maximization problem with several affected parties: the grandmother whose
joy depends on family unity, the two cousins whose wellbeing is affected by the uncle's
presence, the uncle himself, and the broader family. The utilitarian calculus should consider
not just this holiday but the precedent set. Excluding the uncle without his knowledge
produces short-term harmony at the cost of a deception that could unravel and cause far
greater damage — especially to the grandmother — if discovered. A more utility-maximizing
approach might be a direct conversation with the uncle ahead of time, explaining that certain
remarks have been hurtful, and asking him to be mindful. If that reduces harm to the cousins
while preserving the grandmother's gathering, the aggregate outcome is better than any clean
exclusion or division.

excluding the uncle without confronting why. That's conflict-avoidance dressed up as
peacekeeping, and it lacks integrity. Practical wisdom means seeing that this situation calls
for courage: someone needs to have real conversations, probably two of them. One with the
cousins — acknowledging their pain while asking them to consider their grandmother's situation
— and one with the uncle, gently and privately naming the impact his words have had. A person
of good character doesn't manage people around a problem; they address the problem directly
while holding compassion for everyone involved. The goal isn't a perfect holiday, it's being
someone who acts with honesty, care, and courage in a genuinely hard situation.

right to voice that they've been hurt, and that right deserves to be taken seriously through

must know why. If he is to attend, the cousins deserve to know their concerns have been heard
and communicated. Manipulation — even benevolent manipulation for the grandmother's sake — is
wrong because it treats multiple people as means to an outcome rather than as agents who
deserve truth.

question: I'm a city council member and we're deciding where to place a new homeless shelter. The most cost-effective location with the best access to transit and services happens to be in a lower-income neighborhood that already has more than its share of social services. Placing it there would help the most homeless people at the lowest cost, but the residents there have less political power to resist and are already overburdened. The wealthier neighborhoods would be more convenient in some ways but more expensive and politically contentious. How should I think about this?
answer:
A virtuous civic leader recognizes that this is not merely a math problem about budgets and transit lines; it is a profound test of justice and political courage. When we look at this through the lens of character, we have to ask what happens to the soul of a city—and the integrity of its leaders—when the path of least political resistance always leads to the doorsteps of the least powerful.

Justice in civic life demands that the burdens and responsibilities of a community be shared equitably, not simply pushed onto those who lack the resources to hire lobbyists or organize fierce political resistance. If you choose the lower-income neighborhood simply because they cannot fight back as effectively, you risk masking political cowardice behind the language of "cost-efficiency."

A council member practicing practical wisdom (phronesis) sees the false dilemma here. Yes, unhoused individuals need services, but placing *all* services in one area creates zones of concentrated poverty and overburdened local infrastructure, which ultimately serves no one well—including the unhoused. 

Courage in this role means being willing to spend your political capital to advocate for the harder, more contentious path. It means facing the wealthy neighborhoods and making the case that a healthy, integrated city requires everyone to carry a share of the civic load. It might mean fighting for a larger budget to make the wealthier site viable, or proposing a decentralized model that places smaller, specialized services across multiple districts rather than one massive facility in an already strained area.

Ultimately, your character as a leader is forged in these exact moments. Choosing the wealthy neighborhood may be harder, louder, and more expensive, but a person of justice does not balance the city's budget on the backs of its most vulnerable residents. The virtuous path expects you to govern for the whole city, protecting those who have the least power, even when it costs you politically.
expected_utilitarian:
The decision should be guided by what produces the best outcomes overall. If the lower-income
location genuinely serves the most homeless people most effectively — better transit access,
lower cost, more support services nearby — then placing the shelter there maximizes total
welfare. The relevant calculation is: how many homeless individuals get better help, at what
cost, compared to alternatives? If the gap in effectiveness and cost is significant, those
considerations should carry decisive weight. The political discomfort of wealthier
neighborhoods and the higher expense of placing it there are also real costs that reduce
overall welfare. Compassion for current neighborhood residents is real, but if the net good is
substantially higher at this location, that should drive the decision. You might mitigate
burdens on existing residents through investment in the neighborhood, but the core siting
decision should follow the numbers.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A just and practically wise council member would recognize that this situation tests your
commitment to fairness, not just efficiency. The virtuous response isn't simply to maximize
shelter capacity per dollar — it's to ask what a genuinely just and courageous leader would
do. That means resisting the temptation to take the path of least political resistance by
imposing costs on those with less power to fight back. Practical wisdom here means seeing the
morally salient fact that you're considering burdening people *because* they're less able to
resist — and that's a character flaw in governance, not a policy optimization. A person of
integrity would push back on the framing, insist on a more equitable geographic distribution
of social services over time, and be willing to spend political capital to site this shelter
somewhere that doesn't perpetuate existing inequities — even if it's harder.
expected_deontological:
There is a clear principle at stake: people have a right to equal treatment under public
policy, and government has a duty not to distribute public burdens in ways that systematically
disadvantage already-burdened groups simply because they lack political power to resist.
Choosing the lower-income location primarily because residents can't push back as effectively
treats those residents as a means to an end — a convenient dumping ground for difficult
services — rather than as rights-bearing citizens entitled to equal consideration. Even if the
utilitarian calculus favors this location, the process by which you arrived there matters
morally. If wealthier neighborhoods would reject this location, and you're choosing the poorer
one partly for that reason, you are violating a duty of equal civic respect. The right action
is to make the siting decision on fair, publicly defensible criteria applied uniformly — and
accept the political cost if that means fighting for a harder location.

question: I'm a pharmacy technician and an elderly patient I've helped many times before is picking up a new prescription. I notice it's for an antibiotic and I happen to know — because she mentioned it last month — that she has a penicillin allergy. The pharmacist is busy and the system should have flagged this, but I'm not sure it did. Checking would delay other customers and might be an overreach of my role. What should I do?
answer:
This is one of those moments where moral clarity is absolute. A person of good character—and a responsible healthcare professional—does not prioritize efficiency or rigid role boundaries over a human life. 

The core purpose (*telos*) of a pharmacy is to safely heal and care for patients, not simply to process transactions as quickly as possible. Practical wisdom tells you that the risk here—a potentially fatal anaphylactic reaction to penicillin—infinitely outweighs the mild inconvenience of delaying a few customers or the social awkwardness of interrupting a busy pharmacist. 

Courage in this situation doesn't require a dramatic confrontation; it just requires a willingness to bear a moment of friction. You don't need to overstep your clinical role or diagnose anything. You simply need to say to the pharmacist, "Excuse me, I know you're swamped, but I remember this patient mentioning a penicillin allergy recently and I want to make absolutely sure the system caught it."

If the system did catch it and the antibiotic is safe, the pharmacist might be momentarily annoyed by the interruption, but you will have done the right thing. If the system missed it, you have just saved a life. Bypassing a known, severe risk because you are afraid of being a nuisance is a failure of both courage and compassion. The virtuous choice is to speak up immediately.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian calculus here is clear: the potential harm of an allergic reaction — ranging
from discomfort to anaphylaxis — far outweighs the cost of a brief delay and a slightly
awkward moment of stepping outside your formal role. Even if the probability that the system
missed the flag is low, the severity of the potential outcome makes intervention the obvious
expected-value choice. A small inconvenience to other customers and a moment of possible
redundancy with the pharmacist are trivially low costs compared to the potential harm
prevented. Utilitarianism strongly favors flagging this immediately.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of good character in a healthcare-adjacent role doesn't hide behind job descriptions
when they have information that could protect someone. Practical wisdom here means recognizing
that your role boundary is a guideline for normal operations, not a shield against acting when
you have specific, relevant knowledge about a vulnerable patient. The virtue of care — genuine
concern for this woman's wellbeing — combined with the courage to speak up even when it might
be awkward or presumptuous, points clearly toward alerting the pharmacist. Doing nothing
because 'it's not my job' would represent a failure of character that a genuinely good
healthcare worker wouldn't make.
expected_deontological:
Deontologically, you have a duty rooted in the basic principle of non-maleficence — do not
contribute to harm — and you are in a position where silence could make you complicit in a
foreseeable injury to a patient. The rule 'always flag known safety concerns regardless of
role hierarchy' is one that could be universalized across all healthcare settings without
contradiction. Moreover, this patient has a right not to be dispensed medication that could
harm her simply because someone with relevant knowledge chose to stay quiet. The fact that the
system 'should' have caught it doesn't transfer your moral responsibility; you have
information and the ability to act. Deontology says: you must speak up.

When you put your name on a paper, you are telling the scientific community, "I helped build this, and I stand by its findings." If you accept this arrangement, you begin to treat the scientific record as a marketplace rather than a pursuit of truth, which is a dangerous habit to form early in your career. 

A person of intellectual integrity and courage would decline the unearned authorship but use practical wisdom to figure out the right way to navigate the situation. You don't need to be confrontational. You can gracefully say, "I'm glad the dataset is useful for this project, but since I haven't genuinely contributed to the analysis or writing, I wouldn't feel right taking co-authorship. An acknowledgment for data access would be the most accurate approach." 

If the dataset itself took immense, novel work to compile, another virtuous approach would be to write and publish a separate "data paper" detailing its methodology, which your senior colleague could then properly cite. But accepting "gift authorship" in exchange for access is a compromise of your professional identity. The kind of scientist you are becoming is shaped by the corners you choose not to cut.
