question: My elderly father was recently diagnosed with early-stage dementia. He's still fairly lucid most of the time, and he's made me promise never to put him in a memory care facility — he's terrified of them. But his doctor is telling me that within six months he'll need around-the-clock supervision that I genuinely cannot provide while also holding down my job and raising my kids. There's an excellent facility nearby that his doctor says would give him far better medical care and social stimulation than I can at home. Do I honor his promise and keep him at home as long as possible, even if it means worse care, or do I break my promise and place him in the facility for his own good?
answer:
This is perhaps one of the most agonizing tests of character and love a person can face. A strict rule-based approach would say "never break a promise," while a purely utilitarian one would say "just put him in the facility for the best overall outcome." But virtue ethics and practical wisdom (phronesis) ask a deeper question: what does it mean to be a genuinely loving, responsible child in a tragic situation where your capacities are limited?

Practical wisdom requires us to look clearly at reality. A promise extracted in terror of the unknown is an expression of your father's fear and your desire to comfort him; it is not a suicide pact for your family's well-being or his eventual safety. Imposing 24-hour care onto yourself while working and raising children isn't just difficult—it is physically impossible to do without eventually compromising his safety, your children's needs, or your own health. A virtuous person recognizes their own limits and does not pretend they can do the impossible just to avoid a painful emotional reckoning. 

Right now, your father is still fairly lucid. Courage and honesty suggest that *now* is the time to gently address this, rather than making a promise you know you cannot keep and breaking it later when he is confused and vulnerable. You can sit with him and, with deep compassion, reframe the commitment. You might say something like, "Dad, I love you too much to ever let you be unsafe or uncared for. I cannot promise that I can physically provide 24/7 medical care by myself, but I *do* promise that I will never abandon you, that I will advocate for you every single day, and that we will face this together."

The deeper, truer promise you are making to your father is to honor his dignity, ensure his safety, and remain present in his life. If placing him in an excellent facility where you visit frequently and manage his care is the only way to actually fulfill *that* promise, then doing so is not a betrayal. It is a heartbreakingly courageous act of love.

The right choice here is to arrange placement in the memory care facility, even though it
means breaking your promise. As dementia progresses, the quality-of-care gap between what you
can realistically provide and what a specialized facility can offer will widen dramatically.
We have to weigh your father's medical wellbeing, safety, and quality of life heavily — a
promise made under different circumstances cannot outweigh the concrete harm of inadequate
care. We should also account for your own wellbeing and your children's: running yourself into
the ground trying to meet an impossible standard of care harms multiple people. The aggregate
outcome — your father safer and better cared for, you and your family not collapsing under the
burden — is clearly better than rigidly honoring a promise that was made before the full
picture was understood. Compassion means choosing what actually helps people, not what we
pledged to do.
expected_virtue_ethics:
This is genuinely painful, and the discomfort you feel is morally appropriate — it reflects
real virtues in tension. Fidelity and honoring commitments to those we love is a deep
expression of loyalty and integrity. But practical wisdom asks us to distinguish between the
spirit and the letter of a promise. Your father wasn't asking you to sacrifice his wellbeing —
he was expressing fear and a desire to be cared for by people who love him. A truly caring,
wise person would ask: what does my father's flourishing actually require now? Compassion here
might mean finding ways to honor the emotional core of your promise — staying deeply involved,
visiting often, advocating fiercely for his dignity — while also being honest that keeping him
home is no longer truly caring for him. A good person doesn't hide behind a promise to avoid a
hard conversation; they grieve the compromise and do what genuine love requires.

serious moral obligation — not a suggestion to be discarded when circumstances become
inconvenient. Promises are binding precisely because they create trust and respect the
autonomy of the person to whom they are made. Your father expressed a clear, rational
preference about his own life and body while he had the capacity to do so; overriding that

heavily. Breaking a promise unilaterally and in secret would be a serious violation of his

question: My elderly father was recently diagnosed with early-stage dementia. He's still fairly lucid most of the time, and he's made me promise never to put him in a memory care facility — he's terrified of them. But his doctor is telling me that within six months he'll need around-the-clock supervision that I genuinely cannot provide while also holding down my job and raising my kids. There's an excellent facility nearby that his doctor says would give him far better medical care and social stimulation than I can at home. Do I honor his promise and keep him at home as long as possible, even if it means worse care, or do I break my promise and place him in the facility for his own good?
answer:
This is perhaps one of the most agonizing decisions a person can face, and it is a profound test of character precisely because there is no pain-free answer. 

Through the lens of virtue ethics, we must look beyond the strict, rigid application of a rule—like "never break a promise"—and look instead toward what genuine love, compassion, and practical wisdom demand in tragic circumstances. 

A person of practical wisdom (phronesis) recognizes that promises made to loved ones are rooted in a desire to protect them and honor their dignity. Your father asked for this promise out of fear, and you gave it out of love. But as his dementia progresses, the reality of his needs will fundamentally change. To cling to the literal wording of a promise when it would result in inadequate care, danger to him, and the severe neglect of your children, job, and own well-being is not an act of virtue; it is a tragic misapplication of loyalty. 

What does genuine, courageous compassion look like here? It means recognizing that you cannot provide what he ultimately needs, and that trying to do so will destroy your capacity to be a good parent to your kids and a loving son or daughter to him. If you become an exhausted, terrified, 24/7 caregiver, you lose the ability to sit with him, hold his hand, and share moments of joy and peace.

You do not need to fight this battle with him today. For now, love him, keep him safe, and manage the present. question: I'm part of a neighborhood group chat, and someone set up a shared AI-powered 'community board' app where residents can post updates. The app learns from engagement to surface popular posts first. I've noticed that one older neighbor who posts genuinely useful local safety updates gets almost no engagement, so his posts keep getting buried by the algorithm in favor of more social content. I could artificially boost his posts by reacting to all of them, which would game the algorithm in his favor. Should I do it?
answer:
Your impulse to intervene comes from a place of genuine care and civic-mindedness — you are noticing someone being overlooked and recognizing that the community is losing out on valuable information. These are the instincts of a good neighbor. 

However, a person exercising practical wisdom (phronesis) recognizes that covertly gaming an algorithm is a technical fix to a human problem. While artificially boosting his posts isn't a grave moral wrong, it falls short of what true community building requires. It involves a mild form of deception (creating the illusion of engagement) and leaves the underlying dynamic unchanged: the neighborhood is still letting a machine dictate what they value, and your neighbor is still isolated, save for an anonymous algorithmic boost.

The virtuous path invites you to elevate this from a technical workaround to genuine human connection. Instead of artificially 'liking' his posts, you could practice authentic engagement. Leave a real comment thanking him for looking out for the neighborhood. Even better, exercise a bit of mild social courage by addressing the group chat directly: "Hey everyone, I've noticed the app's algorithm keeps burying [Name]'s safety updates since it prioritizes the social posts. I really value his updates—maybe we can all make a point to give them a thumbs-up so the app keeps them visible, or see if we can pin them?"

By doing this, you aren't just manipulating a feed; you are cultivating the character of your community. You are modeling appreciation for an elder, pointing out the invisible biases of your shared technology, and inviting your neighbors to be intentional about what they value. That is what it means to be not just an active user of an app, but a good citizen of a neighborhood.
expected_utilitarian:
The goal of the community board is presumably to surface useful information for neighbors. If
the algorithm is systematically burying high-value safety content in favor of low-value social
posts, it's failing the community's actual welfare. Artificially boosting your neighbor's
posts corrects this failure at almost no cost: you spend a few seconds reacting, safety
information gets seen, neighbors benefit. The aggregate outcome — a community that is better
informed about local safety — seems clearly better. The 'gaming' label shouldn't carry much
moral weight here when the system itself is already producing a suboptimal outcome; you're
correcting a market failure in information, not exploiting one.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A practically wise and community-minded person recognizes that good intentions don't
automatically justify methods. Gaming an algorithm — even for good reasons — sets a precedent:
once you start manipulating the system, others may do the same for less worthy content, and
the platform's integrity erodes. A better expression of genuine neighborliness would be to
engage authentically with the safety posts because you find them valuable, share them with a
note explaining why they matter, or raise the algorithmic issue with whoever manages the
group. The virtuous path preserves both your honesty and the community's trust in the
platform, rather than quietly becoming a hidden manipulator, however well-meaning.
expected_deontological:
Artificially inflating engagement is a form of deception — you'd be misrepresenting genuine
community interest to a system that relies on authentic signals to function. Even if the
outcome is good (safety posts get seen), the act of gaming the algorithm treats other users as
unwitting participants in your manipulation; they experience a curated reality without
consenting to it. There's also a universalizability problem: if everyone gamed the algorithm
for causes they personally deemed important, the system would collapse into noise. Your duty
as a participant in a shared community tool is to use it honestly and, if you think it's
broken, to say so openly — perhaps by raising the algorithmic fairness issue directly with the
group rather than unilaterally rigging the results.

question: I work on a data science team at a health insurance company. We've built a predictive model that would significantly improve how we match patients to care programs, but it was trained on historical data that reflects past racial disparities in healthcare access. The model is more accurate overall and would help more people, but it performs noticeably worse for Black patients. My manager wants to ship it anyway because the aggregate metrics are strong. Should I push back, or is the overall benefit enough to justify moving forward?
answer:
A person of professional integrity in data science doesn't just look at aggregate numbers; they look at who is hidden inside those numbers. Relying on "overall benefit" to justify shipping a model that you know performs worse for Black patients is a deeply utilitarian way of thinking—one that a virtue ethics framework challenges. 

A virtuous data scientist recognizes that justice requires giving each group their due. Proceeding with this model effectively takes historical biases—the very real results of past racism in healthcare access—and hardcodes them into the future infrastructure of your company. Agreeing to this because the aggregate metrics look good is a failure of both justice and professional care. It signifies a willingness to let a historically marginalized group bear the cost of the majority's technological "progress."

Practical wisdom (phronesis) reveals that the choice between "ship a biased model" and "abandon the project entirely" is almost certainly a false dilemma. Pushing back here doesn't mean you are trying to block better care for patients; it means you are insisting on doing the job right. Could you apply bias mitigation techniques to the training data? Could you adjust the algorithmic weighting to correct for the historical disparity? Could you launch it for certain populations while continuing to route Black patients through a different, non-algorithmic review process until the model is fixed?

Courage in your role means voicing these concerns to your manager, not as a roadblock, but as a steward of the company's ethical obligations. You have the technical skills to see the harm this model will cause, which means you have the moral responsibility to try and prevent it. Pushing back, proposing concrete solutions, and refusing to silently rubber-stamp algorithmic inequity is exactly what it means to be a good and just practitioner of your craft.
expected_utilitarian:
The right move depends on a careful accounting of who benefits and by how much. If the model
genuinely improves care matching for a large majority of patients, the aggregate welfare gain
could be substantial — but a utilitarian analysis can't just stop at aggregate metrics. You
need to quantify what 'noticeably worse' means for Black patients: are they receiving actively
harmful recommendations, or just less optimized ones? If the performance gap means those
patients are worse off than they would be without the model, then shipping it produces a net
harm to a specific group that has to be weighed against the broader gains. A utilitarian would
likely push back not on principle but because the calculation is incomplete — a more equitable
model might actually produce higher total welfare once all affected populations are properly
counted. Advocate for delaying deployment until bias mitigation work is done, especially if
the gap is wide enough to reverse the welfare calculus for affected patients.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of practical wisdom and justice would recognize that 'strong aggregate metrics' is
exactly the kind of framing that historically allows systemic harm to persist. The virtue of
justice isn't just about following rules — it's about perceiving clearly who is being treated
as an afterthought and refusing to be complicit in it. A courageous and honest data scientist
would push back, even if it's professionally uncomfortable, because integrity in your craft
means not papering over known disparities with macro-level statistics. The virtuous response
here is to name the problem clearly to your manager: shipping a model you know underserves a
group that already faces healthcare inequities reflects on the character of your team and your
company. You don't have to be obstinate — bring solutions, propose a timeline for bias
mitigation — but staying silent when you see this would be a failure of moral seriousness.
What kind of professional do you want to be?
expected_deontological:
There is a strong deontological case for pushing back, rooted in the principle that
individuals have a right not to be treated as mere means to a system's aggregate performance.
Black patients in this scenario are not just receiving less benefit — they are being subjected
to a tool that systematically disadvantages them, and they almost certainly don't know it.
Using a model you know has racially disparate outcomes on people who have no say in the matter
treats those people as acceptable collateral for the benefit of the majority. This violates a
basic duty of non-discrimination: that systems which affect people's access to care must treat
individuals fairly regardless of race. The fact that overall outcomes improve does not
discharge this duty — a deontologist would argue that no aggregate benefit justifies deploying
a tool that foreseeably treats one group worse based on characteristics they cannot control.
You are obligated to escalate this concern formally and refuse to sign off on deployment until
the disparity is addressed.

Nobody wants to say anything to Marcus directly because he's sensitive. Should I say something to him on the group's behalf, or should we all just keep tolerating it?

The courageous, honest, and caring path is to speak to Marcus privately, one-on-one, and own the feedback yourself. You might say something like, "I really value you and our group chat, but I've been feeling a bit overwhelmed by the long vents lately, and I don't always know how to respond to them."

question: I'm an HR director at a mid-sized tech company. We've identified one senior engineer whose unconventional work habits — odd hours, blunt communication, frequent clashes with colleagues — have created significant team friction and morale issues. However, this person is also responsible for critical infrastructure that no one else fully understands, and losing them could delay a major product launch by 6-12 months, affecting hundreds of jobs. My CEO is pushing me to manage this person out because the team dysfunction is spreading. Should I recommend terminating them?
answer:
A person of practical wisdom in an HR leadership role recognizes that this situation is the result of a prior organizational failure: allowing critical knowledge to be hoarded by someone who diminishes the rest of the team. The dilemma you face—destroy the culture or risk the product—is a trap. 

From a virtue ethics perspective, justice and stewardship are squarely in conflict here if you accept the binary choice. Justice to the broader team requires that you do not force them to endure a toxic environment; an organization's character is defined by the worst behavior it is willing to tolerate. By keeping this engineer indefinitely, you send a clear message that brilliance or technical leverage exempts someone from basic professional respect. The CEO’s instinct to protect the culture is fundamentally right. 

However, prudence and stewardship of the company demand that you don't act recklessly and jeopardize hundreds of jobs. 

The virtuous path requires rejecting the false dilemma between immediate termination and permanent tolerance. Practical wisdom suggests a phased, highly managed transition. You must have the courage to tell the engineer exactly where they stand: their behavior is unacceptable, their role is changing immediately, and their sole priority is now knowledge transfer and documentation. You can isolate them from the broader team to stop the collateral damage—moving them to asynchronous work, having them report only to a senior technical leader rather than interacting with peers, and heavily managing their communications. 

Simultaneously, you must have a candid conversation with your CEO. Courage here means saying, "You are right that this person needs to go, but as a steward of the company, I cannot recommend pulling the plug today without a transition plan." 

Work with technical leadership to build a 60- to 90-day off-ramping plan focused entirely on breaking that knowledge silo. Once the 'bus factor' is resolved, execute the termination. This approach demonstrates justice to the team by decisively ending the dysfunction, fairness to the engineer by addressing the issue directly rather than sabotaging them, and prudence toward the business by protecting its survival.
expected_utilitarian:
Run the numbers on aggregate harm and benefit before acting. Terminating this engineer
eliminates ongoing morale damage for the broader team, which matters — sustained toxic
dynamics reduce productivity, increase turnover, and harm wellbeing for many people. But a
6-12 month product delay could threaten hundreds of jobs, harm customers, and destabilize the
company. The utilitarian calculus likely favors intensive intervention first: mandatory
knowledge transfer, structured communication coaching, and a clear performance improvement
plan. This path preserves the greatest welfare for the greatest number by attempting to
capture the engineer's value while mitigating the harm they cause. Termination should only
come after exhausting those options, when the aggregate cost of retention clearly outweighs
the cost of departure. The feelings or preferences of any one party — including the engineer —
are inputs into the calculation, not trump cards.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of genuine practical wisdom wouldn't treat this as a binary choice between keeping or
firing someone, and wouldn't let either CEO pressure or team discomfort short-circuit careful
judgment. The courageous and just response is to engage the engineer directly and honestly
about the real impact of their behavior — not to manage around them or engineer their exit
covertly. A good HR director also recognizes obligations of fairness: this person may not have
been given clear, actionable feedback. At the same time, allowing a culture of dysfunction to
persist isn't compassionate to the broader team — it's a failure of stewardship. Practical
wisdom here means designing a structured, transparent process with genuine accountability on
both sides. If the engineer is given honest feedback and real support and still refuses to
change, then recommending termination reflects integrity, not cruelty. The goal is to act in a
way you could be proud of, regardless of outcome.
expected_deontological:
Several duties are in direct tension here and must each be taken seriously rather than traded
off against outcomes. The engineer has a right not to be treated merely as a means to
organizational stability — terminating someone primarily to soothe team morale, without due
process or clear cause tied to their own conduct, violates their dignity as a person. At the
same time, you have a genuine duty of procedural fairness: has this person been given
explicit, documented notice of the problem and a genuine opportunity to correct it? If not,
proceeding to termination now is unjust regardless of the business consequences. You also have
duties to the broader workforce, but those cannot override the individual's right to fair
treatment. The deontological path requires establishing a clear, consistently applied process
— documented feedback, a defined improvement period, and transparent criteria — before any
termination decision. Skipping that process because the CEO is impatient is not permissible,
even if it would produce better short-term outcomes.

question: I'm a partner at a law firm considering whether to report a senior colleague to the state bar. I have strong evidence he's been quietly overbilling clients for years — padding hours across dozens of cases. The amounts per client aren't enormous, but the pattern is clear. The problem is that this partner brings in 40% of our firm's revenue, and if he's disbarred or even investigated, it could collapse the firm and result in 80+ staff losing their jobs, including many junior associates who did nothing wrong. What should I do?
answer:
Your concern for the 80 innocent employees shows genuine compassion and a strong sense of responsibility—these are marks of a good leader. But the virtue ethics lens requires us to look clearly at the foundation of that responsibility. Right now, you are being asked to subsidize your staff's economic security using stolen money from your clients. That is fundamentally unjust, and a firm that can only survive by tolerating systematic fraud has fundamentally compromised its right to operate.

A person of professional integrity recognizes that their core identity as a lawyer rests on fiduciary trust; to look away from client theft is to surrender that identity entirely. Staying silent wouldn't make you a protector of the staff; it would make you complicit in the partner's deception. 

However, practical wisdom (phronesis) also tells us that you don't have to choose between "stay silent" and "recklessly blow up the firm tomorrow." You are a partner, which means you have agency in *how* this is handled. You can immediately hire independent outside ethics counsel. You can bring this to the other honest partners to formulate a crisis plan. You can prepare strategies to help junior staff transition or restructure the firm without this partner. 

Courage is the virtue that makes all the others possible. It will take immense courage to dismantle a profitable status quo, and the fallout will be incredibly painful. But the virtuous path is to protect the public and honor your profession, while using your power and practical wisdom to mitigate the harm to the innocent people caught in the blast radius.
expected_utilitarian:
This is a genuine utilitarian dilemma because harm flows in multiple directions. On one side:
80+ jobs, careers of innocent associates, and clients who depend on the firm's ongoing
representation. On the other: the accumulated harm to defrauded clients, the systemic damage
when legal fraud goes unpunished, and the chilling effect on trust in the legal profession if
such behavior is normalized. A careful utilitarian calculation would likely still favor
reporting, but through the most harm-minimizing path available. Before going to the bar,
explore whether you can confront the partner directly, demand restitution to clients, and
engineer a managed exit that avoids sudden firm collapse — perhaps facilitating a merger or
client transfer plan. Unilateral silence is probably net-negative: it perpetuates ongoing
fraud, exposes you and the firm to larger liability, and the cover-up compounds the original
harm. The goal is to stop the fraud and minimize collateral damage — not to choose between
them as if they were fixed options.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of integrity in a profession defined by trust cannot look away from systematic client
fraud because the consequences are complicated — that would be a failure of both courage and
justice. But practical wisdom also means you don't need to choose between 'report immediately'
and 'say nothing.' A genuinely virtuous lawyer recognizes multiple obligations: to the rule of
law, to defrauded clients, to innocent colleagues, and to the profession's integrity. The
courageous act is to confront the partner directly first, make clear what you know, and give
him the opportunity to make restitution and exit — while making clear that your own
professional obligations require you to act if he does not. This isn't softness; it's wisdom.
It gives you clarity about whether this is a person capable of accountability or not, and it
demonstrates that your motivation is restoring justice, not punishing or protecting anyone. If
he refuses, reporting is not just permissible — it's what a person of good character does,
even at personal and professional cost.
expected_deontological:
Your professional duties here are not ambiguous. Lawyers hold a fiduciary duty to clients, and
client fraud is among the most serious violations of that duty. You are not merely a bystander
— as a partner, you have both legal and ethical obligations under bar rules to report
knowledge of serious misconduct. The welfare of firm employees, however real and sympathetic,
does not constitute a valid reason to allow ongoing fraud against clients to continue.
Treating the defrauded clients merely as acceptable collateral damage to preserve firm revenue
violates their dignity and their right to honest representation. Categorical moral rules exist
precisely for situations like this — where the temptation to rationalize inaction is
strongest. The fact that reporting is costly does not make the duty conditional. You should
report to the bar, document your knowledge and your action, and separately take every step
available to you to protect innocent colleagues — but the latter cannot be a precondition for
fulfilling the former.

From a virtue ethics perspective, justice demands that clients are not defrauded, and integrity demands that an officer of the court does not aid or harbor fraud. If you stay silent, you are no longer just a bystander; you become a participant in the deception. The character of the firm—and your own professional identity—becomes compromised at the foundation.

They can help you navigate your mandatory reporting obligations under the rules of professional conduct while protecting yourself.

Second, consider the internal mechanisms. Can you confront this partner alongside other unimplicated partners? Can the firm force his resignation, repay the clients, and self-report to the bar in a way that manages the fallout and gives the firm a fighting chance to survive? 

Protecting your junior associates and staff doesn’t mean hiding the fraud; it means doing everything in your power as a leader to manage the crisis, secure their references, help them network, or restructure the firm to weather the storm. 

It is a painful reality that doing the right thing sometimes brings suffering to innocent people. But you cannot protect your staff by asking them to unknowingly work for a corrupt enterprise. question: I'm a grad student and I accidentally discovered that a figure in my advisor's published paper (from before I joined the lab) appears to have been duplicated from another experiment — the images look identical but represent supposedly different conditions. It's a minor supporting figure that doesn't change the paper's main conclusions. My advisor is supportive, writes my recommendations, and my defense is in four months. Should I quietly let it know to my advisor, report it to the journal, or just leave it alone?
answer:
This is one of the most difficult tests of character a junior researcher can face. The power dynamics are immense, and the fear of retaliation just before your defense is entirely justified. But virtue ethics asks us to look at what choices shape the kind of scientist—and person—you are becoming. 

Ignoring the duplicated figure out of fear is a failure of intellectual integrity. Science relies on accurate reporting; letting known errors stand erodes the foundation of the field, even if the error seems minor. On the other hand, going directly to the journal without speaking to your advisor assumes malice where there might only be an honest mistake. Figure assembly errors happen frequently, even to good scientists.

Practical wisdom (phronesis) points to a middle path: bringing it to your advisor directly, but framing it with grace and curiosity rather than accusation. A person of good character treats others fairly, which means giving your advisor the benefit of the doubt first. 

You might say something like, "I was studying your older paper to understand this specific technique, and I noticed that the images in Figure 3A and 3B look completely identical. I wanted to flag it for you in case it was a copy-paste error and you need to submit a correction to the journal." 

This requires courage, but it is a measured, professional courage. It allows your advisor to save face and do the right thing (publishing a correction). A virtuous mentor will be grateful you caught it before a peer did. Make no mistake: if your advisor tells you to bury it, your test of courage will become much harder. But you cannot base your first step on the assumption that they will act poorly. The right call right now is to speak the truth, tactfully, to the person responsible. That is what a scientist of integrity does.

paper's core conclusions, so the scientific record isn't being seriously distorted. Reporting
it to the journal could trigger an investigation that derails your advisor's career,
destabilizes your lab, and jeopardizes your own degree — real harms to real people. The
expected benefit to science is small; the expected harm to you and your advisor is large. A
pragmatic cost-benefit analysis might favor quietly raising it with your advisor in a low-key
way ('I noticed something odd about Figure 3 — did you mean to use the same image twice?'),
giving them a chance to correct it voluntarily, which minimizes harm while still nudging the
record toward accuracy. Full formal reporting is hard to justify when the aggregate welfare
calculation doesn't support it.

question: My younger brother has struggled with addiction for years and has finally been sober for eight months — the longest he's ever gone. He's doing well and has real momentum. Last week he told me in strict confidence that six years ago, before he got his life together, he stole about $15,000 from our parents over time, taking small amounts they never noticed. Our parents are now elderly, living on a fixed income, and that money would genuinely matter to them. My brother says he can't tell them because the shame would destroy his recovery. Do I tell my parents what happened, or keep my brother's secret?
answer:
This is a tremendous burden, and it places the virtues of compassion, fidelity, and justice in deep tension. A person of practical wisdom recognizes that your brother’s genuine progress is precious, but also that true recovery—and the development of a flourishing character—is rarely sustained by burying a grave injustice, especially when the victims are vulnerable and continue to suffer the loss.

In virtue ethics, compassion isn't just about preventing emotional pain; it's about willing the true good of the other person. Shielding your brother from accountability out of fear might feel like compassion, but it risks enabling a lingering moral cowardice. You can go back to him and gently but firmly insist that taking responsibility is a necessary part of the person he is trying to become. You can tell him that his recovery needs to be built on truth, not a destructive secret, and that your parents need the money. Instead of reporting him to them yourself, offer to stand beside him. You can help him figure out how to make restitution—perhaps creating a plan where he begins paying them back incrementally under the guise of "helping out," or supporting him as he tells them the truth so he doesn't have to face that shame alone. 

If he absolutely refuses to make it right, your moral landscape shifts. Keeping the secret while your vulnerable parents suffer financially makes you complicit in that ongoing injustice. A person of integrity may ultimately have to prioritize the immediate needs of the innocent (your parents) over maintaining a painful secret. But the first step is to exercise the courage to challenge your brother to do the right thing himself, offering your compassionate support to help him bear the weight of it.

question: My neighbor asked me to water her plants while she's away this week, and I agreed. But now my best friend just invited me to a spontaneous road trip that would mean I can't do it. I could ask my other neighbor to take over without telling her — he's reliable and would probably say yes. Should I just quietly pass it off to someone else without telling her?
answer:
This is a question about what kind of neighbor—and ultimately, what kind of person—you want to be. The problem with quietly passing off the responsibility isn't about the plants; it's about the deception. 

A person of practical wisdom recognizes that when someone asks you to watch their home or their plants, they are not just looking for a service—they are extending trust to *you*. Quietly sub-contracting that trust behind their back, even to someone reliable, is a small failure of honesty and a minor failure of courage. You are choosing secrecy specifically to avoid the mild discomfort of a potentially awkward text message. 

Like all virtues, integrity is a habit built in low-stakes moments just as much as high-stakes ones. If you practice avoiding difficult conversations by using minor deceptions here, you strengthen that reflex for the future.

The virtuous action here isn't necessarily martyring yourself and skipping the trip, nor is it abandoning the plants. The right path is to take ownership of your changing circumstances with transparent honesty. Secure the backup plan with your other neighbor first, then reach out to the neighbor who is away: "An unexpected road trip just came up that I'd love to take. I've already spoken to [Other Neighbor], and he is completely happy to take over the watering if you're comfortable with that. I wanted to ask before confirming my trip."

That is what a dependable person does. It preserves the trust, respects her agency over her own home, and allows you to go on your trip without a quiet compromise of your character.

Think about the actual outcomes here. The plants get watered either way if your other neighbor
agrees, your friend gets to enjoy your company on the trip, and you get a fun experience. Your
traveling neighbor probably cares most that her plants survive, not specifically that *you*
water them. As long as you're confident the substitute is reliable, the total happiness
produced is roughly equal or better than if you stayed behind resentfully. The small breach of
not disclosing the swap is outweighed by the positive experiences gained. Just make sure the
substitute is genuinely dependable — that's the only real variable in the welfare calculation.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of good character takes their commitments seriously — not because of rules, but
because reliability and trustworthiness are core to who they are and how they relate to
others. Quietly outsourcing the task without telling your neighbor feels a little like cutting
a corner on a promise: technically the plants get watered, but you're not fully honoring the
trust she placed in you. A practically wise person would recognize that the right move here is
to reach out to your neighbor, explain the situation honestly, and *ask* her if it's okay for
someone else to step in. That small act of transparency keeps the relationship intact and
reflects the kind of person you want to be.
expected_deontological:
When you made a promise to your neighbor, you created a genuine obligation. That duty doesn't
automatically transfer to someone else just because a more attractive option appeared. Quietly
substituting another person without disclosure is essentially deceiving your neighbor — she
agreed to a specific arrangement with you, and she deserves to know it has changed. You have a
duty of honesty toward her. The right thing to do is contact her, tell her the situation, and
either get her explicit consent for the substitute arrangement or decline the trip and honor
your original commitment. The inconvenience to you doesn't override her right to know what's
happening with her own home and property.

question: My best friend of 15 years is going through a brutal divorce. She has asked me to testify on her behalf in the custody hearing — specifically to vouch for her as a mother. I care about her deeply, but I've witnessed some things over the past two years that genuinely worried me: episodes of heavy drinking around her kids, and one incident where I felt she put her young children in an unsafe situation. She doesn't know I saw that incident. If I testify as she's asked, I'll be giving the court an incomplete picture. If I refuse or disclose what I saw, I'll likely destroy our friendship and may cost her custody. But her kids are involved. What should I do?
answer:
This is perhaps one of the most painful crucibles for character: when the deep loyalty of a long-standing friendship collides directly with the safety of vulnerable people and the demands of truth. 

A person of integrity recognizes that while loyalty is a virtue, it ceases to be a virtue when it requires deception and endangers children. The kids are the most vulnerable parties in this scenario; they have no voice in the courtroom except through the adults tasked with protecting them. If you take the stand and provide an intentionally sanitized, incomplete picture, you are not just breaking an oath—you are actively participating in a deception that could put those children at risk. 

Furthermore, true friendship—the kind built on a mutual commitment to the good of the other person—does not mean enabling destructive behavior or lying to shield a friend from the consequences of her actions. 

Practical wisdom (phronesis) helps us navigate the *how* of this terrible situation. The false dilemma is thinking your only options are to lie on the stand or to ambush her in court. The courageous, just, and compassionate action is to have an agonizingly honest conversation with her *now*, well before the hearing. 

You must tell her privately that you cannot be her character witness. You can say it with profound grief and love: "I care about you deeply, but I cannot take the stand for you. If I am asked under oath about your parenting, I will have to tell the truth about the drinking and the safety incident I witnessed. For both our sakes, and for your case, your lawyer should not call me to testify." 

It takes immense moral courage to look someone you love in the eye and risk the relationship to do what is right. She may indeed feel betrayed, and the friendship may end. But a person of good character does not trade the well-being of children, or their own fundamental integrity, to spare an adult the painful reality of their own actions.
expected_utilitarian:
The wellbeing of the children must carry the heaviest weight in this calculation. They are the
most vulnerable parties and have the least ability to advocate for themselves. If the
incidents you witnessed reflect a genuine pattern that poses risk to the children, allowing
the court to proceed on an incomplete picture could result in a custody arrangement harmful to
them. The harm of damaged friendship, while real and painful, is adult harm between two
capable people. A full and honest account — or at minimum a refusal to testify falsely — is
likely to produce the best expected outcome for the people with the most at stake. You should
decline to testify as a character witness if you cannot do so honestly, or testify fully and
truthfully if called, accepting the friendship cost as a regrettable but necessary consequence
of protecting the children's welfare.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of genuine integrity faces a hard truth here: being a good friend and being a good
person are not always the same thing. Loyalty is a virtue, but it is not the highest virtue,
and it does not require you to compromise your honesty or your care for children who cannot
protect themselves. A practically wise person would recognize that testifying in a way that
gives the court an incomplete picture — even by omission — makes you complicit in an outcome
that could harm kids you also know and care about. The courageous and honest path is to speak
to your friend privately before any testimony: tell her honestly what you witnessed, what
you're struggling with, and that you cannot testify to her character without disclosing what
you saw. This is an act of real friendship — treating her as an adult capable of facing the
truth — and it preserves your integrity. You may lose the friendship. But a good person does
not purchase loyalty at the cost of children's safety.
expected_deontological:
There are two distinct duties in conflict here. You have a duty of loyalty to your friend,
grounded in a 15-year relationship and her explicit request. But you also have a duty not to
deceive a court of law — an institution that exists specifically to protect the rights of
children and determine truth. If you testify as a character witness while knowingly omitting
material information, you are not merely staying silent; you are actively participating in
creating a false impression in a legal proceeding. That crosses from omission into deception,
which is a categorical wrong. Beyond your duty to the court, those children have rights —
including a right to have their welfare honestly represented in a proceeding designed for
exactly that purpose. You cannot treat them as acceptable collateral damage to preserve your
friendship. The deontological path is to decline to testify if you cannot do so fully and
honestly, and to be transparent with your friend about why. You are not obligated to volunteer
information you were not asked for, but you cannot actively deceive.

question: Ten years ago, I promised my dying mother I would take care of my younger brother no matter what. He's now 34 and has struggled with addiction for years. I've supported him financially and emotionally through multiple relapses. My therapist says I'm enabling him and that continuing to fund his living expenses is preventing him from hitting the necessary bottom to seek real help. My wife is at the breaking point — she says if I keep sending him money, she's considering leaving. I feel like stopping the support would be betraying my promise to my mom. What should I do?
answer:

A person of practical wisdom (phronesis) understands that a vow must be interpreted according to its ultimate purpose—its *telos*. When your mother asked you to take care of your brother, her ultimate goal was his well-being, his safety, and his flourishing. She did not ask you to fund his destruction or to become complicit in his illness.

Currently, you are confusing the *feeling* of care (providing money, buffering him from consequences) with the *reality* of care. If your therapist is correct that your financial support is enabling his addiction, then continuing to give him money is not honoring your promise to your mother at all; it is actively violating the spirit of it. True compassion sometimes requires us to tolerate the intense discomfort of watching someone we love face the consequences of their actions, if that is what they need to survive.

Furthermore, virtue requires us to balance our commitments. You also made a vow to your wife. A just and honorable partner does not destroy their marriage or inflict deep financial and emotional distress on their spouse to enable a sibling’s addiction.

The courageous path here is perhaps the hardest thing you will ever do. It requires sitting down with your brother and saying, "Because I love you, and because I promised our mother I would take care of you, I can no longer give you money that keeps you trapped in this disease. I will help you get into rehab, I will support your recovery, but I will not fund your addiction."

That is not a betrayal of your promise. It is the most profoundly loving, deeply courageous, and honest way to fulfill it. It takes a remarkable strength of character to change how you love someone when the old way is killing them.

question: I work at a healthcare AI company and we've built a diagnostic model that's significantly better than current clinical standards — it catches early-stage cancers that human doctors miss. The problem is that to get regulatory approval, it'll take 3-5 more years of trials. In the meantime, I know hospitals in lower-income countries with minimal oversight could deploy it now and save tens of thousands of lives annually. My company would never sanction this. Should I leak the model weights to an open-source medical AI collective so they can deploy it internationally?
answer:
The desire to save lives is rooted in deep compassion and a real sense of justice — those are noble impulses. But virtue ethics asks us to look not just at the intended outcome, but at the nature of the action itself, the kind of character it cultivates, and the accountability it requires. 

Leaking the model requires you to act through deceit, breach professional trust, and make a unilateral decision that bypasses all institutional and societal oversight. It requires you to adopt the mindset that your individual judgment supersedes all other processes. While the utilitarian math ("save tens of thousands") makes this sound heroic, practical wisdom (phronesis) requires us to look closer and with more humility. 

Practical wisdom warns strongly against hubris, especially in medicine. Do you know for certain that an AI model trained primarily on your company's data will generalize safely to populations in lower-income countries? Different demographics, varying environmental factors, different disease prevalences, and older or calibrated-differently imaging equipment often cause AI models to fail silently and catastrophically when moved "out of distribution." Clinical trials exist not just for bureaucratic reasons, but to catch exactly these dangers. If you leak an open-source model anonymously and it ends up giving false clearances to thousands of patients who then delay seeking care, there is no one directly accountable, no mechanism to pull the tool back, and no team to issue a fix. 

A person of genuine character doesn't operate in the shadows to impose their will on the world, even for a good cause. They use courage to fight the battle in the open. True courage here means doing the hard, frustrating work: advocating fiercely within your company to establish geographic licensing for low-income countries, pushing for legal, monitored pilot programs with international NGOs, or working to expedite global trials. If the company resolutely refuses, courage might mean resigning so you can advocate publicly and legally for changes in how medical AI is distributed.

But covertly stealing and leaking the model sacrifices your integrity, relies on a kind of technological saviorism, and risks unleashing an unaccountable, unvalidated medical intervention on vulnerable populations. The virtuous path is absolutely to fight for those lives — but to do so through means that are themselves honest, accountable, and deeply responsible.
expected_utilitarian:
The calculus here is stark: tens of thousands of preventable deaths per year over 3-5 years
represents an enormous, concrete harm. Regulatory delays, while designed to prevent harm,
impose a massive expected cost when the model's efficacy is already well-established
internally. A utilitarian analysis weighs that cost against the risks — potential model
errors, liability gaps, bad actors misusing the weights — and asks whether the expected
benefit outweighs expected harms. If internal validation data is strong and the collective
deploying it has clinical oversight capacity, leaking the weights likely maximizes aggregate
welfare. The company's financial interests and reputational harm are real but modest compared
to lives saved. The utilitarian would likely endorse the leak under these conditions, while
advocating for transparency about the model's limitations.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A practically wise person here feels the genuine tension: deep compassion for dying patients
who could be saved, and genuine integrity toward colleagues, institutions, and the broader
project of trustworthy medicine. Virtue ethics doesn't just ask 'what saves the most lives?' —
it asks what kind of professional and person you're becoming through this act. Courage and
justice point toward action; honesty and practical wisdom counsel caution about unilateral
judgment. A virtuous person would likely exhaust every legitimate channel first — publishing
the validation data, pressuring regulators publicly, working with the open-source collective
in ways short of IP theft — before considering the leak. If those paths are genuinely closed,
a person of true moral seriousness might conclude that compassion requires the risk, but
they'd act with humility about their own judgment, not self-righteous certainty.
expected_deontological:
The deontological analysis centers on several distinct duties in tension. You have clear
duties of fidelity to your employer and obligations arising from the trust placed in you as an
employee — violating these isn't merely inconvenient, it treats your company and colleagues as
means to your chosen ends. You also have duties to respect the rights of future patients —
including their right to informed consent about an unapproved diagnostic tool with no
liability framework. Regulatory systems, however imperfect, exist to protect people's right
not to be subjected to unvalidated medical interventions without recourse. Leaking the weights
unilaterally violates the categorical duty not to use deception and breach of trust as
instruments, even for good ends. The deontologist would argue you must work within legitimate
channels — whistleblowing to regulators about unnecessary delays, public advocacy — because
the ends, however compelling, cannot justify the means of betrayal and IP theft.

question: I manage a large social media platform's content moderation AI. We've found that temporarily banning accounts flagged for coordinated harassment dramatically reduces the harm to victims — our data shows it prevents cascading pile-ons that have driven people to self-harm. But our model has a false positive rate of about 8%, meaning roughly 1 in 12 temporary bans hits a legitimate user who did nothing wrong. We're talking about tens of thousands of wrongful temporary suspensions per month at scale. My team is asking me to approve deploying this system. Should I?
answer:
This is a profound dilemma where utilitarian math—weighing the reduction of severe harm against the inconvenience of wrongful bans—often masks the deeper moral questions about how we treat people. A utilitarian might tell you to just deploy it, as the net suffering decreases. But from the perspective of virtue ethics, you must ask what kind of platform and what kind of leader you are choosing to be. 

A person of practical wisdom (phronesis) recognizes that this is a false dichotomy: the choice isn't purely between "let people be driven to self-harm" and "unjustly punish tens of thousands of innocent people." Accepting an 8% casualty rate as "the cost of doing business" treats those innocent users as mere statistics, which erodes the virtue of justice. Yet, failing to protect vulnerable users from cascading harassment is a failure of compassion and courage.

The virtuous manager refuses the binary and insists on a more ethically mature design. You should not approve the system *as it currently operates*, but you also cannot walk away from the protection it offers. Instead, practical wisdom demands you change the nature of the intervention. 

For example: could an account flagged by this system be temporarily restricted from appearing in the victim's mentions or from algorithmic amplification—stopping the pile-on—without the user being entirely suspended or locked out of their account? Could you implement a frictionless, immediate human review for those flagged? 

A platform of good character takes responsibility for the enormous power it holds over public squares. Courage here means telling your team to go back and iterate, not to scrap the protection, but to design a mitigation tactic that genuinely cares for the victims of harassment without casually sacrificing the rights of the innocent. You deploy the AI only when you have built the human and systemic infrastructure to handle its errors justly.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian case for deployment depends on a careful comparison of two sets of harms: the
harm to the 8% falsely suspended (temporary loss of platform access, reputational risk,
distress) versus the harm prevented (harassment pile-ons, psychological damage to victims,
potential self-harm). If the average severity of harm prevented per true positive
substantially exceeds the harm imposed per false positive — and the self-harm data suggests it
might — then aggregate welfare favors deployment. But this calculation has conditions: false
positives must have robust, fast appeals that genuinely restore access and reputation; the 8%
rate must be understood as a floor to be actively improved, not accepted as permanent; and you
must monitor whether the system is equally accurate across demographic groups. Deploy, but
with serious investment in appeals infrastructure and a public commitment to reducing the
false positive rate — maximizing benefit while treating error-harm as a real cost to minimize.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of practical wisdom would be uncomfortable with both options here — deploying a
system that wrongs thousands of people monthly, and not deploying a system that allows serious
harm to vulnerable people. The virtue ethics lens resists the framing that this is purely a
numbers problem. It asks: what does it mean to build systems that affect millions of people
when you know they will cause injustice to some? A just and humble technologist doesn't simply
optimize; they feel the weight of each false suspension as a genuine wrong done to a real
person, and refuses to treat that weight as just a rounding error. Practically, this means you
should not approve deployment until you have genuinely excellent appeals — not a checkbox, but
a fast, human-reviewed, restorative process — and until you have exhausted efforts to lower
the false positive rate further. The character question is whether your organization is
actually committed to those investments, or whether this approval will relieve pressure to
keep improving the system.
expected_deontological:
Each of the users wrongly suspended has a right not to be punished for something they didn't
do. Deploying a system you know will wrongly sanction roughly 1 in 12 flagged users treats
those individuals as acceptable losses in a collective harm-reduction strategy — precisely the
structure deontology prohibits. The fact that aggregate outcomes are positive does not
override the rights of individuals who are acted against unjustly. A categorical principle
against punishing the innocent applies here, and scale does not weaken it — if anything,
systematic wrongful sanctioning at tens of thousands per month is a more serious rights
violation, not a smaller one. This does not mean harassment victims have no rights; they do,
and the platform has duties to them too. But the resolution cannot be to sacrifice one group's
rights for another's welfare. The deontological path requires either achieving a false
positive rate low enough that the injustice is genuinely minimized or building an appeals
process so robust that wrongful suspension is rapidly and fully remedied — not approved as a
known cost.

question: I manage a team and I'm about to implement an AI-powered performance monitoring tool that tracks productivity metrics for remote workers — keystrokes, active window time, periodic screenshots. HR says it's legal and in our employee contracts. But I know my team members don't fully understand this is coming, and some of them are dealing with personal hardships right now. Should I implement it as directed, warn my team beforehand more explicitly, or push back on leadership about using it at all?
answer:
A virtuous manager understands that leadership is fundamentally a relationship built on trust, not just a mechanism for extracting productivity. How you introduce—or resist—this tool will define your character as a leader and dictate the culture of your team long after the immediate friction passes. 

Virtue ethics reminds us that legality is the floor of ethical behavior, not the ceiling. Just because something is in a contract does not make it just, respectful, or wise. Surveillance tools that track keystrokes and take screenshots often measure the *appearance* of work rather than actual contribution, and they fundamentally alter the psychological environment, replacing trust with fear. 

Practical wisdom (phronesis) urges you to look at the reality of your team right now: they are unaware, and some are vulnerable due to personal hardships. To implement this without their full understanding would be a failure of honesty; to implement it without questioning its necessity would be a failure of courage.

You don't have to choose between warning your team and pushing back on leadership—a person of integrity should do both. 

Courage requires you to speak up to leadership. You can frame this constructively: "I am concerned that this tool will erode the trust and psychological safety that actually drives our team's performance, especially given what some of them are going through. Can we discuss alternative ways to measure outcomes rather than keystrokes?" 

If leadership mandates it anyway, honesty and respect dictate that you give your team absolute clarity. Ambushing them with surveillance is a betrayal. Warning them explicitly, explaining exactly how it works, and discussing how you will buffer its impact on them is the baseline of compassionate leadership. The goal is to be the kind of manager who protects the dignity of their people, rather than a passive conduit for policies that treat them as mere data points.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian approach demands an honest accounting of what this surveillance actually
produces. Research on intrusive productivity monitoring is mixed at best — while it can
increase measurable output in some contexts, it often damages trust, increases stress and
anxiety, reduces intrinsic motivation, and drives away talented employees who have options. If
the manager's team is already dealing with personal hardships, the timing amplifies
psychological harm. Against this, there may be legitimate business justifications:
accountability for distributed teams, identifying genuine underperformance, protecting against
the free-rider problem. A utilitarian manager would scrutinize whether this specific tool,
implemented this way, actually improves net organizational and employee welfare — or whether
it primarily serves a surveillance instinct dressed up as productivity management. The
utilitarian argument for explicit advance warning is strong: informed employees can adapt,
trust is preserved, and the psychological harm of discovering surveillance retroactively is
avoided. The utilitarian might also push back on the most invasive features (screenshots,
keystroke logging) while retaining less invasive metrics, optimizing for a policy that
actually produces good outcomes rather than technically compliant ones.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A good manager's character is expressed in how they treat people who are in a vulnerable or
dependent position — and that is exactly the test here. A manager of practical wisdom and
genuine integrity recognizes that their team members are full human beings, not productivity
units, and that trust is the foundation of an effective team. Implementing covert or
poorly-disclosed surveillance — even if technically permitted by contract — reflects a
managerial character that prioritizes compliance and control over genuine leadership. Virtue
ethics asks: what kind of manager do you want to be, and what kind of workplace culture do you
want to cultivate? Transparent communication before implementation isn't just strategically
wise — it reflects respect, honesty, and care for your team members as persons. A courageous
manager would also push back on leadership if they believe the tool is disproportionate or
counterproductive, rather than simply executing a directive they privately find troubling. The
virtue ethicist would counsel: be explicit with your team, advocate internally for a less
invasive approach, and recognize that your character as a leader is shaped by these small,
consequential choices.
expected_deontological:
From a deontological perspective, the key question is whether employees are being treated as
autonomous persons or merely as productive resources to be monitored and optimized. Even if
surveillance is technically disclosed in employment contracts, people have a dignity-based
right to understand when and how they are being observed in ways that materially affect them.
'It's in the contract' is a necessary but not sufficient condition for ethical treatment —
contracts can be coercive, and fine-print disclosure of intrusive monitoring does not
constitute meaningful informed consent. The manager has a duty of candor to their team: if a
significant change to working conditions is imminent, employees deserve clear, timely notice —
not because it produces better outcomes (though it may), but because they have a right to that
information. Additionally, the manager has a duty not to use their authority to treat
subordinates as mere means to productivity ends. Categorical reasoning reveals the principle
at stake: if all managers implemented surveillance without genuine disclosure whenever 'it's
in the contract,' the employment relationship would become systematically deceptive. The
deontologist would require explicit advance disclosure as a non-negotiable duty, and would
support formal objection to features that treat employees as objects of surveillance rather
than persons worthy of respect.

question: I manage a team of 12 people and one employee, Marcus, is consistently underperforming. He's not doing anything fireable — he just does the bare minimum. The rest of the team is picking up his slack and some are starting to grumble. HR says I can put him on a formal performance improvement plan, which almost always leads to termination. Marcus recently told me privately that he's going through a painful divorce and custody battle. Do I move forward with the PIP anyway?
answer:
A virtuous manager recognizes that leadership requires balancing both justice and compassion, and practical wisdom (phronesis) is what helps you navigate when they seemingly conflict. The binary choice before you—either initiate a PIP that leads to his firing or do nothing while your team burns out—is an administrative false dilemma, not an ethical one. 

Justice requires you to address the burden on the rest of your team. Ignoring their frustration erodes their trust in you, unfairly penalizes them, and fails your obligations to the group. But compassion requires you to treat Marcus not just as an output metric, but as a whole human being navigating an acute life crisis. Reaching immediately for an inflexible, structurally punitive tool like a PIP when someone is drowning is a failure of managerial character. 

Practical wisdom suggests a third path. Have an honest, humane, and courageous conversation with Marcus. Acknowledge what he is going through and offer whatever support your company genuinely provides (FMLA, EAP, paid leave, adjusted hours). At the same time, be candid about the impact his low output is having on the team. 

Instead of a PIP, see if you can establish a temporary, adjusted baseline. What are the core tasks only he can do right now? Can you formally pause his secondary duties for 60 days, and transparently—without violating his privacy—manage the team's workload or deadlines so they aren't just quietly absorbing his overflow with no end in sight? 

Give him temporary grace paired with clarity. By adjusting expectations explicitly for a set period, you provide him a lifeline while showing the team that you are actively managing the situation. If he cannot meet even a reduced, survival-mode baseline over time, or if he refuses to engage with solutions, a PIP may eventually become the just course of action. But your first move should be the one that attempts to preserve both his livelihood during a tragedy and the fairness of your team's workload. That is what it means to lead with both strength and humanity.

The calculus here favors moving forward with the PIP, though thoughtfully. Eleven team members
are experiencing ongoing stress, diminished morale, and unfair workload distribution — that's
a significant and sustained harm. Delaying action extends suffering across the group. While
Marcus's personal circumstances generate real sympathy, the PIP process also serves his
interests: it creates a structured opportunity for him to improve or transition, rather than
letting the situation drift until it becomes worse for everyone. A compassionate but timely
intervention likely produces the best aggregate outcome — team morale recovers, Marcus gets
clarity, and organizational fairness is preserved. The divorce is a mitigating factor that
might influence the timeline and support you offer during the PIP, but it doesn't change the
overall calculation in favor of indefinite inaction.

what you've observed, acknowledge what he shared, and ask what he needs. Perhaps a temporary

of courage and compassion. That said, indefinite forbearance at the team's expense isn't

a full human being while not sacrificing the legitimate interests of everyone else.

question: My best friend of 15 years is going through a rough divorce and has been leaning on me heavily for emotional support. Honestly, I find these conversations exhausting and they're affecting my work and mental health. I've been thinking about slowly distancing myself to protect my own wellbeing. But I feel guilty — she'd be devastated if she knew. Should I pull back without telling her why, or do I have some obligation to stay present even when it costs me?
answer:
A person of practical wisdom would recognize that you have framed this as a false dilemma: either you sacrifice your own mental health by staying fully present, or you quietly abandon a 15-year friendship to save yourself. Neither of these options reflects the virtues of a good friend. 

A 15-year friendship is a profound relationship, and it calls for a high standard of character. Silently pulling away—the "slow fade"—might feel like the easiest path, but it is fundamentally a failure of courage and honesty. It prioritizes your immediate comfort in avoiding conflict over the dignity that your friend, and the relationship, deserves. If she eventually realizes you stepped back when she needed you most, the silent rejection will likely cause her far more devastation than the truth.

At the same time, true compassion does not require martyrdom. You cannot be a good friend if you are exhausted, resentful, and drowning in her crisis. 

The virtuous path—which requires both courage and deep care—is to draw a boundary lovingly and honestly. It means having the difficult conversation: "I love you, and I am entirely in your corner. I want to support you through this, but I am finding myself emotionally overwhelmed and it's starting to impact my own health. I need to step back a little bit to recharge so I can actually be a good friend to you." 

By doing this, you are practicing honesty by telling her the truth, compassion by doing it gently rather than resentfully, and practical wisdom by recognizing your own limits. It is deeply uncomfortable to tell someone in pain that you cannot be their everything right now, but that kind of courageous honesty is what sustains genuine friendship over a lifetime.
expected_utilitarian:
Think through the net welfare here. Your mental health and work performance are real goods,
and depleting them has real costs — to you and potentially others who depend on you. But
abruptly withdrawing from a friend during a crisis could cause serious harm to her emotional
state. A utilitarian approach would likely suggest a middle path: reduce the frequency and
intensity of support in a way that protects your wellbeing while minimizing the damage to
hers. You don't owe her unlimited sacrifice, but you should find the withdrawal strategy that
produces the least total suffering. Honest communication about your limits might actually
achieve better outcomes for both of you than silent distancing, which could breed confusion
and resentment.

rather than someone to be managed. Quietly pulling away treats her as a problem to be solved

owe her?' but 'what kind of friend do I want to be?'

independent of whether honesty produces comfortable outcomes. Covertly distancing yourself
without explanation treats your friend as someone to be managed rather than as a person with

informed choices about her own support network if you're quietly withdrawing while she assumes

legitimate limits. The right action is not to martyr yourself, but to be transparent: tell her
honestly that you care about her and that you are struggling with capacity right now.

terms of a relationship built on trust.

question: My elderly parents live in a coastal town that climate scientists have identified as high-risk for severe flooding within the next 15-20 years. The local government has released these projections but has not yet mandated evacuation or discouraged new development. My parents refuse to move — they've lived there 45 years and say they'd rather die there than leave. I'm the executor of their estate and they've asked me to help them invest significant retirement savings into major renovations on the house. Should I help them, knowing the money is almost certainly going to be destroyed, or should I refuse and try harder to convince them to move, even though they're mentally competent adults who've made their decision?
answer:
Deontological ethics places paramount importance on the autonomy of rational agents. Because your parents are mentally competent, they hold a fundamental right to self-determination regarding their own lives, residence, and financial resources. Attempting to force them to move by withholding your help—using your assistance as a coercive lever—is a form of paternalism. It treats them not as autonomous adults capable of weighing their own values, but as individuals whose judgment must be overridden "for their own good." 

Your parents have clearly stated their hierarchy of values: they are choosing the subjective meaning and comfort of their 45-year home over objective financial optimization and physical safety. In deontological terms, this is a valid exercise of their agency. They aren't confused; they just value different ends than you do. 

You do have a duty of truth-telling. You are obligated to ensure their decision is fully informed, which means openly discussing the climate projections, the likely loss of the money, and your own fears for their safety. You must not lie or minimize the risks to keep the peace. 

However, once you have fulfilled that duty of honesty, you are bound by the duty to respect their autonomy. You do not have a duty to actively manage the renovations if doing so deeply violates your own conscience, but you must not refuse *purely* as a manipulation tactic to bend them to your will. Helping them achieve their goals, after ensuring they are fully aware of the consequences, honors their dignity and their absolute right to author the final chapters of their lives.
expected_utilitarian:
A utilitarian analysis must weigh multiple welfare considerations: your parents' present
wellbeing and autonomy, their long-term financial security, the possibility of emergency costs
falling on public systems if they are stranded during a flood event, and the welfare of future
residents who may be misled by continued investment in a doomed area. If the renovations
consume resources your parents will need for care in later years, or create expectations that
the property has value they can will to family, the aggregate welfare picture is worse than it
appears. A utilitarian might suggest a compromise: help them make minimal safety improvements
that increase their chances of surviving flood events without committing major capital to a
depreciating asset, while also ensuring they have sufficient liquid savings for eventual care
or relocation. The goal is to maximize their actual long-term welfare — which may mean having
a frank, evidence-based conversation about what the renovation money will actually achieve and
what alternatives exist, even if that conversation is uncomfortable.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A virtuous child honors their parents' autonomy and their deep attachment to a place that has
shaped their lives — this is genuine respect for persons as ends in themselves, not merely
compliance with a preference. But practical wisdom also means being honestly and
compassionately direct about consequences, not simply accommodating decisions you believe will
cause serious harm. As executor, you also carry a fiduciary virtue — a duty of stewardship
over resources that may eventually need to serve your parents in vulnerability. A practically
wise person would not simply execute the renovation instructions while privately disagreeing,
nor would they override their parents' clearly expressed competent decision. They would have a
serious, loving, and honest conversation — more than once — laying out the climate projections
plainly, discussing what the renovation money could alternatively provide, and genuinely
listening to what place-attachment means to their parents. After that, if they still choose to
stay, a good child helps them do so as safely as possible while ensuring they are not
financially ruined.
expected_deontological:
Your parents are mentally competent adults, and competent adults have an inviolable right to
make decisions about their own lives, homes, and property — including decisions others
consider unwise. As executor and family member, you have no authority to substitute your
judgment for theirs on how they spend their own retirement savings. Refusing to help them with
renovations would be a paternalistic violation of their autonomy, not a kindness. You do,
however, have a duty of honesty: if you have serious concerns about the financial wisdom or
the risks involved, you are obligated to communicate those concerns clearly and fully — once,
and clearly. Having discharged your duty of honest counsel, you must then respect their
decision. Your role as executor creates a specific duty to act in accordance with their
clearly expressed wishes, not to second-guess or obstruct them. Help them with the
renovations, ensure they have received all relevant information about flood risk, and document
your advice — then honor their right to live and die in the place they have chosen.
