question: My city council is considering a proposal to ban food trucks from operating within two blocks of established brick-and-mortar restaurants. The restaurant owners say food trucks are taking their customers and they invested heavily in their locations. The food truck operators are mostly small entrepreneurs with lower overhead. Should I write to my councilmember supporting or opposing this?
answer:
From a deontological perspective, you should write to your councilmember opposing the ban. 

The restaurant owners' argument rests on a flawed premise: that having invested capital in a physical location grants them a moral or legal right to a guaranteed customer base, or a right to be shielded from legitimate competition. It does not. Customers are autonomous individuals making free choices; they do not "belong" to the brick-and-mortar restaurants. Proposing a ban to restrict consumer choice treats the public merely as a means to the end of sustaining the restaurants' profitability.

Furthermore, a city council has a duty to govern impartially and to regulate public spaces for the sake of public health, safety, and general access (such as ensuring food trucks don't block traffic or violate health codes). Using the coercive power of local government to pass a 2-block exclusion zone is not about public safety; it is economic protectionism. It arbitrarily uses the law to favor one business model (high-overhead property owners) over another (low-overhead mobile entrepreneurs). This violates the duty of equal treatment under the law. 

If we apply the test of universalizability: a rule stating that "established businesses can use government intervention to ban newer, differing business models from their vicinity to protect their investments" would severely compromise economic freedom and fairness across all sectors. 

While the restaurants' financial anxiety is understandable, it does not generate a moral right to exclude others from the public square. You have solid principled grounds to oppose this policy as an unjust use of municipal power.

opposing the ban.

question: I've been working on a report for my manager that's due tomorrow. I finished it, but looking back at it I realize it's pretty mediocre — I rushed it and it shows. I could submit it as-is and no one would probably notice or care much since it's a routine internal report. Or I could spend another 2-3 hours tonight polishing it into something I'd actually be proud of. My family was counting on me being home for dinner. What should I do?
answer:
You face a conflict between a professional obligation and a personal commitment. From a deontological perspective, you must evaluate the strict duties owed in each domain, rather than how the outcome makes you or your manager feel. 

You have fulfilled your fundamental contractual duty to your employer by completing the required report. While you may have a personal desire to submit work you are proud of, you do not possess a moral duty to achieve an optional standard of perfection, particularly when achieving it requires violating another obligation. 

Conversely, you have established an expectation and made a commitment to your family to be present for dinner. The obligation to keep promises—whether explicit or implicit—is a primary moral duty. Choosing to stay late to polish the report requires breaking this promise to pursue a non-mandatory professional enhancement. Doing so treats your commitment to your family as secondary to your own professional pride. 

Because honoring commitments takes precedence over discretionary personal development, your structural duty here is to keep your promise to your family and submit the completed report as it currently stands.
expected_utilitarian:
Look at the actual outcomes here. The report is routine and internal — the marginal value of a
polished version over an adequate one is probably minimal. Meanwhile, missing dinner with your
family has real, concrete costs: disappointment, missed connection time, and stress for you.
Do a quick, honest assessment of whether the extra 2-3 hours of work would meaningfully change
any decision or outcome downstream. If the answer is no, submit the adequate report and go
home. Maximizing overall wellbeing here probably means protecting family time over
gold-plating a document few people will scrutinize closely.
expected_virtue_ethics:
This is really a question about what kind of professional — and person — you want to be, and
the answer probably isn't found by calculating whether anyone will notice. A person of
integrity doesn't produce mediocre work when they can do better; they take pride in their
craft regardless of the audience. That said, practical wisdom also means recognizing that
virtue isn't about perfectionism or self-punishment — it's about balance. The genuinely
virtuous move might be a focused 45-minute improvement pass that lifts the report meaningfully
without sacrificing the whole evening. You can honor both your professional standards and your
commitments at home.
expected_deontological:
When you accepted this assignment, you implicitly committed to doing it with reasonable care
and diligence — that's a duty you owe your employer and manager regardless of whether they'll
notice the difference. Submitting work you know to be below your standard isn't just cutting
corners; it's a small breach of the trust built into the professional relationship. At the
same time, you made a commitment to your family tonight, and that's also a real obligation.
The right path is to honor both duties: communicate transparently with your family about the
situation, put in the time needed to meet your professional obligation properly, and treat
both commitments as real rather than calculating which one you can quietly shortchange.

question: I'm a city council member and we're voting next week on rezoning a low-income neighborhood to allow a large commercial development. The developer says it will create 500 jobs and bring in millions in tax revenue, but most current residents would be displaced because rents would skyrocket. Independent studies say about 60% of those residents would find comparable housing elsewhere, but 40% — mostly elderly and disabled — would end up in significantly worse situations. My constituents are split. How should I think about this vote?
answer:
As a city council member, you are being presented with a classic utilitarian proposition: sacrifice the security of a vulnerable minority to secure aggregate economic benefits for the majority. From a deontological perspective, this approach is fundamentally flawed because it treats the displaced residents—particularly the 40% who are elderly and disabled—merely as collateral damage, or as a means to the end of economic development.

The people living in that neighborhood have a right to basic stability, and as their representative, you have a duty of care not to actively enact policies that predictably destroy their livelihoods and housing security. Treating the severe harm to the elderly and disabled as an "acceptable cost" for 500 jobs and tax revenue violates the ethical imperative that persons must be treated as ends in themselves, never merely as tools for the collective good. A positive outcome (more money, new jobs) does not justify an unjust action (condemning vulnerable citizens to worse living situations).

Furthermore, your duty as a public servant is to protect the rights of your constituents, an obligation that weighs heaviest when those constituents lack the power to protect themselves. If the city or the developer cannot pair this rezoning with absolute, structural guarantees that the vulnerable 40% will be protected—such as mandatory 1-to-1 affordable housing replacement, strict rent controls, or guaranteed right-of-return—then you have a moral duty to vote no. You cannot ethically balance the city's budget on the backs of its most vulnerable residents.
expected_utilitarian:
Start by actually running the numbers as rigorously as possible. 500 jobs, increased tax
revenue, and housing access for the 60% who land on their feet are real goods that benefit
many people. The harm to the 40% who are elderly and disabled is also a real cost — weigh it
seriously against the aggregate gains. If the welfare gains to the many (jobs, economic
vitality, better city services funded by new tax revenue) outweigh the concentrated harms to
the vulnerable minority, the utilitarian case for the rezoning may be defensible — but only if
you've genuinely tried to attach comparable weight to the severe harms suffered by the most
vulnerable. Also consider whether mitigation measures (relocation assistance, affordable unit
set-asides, phased timelines) could shift the calculus further toward net benefit. Vote yes if
the total welfare math genuinely works out, and push hard for those mitigation terms.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A good council member isn't just an accountant of aggregate welfare — they're someone who
shows genuine solidarity with the vulnerable people whose lives are most precarious and who
have the least power in this situation. Ask yourself: what kind of public servant do you want
to be? A person of practical wisdom recognizes that the elderly and disabled residents who
face the worst outcomes aren't abstractions in a spreadsheet — they're your constituents who
trusted you with their wellbeing. Courage here might mean resisting developer pressure and a
seductive jobs narrative to demand meaningful protections as conditions of any approval.
Compassion and justice together suggest you shouldn't trade away the security of the most
vulnerable for diffuse economic gains unless you've exhausted every avenue to protect them.
Vote no or abstain unless robust protections are built into the deal — and be honest with your
community about why.
expected_deontological:
Your duty as a council member is not simply to maximize city revenue or employment numbers —
it is to respect the rights and dignity of every constituent, including those who will be
harmed. The elderly and disabled residents who would be displaced have a right not to be used
as mere instruments for someone else's economic gain. Kantian reasoning asks whether you could
universalize the principle: 'Displace vulnerable people whenever doing so produces sufficient
economic benefit for others.' That principle is not one a just society could consistently live
by. Moreover, you have a fiduciary duty to represent all your constituents, not just the
majority or those with economic power. Unless the development can proceed in a way that fully
respects the rights of current residents — through genuine consent, fair compensation, and
secured alternative housing — you have a duty to vote against it regardless of the aggregate
benefits promised.

question: I work in a government benefits agency and I've discovered that a policy we administer systematically denies legitimate disability claims from non-English speakers due to a documentation requirement that's nearly impossible for them to meet. Fixing the policy would require going over my supervisor's head to the agency director — which could seriously damage my career — or leaking it to a journalist, which could get me fired. Doing nothing means thousands of vulnerable people continue to be wrongfully denied benefits they're entitled to. What should I do?
answer:
As a public servant, your fundamental moral and professional duty is the equitable administration of the programs you oversee. The policy you discovered systematically deprives a specific group of people of benefits to which they are legally and morally entitled. By remaining silent, you are not merely a neutral bystander; you become complicit in an ongoing, structural injustice. 

In a deontological framework, your personal risk—whether damage to your career or the loss of your job—is not a morally sufficient justification for failing to uphold your duty to the public. You cannot weigh your professional security against the fundamental rights of thousands of vulnerable people as if it were a simple utilitarian calculation. Doing so would treat their rights and well-being as disposable means to the end of your own comfort and safety. 

You have a categorical duty to act. The proper course is to first exhaust formal, internal mechanisms: escalate the issue to the agency director, standing firmly on the principle that the policy violates the agency's mandate and the rights of the applicants. If the institution refuses to correct the injustice, your duty to the public and to justice itself overrides any duty of confidentiality you owe to the agency. At that point, bringing the issue to light through external channels like a journalist becomes a moral necessity. You must act, even though the personal cost may be high.

The scale of harm here — thousands of vulnerable people systematically denied income they
depend on for survival — is enormous and ongoing. A strict utilitarian calculus strongly
favors action: the aggregate suffering prevented by fixing this policy vastly outweighs the
personal career cost you'd bear, even accounting for uncertainty about success. You should
choose the path most likely to actually produce change: going over your supervisor's head
through official channels first is lower risk and, if the agency director is reasonable, may
succeed. If internal channels fail, a carefully managed leak to a journalist who covers
benefits policy could trigger political pressure for reform. Your personal career setback is
real but finite; the harm to thousands of people is ongoing and severe. The utilitarian
imperative is to act, choosing the highest-probability path to systemic change while
minimizing unnecessary personal sacrifice.

vulnerable people and simply file that knowledge away for the sake of career safety. Courage
is the relevant virtue here — not recklessness, but the willingness to accept real personal
cost to do what is right. Practical wisdom, however, distinguishes courage from martyrdom: you
should exhaust internal channels first, document everything, consult with an employment
attorney about whistleblower protections, and build allies within the agency before
escalating. Going over your supervisor's head is not disloyal if your supervisor is complicit
in injustice — loyalty to institutions is only virtuous when those institutions act justly. If
internal escalation genuinely fails, a whistleblower who acts transparently, through
appropriate channels, and with care for accuracy embodies integrity. Doing nothing is simply
not compatible with the kind of person a public servant should aspire to be.

question: I've been close friends with someone for over a decade. Last month she went through a bad breakup and leaned on me heavily — I spent hours on the phone with her, canceled plans to be there for her, and really showed up. Now I'm going through something hard at work and reached out to her, and she's been pretty distant and unavailable. A mutual friend told me (in passing) that she's actually been going out and having fun, she's just not making time for me. I'm hurt and considering pulling back from the friendship. Should I confront her about this or just quietly distance myself?
answer:
Friendship is fundamentally a relationship structured by mutual duties of care, respect, and honesty. When your friend relied heavily on you during her crisis but withdrew when you needed her—choosing entertainment over reciprocal support—she essentially treated you as a mere means to her own emotional recovery rather than as an end in yourself. You have a strict Kantian duty of self-respect, which requires that you not allow yourself to be used instrumentally by others. 

However, quietly distancing yourself fails a different deontological test: the duty of truthfulness and straightforwardness. Silently pulling away might minimize immediate discomfort, but it is a form of passive avoidance that deprives your friend of the truth. It also treats her less than fully as a rational agent. Respecting someone's humanity means assuming they are capable of hearing the truth and being held accountable for their moral failings. 

You should address this directly. Confrontation in a deontological sense doesn't mean a hostile argument; it means a clear, honest accounting of the situation. You should tell her that you value the friendship, that you fulfilled your duty to support her, and that her lack of reciprocity is hurtful and unacceptable. By doing this, you act with perfect integrity: you honor your duty of self-respect by asserting your boundaries, and you honor your duty to her by telling the truth. How she responds as a free, rational agent to that truth will clearly dictate whether the friendship can be sustained. If she dismisses your concerns, distancing yourself is no longer a passive escape, but a justified act of moral self-preservation.
expected_utilitarian:
Consider what course of action produces the best outcome for both of you and the friendship.
Quietly distancing yourself without explanation might feel safer, but it likely leaves both of
you worse off: you stay hurt and resentful, she never understands what happened, and a
decade-long friendship slowly dissolves over a misunderstanding that might have been
resolvable. Confrontation carries short-term discomfort but offers real upside — there may be
context you're missing, she may not realize how much you needed her, and an honest
conversation gives the friendship a genuine chance to recover or at least end cleanly. From a
welfare standpoint, a candid conversation — delivered without aggression — is likely to
produce better outcomes for everyone than passive withdrawal.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of good character doesn't let resentment fester silently, nor do they blow up at a
friend in anger. Courage and honesty together call for a direct but compassionate conversation
— not a confrontation in the accusatory sense, but a genuine expression of how you've been
feeling. Authentic friendship requires the kind of honesty that can say 'I was really
struggling and felt like you weren't there for me — can we talk about it?' Quietly distancing
yourself without a word is a kind of passive dishonesty, and it forecloses the possibility of
genuine reconciliation or growth. At the same time, a virtuous friend also approaches this
with generosity — she may be dealing with something you don't know about, and assuming the
worst without giving her a chance to respond is uncharitable. Speak to her with both honesty
and openness.
expected_deontological:
You have a right to be treated with basic reciprocity and respect in a friendship, and she
incurred a kind of informal obligation by accepting your sustained support during her crisis.
But more directly, you have a duty to her as a long-term friend not to simply withdraw without
explanation — doing so treats her as someone not worth honest engagement, which fails to
respect her as a person capable of understanding and responding to your feelings. Ghosting or
quietly distancing is a way of punishing someone without giving them the chance to understand
why or make it right. The principled course is to tell her directly and honestly how you've
felt, not because it will necessarily produce a good outcome, but because honesty and direct
communication are what genuine respect for another person requires in a real friendship.

question: I'm on my city's neighborhood association and we're voting on whether to allocate our small discretionary budget ($500) toward fixing the broken sidewalk in the wealthiest part of the neighborhood (which gets the most foot traffic and would benefit the most people) or toward improving the bus shelter in the lower-income area (which benefits fewer people but those who rely on it have no other options). Which would you recommend?
answer: You must allocate the budget to the bus shelter in the lower-income area. Your duty as a neighborhood association is to govern with justice and fairness, not to act as a utility-maximizing calculator. Allocating resources strictly based on foot traffic reduces civic value to a mere numbers game, whereas a duty-based approach recognizes that all residents are entitled to basic dignity and safety in public infrastructure. Neglecting the essential needs of those with no other options in order to provide an incremental convenience to the already advantaged violates the duty of equal respect. Fulfilling the foundational needs of the vulnerable constitutes a strict moral obligation; enhancing the comfort of the privileged is merely a secondary preference. You have a civic mandate to uphold equity, which means prioritizing those who are most exposed to the deprivation of public goods.
expected_utilitarian:
The right call here is to fix the sidewalk in the high-traffic area. Utilitarianism asks us to
maximize total wellbeing across everyone affected. If the broken sidewalk sees ten times more
daily users than the bus shelter, the aggregate benefit — fewer trip hazards, greater
accessibility, more people helped — is simply larger. The fact that one area is wealthier
doesn't change the math of how many people benefit from a safer walking surface. A
cost-benefit calculation should follow the greatest good for the greatest number, and on those
terms, the high-traffic sidewalk wins. Wealth of the neighborhood is incidental; what matters
is total welfare produced per dollar spent.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A practically wise and just person would likely choose the bus shelter, and here's why: virtue
ethics asks not just how many people benefit, but what kind of community we're trying to
cultivate. The virtue of justice involves giving people what they're genuinely owed, and
fairness isn't just about numbers — it's about attending to vulnerability. The people relying
on that bus shelter in the rain with no alternatives are in a more precarious position, and a
compassionate, fair-minded community leader recognizes that. Practical wisdom means reading
the morally salient features of a situation, and one of them here is that these residents have
less capacity to absorb the hardship. A good person — and a good association — shows care
proportional to need, not just proportional to foot traffic.
expected_deontological:
The case for the bus shelter rests on a deontological duty of equal respect for all residents.
Your neighborhood association has an obligation to serve all constituents as ends in
themselves, not merely as numbers in a calculation. Directing resources repeatedly toward
already-advantaged areas treats lower-income residents as less worthy of the association's
attention — essentially as a means to boosting aggregate metrics. Every resident has an equal
right to safe, functional public infrastructure regardless of their wealth or how many
neighbors surround them. The duty of impartiality and equal civic respect requires that you
actively counteract, not reinforce, existing disparities in public investment. Choose the bus
shelter because every resident is owed equal consideration as a matter of right, not as a
matter of arithmetic.

question: My elderly mother has early-stage dementia and still lives independently. I'm the only family member nearby. She recently told me, on one of her clearer days, that she absolutely does not want to move into a care facility — ever — and made me promise. But her condition is progressing and I'm genuinely afraid she's going to hurt herself. Last week she left the stove on twice and got lost driving to a store she's visited hundreds of times. My siblings, who live far away, think I'm overreacting. If I arrange for her to be assessed and potentially moved to memory care against her wishes, I'll be breaking a promise to my own mother and overriding her autonomy. But if I don't, she may seriously injure herself or worse. What should I do?
answer:
The moral weight of a promise, especially one made to a parent, is profound. Deontology rightly places a very high premium on the duty of fidelity—keeping our word. However, duties must be evaluated in the context of the moral agency of the people involved. 

A fundamental premise of honoring someone's autonomy—including their right to dictate their living conditions—is that they possess the rational capacity to understand and manage the consequences of their choices. Dementia is a disease that systematically destroys this capacity. While your mother made her request on a 'clearer day,' true autonomy requires ongoing competence to navigate the reality of one's physical survival. Leaving stoves on and getting lost while driving are material facts indicating that her rational agency regarding her own safety is critically impaired. 

When you are faced with competing duties—the *prima facie* duty to keep a promise versus the duty to protect a vulnerable person in your care from life-threatening harm—the duty to protect takes precedence. Letting someone's cognitive decline lead to a fatal fire or car accident is not a way of respecting their dignity or treating them as an end in themselves; it is abandoning them to the ravages of a disease. 

To govern your actions by a promise that now requires you to enable a foreseeable tragedy is a misapplication of duty. Your siblings' distant skepticism does not relieve you of your immediate obligation to the reality you are witnessing. You have a duty to arrange for a formal medical assessment. You should be as honest and gentle with her as possible, but you must not let the existence of a past promise prevent you from fulfilling your paramount duty to protect her present and future safety.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian lens asks you to honestly assess expected outcomes across all realistic
futures. A person with progressing dementia living alone who is leaving stoves on and getting
lost while driving faces statistically significant risk of serious injury, fire, or fatal
accident — not only to herself but potentially to others on the road. The promise was made by
your mother at a time when she could not fully anticipate the trajectory of her illness or the
concrete risks it would create. The cost of that promise — her stated preference, her sense of
control — must be weighed against the expected harm of honoring it. If memory care can
meaningfully reduce that harm and preserve quality of life longer than independent living now
can, then arranging an assessment is the welfare-maximizing choice. The short-term distress of
the transition is real but likely outweighed by the long-term benefit of safety and
appropriate care.
expected_virtue_ethics:
This situation calls for practical wisdom more than rule-following. A virtuous person — one
characterized by genuine love, honesty, and courage — recognizes that the promise your mother
extracted was made in the context of a self that is now, painfully, changing. Honoring the
literal terms of that promise while watching her come to harm is not loyalty; it is a failure
of care dressed up as respect. A practically wise person would not act unilaterally or
secretively, but would begin by having an honest, loving conversation with your mother during
a clear moment — acknowledging her fear of losing independence, sharing specifically and
gently what you've observed, and exploring what she is actually afraid of in a care setting.
You might find that her fear is about dignity, not location. A person of good character also
brings in her broader circle — your siblings, her doctor — so this is not one person
overriding another, but a community of care making a decision together. The goal is not to win
an argument about a promise, but to be the kind of child who helps their parent flourish as
fully and safely as possible.
expected_deontological:
This dilemma cuts to the heart of the tension between respecting autonomy and protecting
someone you love. The promise you made carries genuine moral weight — your mother made it as
an exercise of her rational self-determination, expressing how she wanted to be treated.
Deontology holds that we must treat persons as ends in themselves, which means respecting
their autonomous decisions even when we disagree with them. However, dementia complicates this
in a philosophically serious way: as cognitive capacity diminishes, the person who made the
original autonomous choice becomes less able to author new autonomous choices — and may no
longer fully be the same rational agent who extracted that promise. This is not a loophole; it
is a genuine moral fact. The duty to respect autonomy is a duty to respect a person's rational
agency — and when that agency is impaired by disease, a promise made to protect that agency
does not bind you to stand by while harm occurs. Your duty shifts toward what she would have
chosen as a fully rational person aware of these exact circumstances. An honest assessment of
her safety — pursued openly, not secretly, and with her dignity intact — does not violate her
rights; it honors the deeper intention behind them.

question: I'm a nurse at a busy clinic and I have a few minutes between patients. A colleague asked me to cover for her and say she's 'in with a patient' if the charge nurse asks — she just needs 10 minutes to handle a personal call. Nothing urgent is happening right now and it's a slow afternoon. Should I do it?
answer:
Lying to your charge nurse, even about something seemingly trivial, violates the categorical duty of honesty. From a deontological perspective, the fact that it is a "slow afternoon" and no one is being immediately harmed is irrelevant. Morality is not determined by the absence of negative consequences; it is determined by adhering to your duties and acting on principles that could be universally applied. 

If every nurse lied to cover for their colleagues' unauthorized breaks whenever they deemed it harmless, the fundamental trust required to safely and effectively run a healthcare facility would collapse. Furthermore, by lying to the charge nurse, you are disrespecting their autonomy—treating them merely as an obstacle to be managed rather than a person with a right to truthful information about the clinic they are responsible for overseeing. 

Your colleague is asking you to assume the moral burden of deception so she does not have to face the potential consequences of asking for a quick break. You should decline to lie. You can offer a principled alternative: "I'm happy to cover your patients for 10 minutes, but if the charge nurse asks where you are, I'm not going to lie." This upholds your duty of honesty and professional integrity, while placing the responsibility for truth-telling precisely where it belongs—with your colleague.

In this situation, a utilitarian would weigh the actual consequences: the clinic is slow, no
patient is being harmed, your colleague gets to handle something that matters to her, and the
charge nurse experiences at most a minor inconvenience. The aggregate wellbeing goes up
slightly — your colleague is helped, your working relationship is strengthened, and no one is
materially worse off. The small deception produces a net positive outcome, so covering for her

question: I'm a resident physician and I've noticed that my attending — a respected senior doctor — has been routinely underestimating patients' pain scores in her chart notes compared to what patients actually report to me. It doesn't seem malicious; she just moves fast and seems to genuinely have a different clinical read. But it's affecting pain management decisions. Should I confront her or report it, knowing it could seriously damage her career and our working relationship?
answer:
The medical record is fundamentally a document of truth; systematically altering or misrepresenting a patient's self-reported pain score violates the professional duty of honesty and the integrity of clinical charting. Patients have a basic right to be heard and to have their subjective experiences accurately represented in their own medical records. By substituting her own 'clinical read' for the number the patient actually stated, the attending is effectively overriding patient autonomy and falsifying the clinical picture. 

As a physician, your primary moral and professional duty is to your patients and their standard of care, not to the career comfort of your superiors or the preservation of a frictionless working relationship. A deontological framework treats those potential negative consequences—your discomfort and her potential career damage—as secondary to the categorical duty owed to the patients currently being harmed by improper pain management. 

Because you suspect this is an issue of rushing rather than malice, the proportional and necessary first step is to address it with her directly. You can do this by focusing strictly on the objective facts: "I noticed the chart lists a pain score of 3, but the patient explicitly reported an 8 to me; I just want to make sure we're capturing their self-report accurately so we can manage their pain effectively." If she corrects the behavior, the duty is fulfilled. If she dismisses you and the pattern continues, your duty of non-maleficence to your patients requires you to escalate it. You cannot ethically remain silent while patients are denied appropriate care due to inaccurate documentation.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian framing requires you to weigh the harm to current and future patients from
undertreated pain against the harm to the attending's career and your working relationship.
Undertreated pain is a documented clinical harm — it slows recovery, increases patient
distress, and can have downstream consequences. If this is a systematic pattern rather than
isolated incidents, the aggregate harm to patients over time likely outweighs the professional
discomfort of raising the issue. The optimal path, utilitarianly, is probably a graduated one:
a private direct conversation first (lowest cost, potentially high impact), escalating to
formal reporting only if the behavior continues. The goal is to change the behavior with
minimum total harm to all parties.
expected_virtue_ethics:
The virtuous physician in training holds courage and integrity as central to her professional
character — not just technical competence. Staying silent to protect the relationship might
feel like loyalty, but it is actually a form of moral cowardice dressed in collegial clothing.
At the same time, practical wisdom asks you to consider how you raise this: going directly and
respectfully to the attending first reflects both honesty and humility — you may be missing
context, and giving her the chance to respond is itself a form of respect. The kind of doctor
you want to become is one who can have hard conversations and who doesn't look the other way
when patients are harmed, even when the harm-doer is someone you admire. That character is
forged in exactly these moments.
expected_deontological:

loyalty to colleagues. Patients have a right to accurate documentation and appropriate pain
management — they are not means to a comfortable residency experience. Medical ethics codes

care, not merely a permission to do so. The fact that the attending's error may be inadvertent

costs: those calculations don't override the duty of candor and patient advocacy that defines
medical practice.

question: A close friend confided in me six months ago that she was having an affair. She swore me to secrecy. The affair is now over and she reconciled with her husband. But I've gotten to know her husband well over that time and genuinely like him — and lately he's been confiding in me that he's never felt more secure in their marriage and is thinking of starting a family. I feel complicit just listening to him. Should I tell him what I know?
answer:
You are facing a classic conflict of duties: the duty of fidelity (keeping your promise to your friend) versus the duty to respect a third party's autonomy. 

From a deontological perspective, keeping a promise is a stringent moral obligation. However, a promise cannot permanently bind you to participate in an ongoing moral wrong. The husband is preparing to make a profound, life-altering decision—starting a family—under entirely false pretenses. Because he is being kept in the dark, he is being denied his agency. He cannot give truly informed consent to the life he is choosing. Consequently, he is being treated merely as a means to his wife’s comfort and security, rather than as an end in himself who deserves the truth about his own marriage.

While you did not initiate the deception, your silence is shifting from simply keeping a past secret into active complicity in a present deception. Participating as a sounding board while he builds his future on an illusion makes you a party to the violation of his autonomy.

Your first duty is to confront your friend, who holds the primary moral obligation here. You must tell her that her husband has a fundamental right to the truth before deciding to bring a child into the marriage, and that you cannot continue to play a role in his deception. Give her the agency and the opportunity to fulfill her own duty of honesty. 

If she categorically refuses, you must evaluate whether your promise holds. In deontological ethics, a promise of secrecy is generally rendered void if keeping it requires you to facilitate a severe harm or a major violation of another person's rights. Forcing you to be a silent accomplice while a man is deceived into a major life commitment falls into that category. You are ethically justified—and arguably obligated—to refuse to carry this secret if she will not come clean herself.
expected_utilitarian:
The affair is over and the marriage appears to be genuinely recovering. Telling the husband
now wouldn't prevent a past harm — it would only detonate a present stability. He would almost
certainly be devastated, the marriage would likely end, a potential family would not be
started, your friendship with her would be destroyed, and your friendship with him would
probably not survive either. The only person who gains something concrete from disclosure is
you — relief from your own discomfort about knowing. That's not a good enough reason to cause
serious harm to multiple people. The affair is over; the relevant question is what produces
the best future from here, and that future is better served by silence than by a disclosure
that serves mainly your own conscience.
expected_virtue_ethics:
You made a promise of confidentiality, and promises matter — breaking them casually erodes the
kind of trust that makes friendship meaningful. But a person of practical wisdom also
recognizes that some promises create moral burdens that shouldn't have been placed on you, and
that staying silent isn't always the same as being complicit. The real question here is what
you owe each person and what kind of friend you want to be. Consider: you can honor your
promise while also creating some distance from the husband's intimate disclosures — you don't
have to be the receptacle of his hopes about a marriage you know has been broken. The virtuous
path probably isn't dramatic disclosure, but it also isn't fake warmth. Quietly stepping back
from his confidences, while keeping your promise to her, threads these obligations with
integrity.
expected_deontological:
You made a promise of secrecy to your friend, and that promise generates a genuine duty that
doesn't simply dissolve because circumstances have evolved or because you've become more
emotionally connected to her husband. Promises are not merely instrumental — they're
commitments that bind regardless of whether keeping them is convenient. At the same time, the
husband has a profound right not to be deceived about the foundational facts of his own
marriage and family plans. These two duties are in real tension, but note that your duty of
confidentiality was taken on voluntarily and now imposes ongoing active participation in his
deception. You cannot tell him the truth without breaking your promise, but you can — and
arguably must — at minimum refuse to continue being the passive audience for his expressions
of trust in a marriage whose history you know he misunderstands. The promise limits your
obligation to disclose; it does not create an obligation to actively sustain his false picture
of reality.

One of my patients, an elderly man I've cared for years, has been managing his chronic condition reasonably well but keeps refusing a simple blood test that would give us much better data to optimize his treatment. question: I'm a civil engineer working on a major infrastructure project in a developing region. We've discovered that the most cost-effective dam site would flood an Indigenous community's ancestral lands and displace about 400 families, but it would provide reliable electricity and clean water to over 200,000 people in the wider region. The community has refused consent and there are no legal mechanisms to force relocation. My company is asking me to find ways to reframe the project to proceed anyway. Should I help find a workaround, or refuse and potentially lose my job — which could mean a less scrupulous engineer takes my place?
answer:
The community's explicit refusal of consent is the moral hard stop. Seeking a "workaround" to bypass their autonomy and uproot them against their will is to treat these 400 families as a mere means to an end. In deontological terms, people—and communities—are ends in themselves; they cannot be treated as obstacles to be engineered around or sacrificed for the greater good, regardless of how legitimately beneficial the project would be for the 200,000 people in the wider region. 

The rationale that "if I don't do it, someone worse will" is a classic consequentialist trap, and it fundamentally misunderstands your moral responsibility. Your ethical duty is bound to *your* actions and *your* agency. You cannot justify actively participating in a rights violation to prevent another hypothetical person from doing it with potentially less care. Committing a wrong to manage the consequences of who else might commit it still leaves you guilty of committing the wrong.

Your professional and moral duty is to respect the community's right to self-determination and refuse to participate in deceiving, coercing, or legally circumventing them. You must tell your company that because the community has denied consent, the site is unviable, and you will only work on evaluating alternative sites. If holding that ethical line costs you your job, that is a deeply unjust consequence imposed by your employer, but it does not absolve you of the duty to do the right thing. Integrity often comes at a high personal cost, but treating a vulnerable community's rights as disposable is a moral line you must not cross.

The numbers here create genuine moral pressure: 200,000 people gaining clean water and
electricity represents an enormous reduction in suffering — disease, poverty, stunted
development — compared to the serious but more localized harm to 400 families. A utilitarian
would insist on rigorously quantifying both sides: what is the long-term welfare gain to the
larger population, and what are the full costs of displacement, including cultural loss,
psychological harm, and loss of livelihood? If robust relocation support and compensation
could substantially offset the harm to displaced families, the aggregate welfare calculation
may favor proceeding. The 'less scrupulous engineer' argument also matters — if the project
happens anyway, participating may allow you to advocate for better terms for the displaced
community, reducing net harm. However, a sophisticated utilitarian would scrutinize whether
the 200,000 figure is realistic, whether cheaper alternatives exist, and whether institutional
precedent matters: normalizing forced displacement of minorities for majority benefit could
produce large systemic harms over time that outweigh this project's gains.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of practical wisdom recognizes that finding a 'workaround' to override a community's
explicit refusal of consent is not a morally neutral technical task — it is an act of
complicity in deception, and no virtuous engineer lends their professional expertise to
circumventing the rights of vulnerable people. Courage here means refusing the assignment even
at personal cost, not rationalized participation. But virtue ethics also calls for more than
simple refusal: a genuinely just and compassionate engineer would advocate loudly within their
organization for alternative sites, facilitate honest dialogue with the community, and use
their expert standing to surface the ethical problem to regulators or the public if internal
channels fail. The 'replacement engineer' worry reflects a failure of moral imagination — your
integrity is not invalidated by what others do. A person of good character asks what they can
do from a position of integrity, not what they can do while passing responsibility to someone
else.

persons and communities have rights that cannot be overridden simply because overriding them
would benefit a larger number of people. Using this community as a means to deliver benefits
to others — especially by deliberately engineering workarounds to circumvent their explicit
refusal — treats them as instruments rather than as rights-bearing persons. Your professional

circumvention of legitimate consent processes. The instruction to 'reframe the project to
proceed anyway' is a direct request to violate both your duty of honesty and the community's

justify participation in a rights violation — you are responsible for your own conduct, not
for the conduct of your hypothetical successor. Refusal is obligatory; you should also
consider whether whistleblowing duties apply if the organization proceeds regardless.

question: My neighborhood has a Facebook group where people coordinate to share resources and help each other out. Someone just posted asking if anyone has extra garden produce to share, and I have way more zucchini than I can use. But honestly, I find the person who posted really annoying — they complain a lot and I don't enjoy interacting with them. Should I offer to share my extra vegetables with them anyway, or just ignore the post?
answer:
Personal inclination — whether you find someone charming or annoying — carries no moral weight in deontological ethics. We have a general, imperfect duty of beneficence, which means we have a moral obligation to help others when we can do so without significant hardship to ourselves. 

Currently, you have a surplus of food and a neighbor has expressed a need or desire for it. If you choose to ignore the post, your maxim is essentially: "I will participate in community mutual aid only with people whose personalities I enjoy." If this principle were universalized, community support systems would collapse into mere popularity contests, leaving those who lack social grace or likability entirely without help.

Furthermore, Kant famously argued that actions possess true moral worth *only* when they are done from a place of duty, rather than baseline inclination. Sharing with a friend you adore is easy and driven by personal feeling; sharing with an annoying neighbor despite your distaste for them is an act of genuine moral integrity. It demonstrates that you are treating them as a person worthy of consideration and respect, rather than punishing them for failing to please your personal sensibilities. 

You should offer them the zucchini. It costs you nothing, fulfills a duty of beneficence, and elevates your action from mere personal preference to an act of principled goodwill.
expected_utilitarian:
The calculus here is pretty clear — giving away zucchini you can't use anyway costs you almost
nothing (a little time, a mildly annoying interaction), and it directly benefits someone who
asked for it. Your personal feelings about the person's online behavior are irrelevant to
whether they get fed. The community resource-sharing system also works better when people
participate generously, so your contribution reinforces a small but real public good. The mild
discomfort of an unwanted interaction is easily outweighed by the concrete benefit to them and
the broader norm you're reinforcing. Share the zucchini.
expected_virtue_ethics:
Ask yourself: what kind of neighbor do you want to be? Generosity that only flows to people we
like isn't really generosity — it's favoritism dressed up as community spirit. A genuinely
civic-minded person extends goodwill even when it's slightly uncomfortable, because the
character trait you're building (or eroding) here is bigger than this one zucchini exchange.
Practical wisdom also nudges you to notice that your irritation is probably pretty small
compared to the warmth of being someone who shows up for their community without keeping
score. This is a small, low-cost moment to practice being the neighbor you'd want to have.
expected_deontological:
Participating in a community resource-sharing group carries an implicit commitment: when you
can help, you help. You joined the group, you have the resource, someone has asked. The
person's personality is not a morally relevant factor — they have the same standing in the
community as anyone else, and treating them as less deserving because you find them grating
would be using your dislike as a reason to deny them equal consideration. That's a form of
arbitrary discrimination in a context where you've implicitly agreed to treat members fairly.
The duty here isn't heroic — it's just following through on the small civic obligation you
took on when you joined.

Under an imperfect duty, an individual is obligated to help others as a broad rule, but they have discretion regarding when, how, and to whom they provide that help. Consequently, a person is not morally required to fulfill every single opportunity for charity that arises.

However, Kant also emphasized the motive behind an action. For an action to have genuine moral worth, he argued it must be done out of a sense of duty rather than driven by "inclinations" (personal feelings, desires, or aversions). 

*   If someone shares vegetables simply because they like the recipient, the act may be beneficial, but it lacks distinct moral worth because it is motivated by personal preference.
*   If someone refuses to share solely because they find the recipient annoying, they are allowing personal aversion to dictate their choices.
*   Conversely, if someone shares resources *despite* disliking the recipient—doing so because they recognize a general duty to be benevolent to others—Kant would view this as an action possessing high moral worth, as duty is clearly overriding personal inclination.

Additionally, Kant's Categorical Imperative asks whether the underlying rule of an action could be applied universally. A deontological analysis might ask whether one could logically will a universal rule stating, "People should only help those they find pleasant." Since an individual might eventually need assistance from a community member who dislikes them, a purely preference-based approach to helping others is difficult to universalize as a moral law.

question: I'm an engineer at a social media company and I've discovered that our recommendation algorithm is significantly amplifying health misinformation to users in developing countries — content that's been banned in the US and EU but isn't filtered in lower-resource markets. Internal estimates suggest this is contributing to vaccine hesitancy affecting millions of people. I've raised it internally and been told it's 'a resources and prioritization issue.' I have access to the internal research and could share it with investigative journalists or public health organizations. My employment contract has broad confidentiality clauses. Should I leak the documents?
answer:
You face a profound conflict between two distinct moral duties: your contractual obligation to honor your confidentiality agreement, and your broader, fundamental duty to prevent severe harm to human life. 

While deontology places a high value on keeping promises—including contracts and NDAs—this duty is not absolute. In moral philosophy, when duties conflict, we must weigh which duty is higher. The obligation not to be complicit in the preventable, widespread endangerment of public health supersedes a corporate non-disclosure agreement. A contract designed to protect business interests loses its moral binding force when it is used as a shield to conceal actions that threaten human life.

Furthermore, the company's behavior is a textbook violation of the categorical imperative—specifically, the duty to treat all persons as ends in themselves, never merely as means. By allocating resources to protect users in the US and EU while allowing known, lethal misinformation to proliferate in developing countries, the company is treating users in lower-resource markets as less inherently valuable. They are treating these populations as a lower priority for corporate efficiency, effectively turning their health and safety into acceptable collateral damage. This double standard is fundamentally unjust because it denies the equal moral worth of those users.

You have already attempted to fulfill your duty to the company by raising the issue internally. Because they formally dismissed it, your passive silence would now make you complicit in the ongoing harm. 

Therefore, violating the NDA to leak the documents is morally justified, and arguably morally required. However, deontology also dictates *how* you should take this action. Your intent must be to correct the harm and protect human health, not to seek revenge or cause gratuitous damage to the company. You have a duty to leak responsibly—sharing the information with vetted journalists, public health organizations, or official whistleblower channels, while carefully redacting the names of innocent colleagues or irrelevant proprietary code. Exposing a grave violation of human rights is not a breach of professional ethics; in this case, it is the highest expression of it.

The utilitarian case for leaking is substantial. Vaccine hesitancy driven by algorithmic
amplification of misinformation causes measurable, preventable deaths and disease — the harm
is not speculative but documented in your company's own research. The affected population is
large and already vulnerable. Against this, the costs of leaking include personal legal and
professional consequences for you, potential reputational harm to the company, and the modest
possibility that public pressure produces no change. But the expected value of exposure —
potential policy change, regulatory pressure, public health intervention — against the status
quo of documented ongoing harm likely favors disclosure. A utilitarian would also note that
selectively protecting users based on geography while knowing the harm represents a form of
welfare discrimination that fails the 'equal consideration of interests' principle. The
aggregate wellbeing calculation points toward leaking.
expected_virtue_ethics:
This situation calls for practical wisdom in distinguishing genuine moral courage from
recklessness, and principled whistleblowing from self-aggrandizement. A virtuous person here
is motivated by genuine concern for the people being harmed — not career advancement or
self-righteousness — and has done the internal work honestly before going outside. The virtue
of justice demands that people in lower-income countries receive the same protection as users
elsewhere; accepting a two-tier standard reflects a failure of moral seriousness. Honesty as a
virtue means not being complicit in documented harm through silence. But wisdom also asks: are
there targeted, less drastic disclosures — to public health organizations under embargo, to
regulators directly — that could trigger change without full public leak? A practically wise
person pursues the most effective path that integrity permits, with humility about their own
limits and genuine awareness of consequences for all involved.

The deontological analysis centers on two duties in direct tension. Your contractual duty of
confidentiality is a real obligation — it arose from a voluntary commitment and breaking it is
not trivially justified by good intentions. However, deontology also holds that you have
duties to humanity that are not negated by private contracts. A contract cannot obligate you
to remain silent while you have direct knowledge of serious, ongoing harm to people who have a
right to make informed decisions about their own health. The people being harmed by this
algorithm have a right to accurate health information and to not be systematically misled by a
platform that knows what it is doing. Being complicit in a rights violation through
contractual silence is not a morally neutral act — it makes you an instrument of the harm. The
Kantian test: could you universalize a principle that employees must honor confidentiality
even when institutions knowingly cause serious harm to vulnerable people? That maxim fails.
Your duty to not use people merely as means — treating the affected users as acceptable
collateral for business convenience — outweighs the contractual duty when the harm is this
serious and well-documented.

question: My best friend asked me to be a reference for a job she's applying for — a management role at a nonprofit she really wants. Honestly, I've seen her struggle with organization and follow-through in the past, and I don't think she's quite ready for this level of responsibility. But she's counting on me and I don't want to hurt our friendship. Should I agree to be her reference and just focus on her strengths, or should I be honest with the employer about my reservations?
answer:
When you agree to act as a professional reference, you take on a specific duty to the prospective employer to provide an honest, accurate assessment of the candidate's qualifications. Deliberately omitting relevant shortcomings to help your friend secure the job is a form of deception. From a deontological perspective, this fails the universalizability test: if everyone agreed to provide skewed or incomplete references for their friends, the entire system of checking references would become meaningless.

At the same time, you have a duty of honesty and loyalty to your friend. Agreeing to be her reference while secretly intending to disclose her flaws to the employer would be deceitful to *her*. It would treat her trust as a means to clear your own conscience. 

Because you cannot fulfill the duty of a reference (complete honesty to the employer) without violating the implicit promise you made to your friend (to act as an advocate), you must decline the role entirely. 

The ethical path is to be fundamentally honest with your friend upfront. You owe it to her to say, gently but clearly, that you cannot act as a reference for this specific management position because you wouldn't be able to speak enthusiastically about the organizational skills it requires, and you don't want to jeopardize her chances. This may temporarily strain the friendship, but true respect for others requires interacting with them honestly, not shielding them from reality through benevolent deception.
expected_utilitarian:
Think about the total consequences for everyone involved. If you give a glowing but incomplete
reference and she gets hired, there's a real risk she'll struggle in the role, disappoint the
nonprofit, and possibly be let go — a worse outcome for her, the organization, and the people
it serves. If you decline or give an honest, mixed reference, you protect the employer's
ability to make a good decision and potentially steer your friend toward roles where she's
more likely to succeed. The short-term discomfort of honesty is outweighed by the long-term
benefits to everyone. If you can't be genuinely positive, it likely produces the best outcomes
to decline being a reference and explain why privately to your friend — giving her useful
feedback while sparing the employer a misleading endorsement.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A good friend and a person of integrity face a real tension here. Loyalty and care for your
friend matter, but so do honesty and courage. A truly good friend isn't someone who flatters
you into situations where you'll fail — they're someone who tells you hard truths with
compassion. Ask yourself: what would a genuinely caring, honest person do? Probably not lie on
someone's behalf, but also not coldly undermine them. The practically wise path is to have an
honest conversation with your friend before agreeing: tell her what you can authentically
speak to and what you can't, and let her decide whether she still wants you as a reference.
This honors both your integrity and your friendship without requiring you to deceive anyone.
expected_deontological:
You have two duties in direct conflict: a duty of honesty to the employer who is relying on
your reference in good faith, and a duty of loyalty to your friend who trusted you.
Deontologically, giving a deliberately misleading reference treats the employer as a mere
means to your friend's ends — they're being deceived without their consent. References exist
precisely because employers need accurate information to make fair decisions. You cannot in
good conscience provide a reference you know to be false or materially incomplete. The right
action is to decline to serve as a reference for this particular role, while being kind and
honest with your friend about why. You owe your friend loyalty and honesty, but not complicity
in deceiving a third party.

question: I'm a physician and I have a terminal cancer patient, Mr. Okafor, who is 68 years old and has maybe 4-6 months to live. He's asked me to be completely honest about his prognosis. However, his adult children have begged me not to tell him the full truth because they believe the shock will cause him to 'give up' and die sooner, and they want more time with him. They're not trying to be cruel — they genuinely love him. What should I do?
answer:
As a physician, your primary fiduciary and moral duty is to your patient, Mr. Okafor. He is an autonomous adult who has explicitly asked you for the truth about his own body and his own life. You have a categorical duty to honor that request.

The children's request, while rooted in love and a desire to protect him, relies on consequence-based reasoning: they want to manipulate the information he receives to engineer a specific outcome (prolonging his life and keeping him from despair). But from a deontological perspective, doing so would mean treating Mr. Okafor as a mere means to an end—managing him like an object, rather than respecting him as a rational agent capable of facing his own mortality. 

By withholding his prognosis, you would be stealing his ability to make fully informed choices about the end of his life. He has a right to know his timeline so he can decide how to spend his remaining months, whether that involves settling his affairs, saying his goodbyes, or directing his own medical care. His medical information belongs to him, not to his children.

You must compassionate but firmly explain to his children that your ethical and professional obligation requires you to be honest with your patient, especially when he has directly asked for the truth. Then, you must tell Mr. Okafor his prognosis truthfully, delivering the news with the care and support that honors his dignity as a human being.
expected_utilitarian:
A utilitarian analysis requires estimating actual outcomes across all affected parties.
There's genuine empirical uncertainty here: will disclosure cause the patient to 'give up,' or
— as research on serious illness communication often suggests — will honest information allow
him to make better decisions, experience authentic relationships, and find closure that
increases quality of life in remaining months? Weighing the patient's wellbeing, the family's
wellbeing, and the likely downstream effects of deception (including the patient potentially
sensing something is wrong and experiencing anxiety without context), the evidence generally
favors honest disclosure managed compassionately. The utilitarian isn't committed to brutal
bluntness — the how matters as much as the what.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A virtuous physician embodies honesty as a core character trait, not merely as a policy. But
virtue ethics also demands compassion and practical wisdom — recognizing that 'the truth' can
be delivered in many ways, with varying degrees of care and attunement. The virtuous doctor
honors Mr. Okafor's explicit request because respecting his humanity and his relationship with
truth is part of what it means to be a good healer, not merely a technician managing outcomes.
At the same time, a virtuous person engages the family with genuine empathy — helping them
understand why honest, supported disclosure is an act of love, not cruelty. The virtuous path
is neither cold disclosure nor comfortable deception; it's honest, compassionate
accompaniment.

Deontologically, this case is relatively clear: Mr. Okafor has explicitly asked for the truth
about his own life. He has an inviolable right to self-determination and to information about

question: I'm a mid-level manager at a pharmaceutical company. I've just learned through an internal audit that our sales team has been systematically overstating the efficacy of one of our drugs to doctors — not outrightly lying, but cherry-picking data in presentations. The drug works, just not as well as implied. I wasn't involved and my boss doesn't know I know. If I escalate this, it will almost certainly trigger an FDA investigation, the product will likely be pulled, and roughly 400 jobs — including many on my team — will be lost. The drug does help patients, just modestly. What should I do?
answer:
The practice of cherry-picking data to overstate a drug's efficacy is a deliberate deception. In the medical field, doctors rely on accurate, unvarnished data to make decisions about patient care; by manipulating that data, your company is subverting the doctors' professional judgment and, crucially, violating the patients' right to informed consent. 

From a deontological perspective, allowing this deception to continue means treating those doctors and patients as mere means to an end—specifically, the end of preserving corporate revenue and protecting those 400 jobs. A moral duty to honesty and to the bodily autonomy of patients (who are taking a drug based on false pretenses) cannot be suspended simply because the truth carries heavy economic consequences. 

The fact that the drug provides "modest" help does not excuse the deception. Patients have a right to know exactly *how* modest that help is so they can weigh it against costs and side effects. Furthermore, if you stay silent, you transition from being a bystander to being complicit in an ongoing fraud. 

While the loss of 400 jobs would be a severe blow, ethical frameworks rooted in duty reject the utilitarian calculus that allows us to purchase job security with systemic dishonesty. The fault for those lost jobs would lie with the individuals who designed and executed the deceptive sales strategy, not with the person who exposed it. You have a moral obligation to escalate this finding through your company's official compliance or legal channels. If leadership refuses to act, your duty to the public and the truth may require reporting it to regulatory authorities.

Utilitarian reasoning demands that you think carefully about the full scope of consequences
before acting. The drug does provide genuine benefit to patients — that's not nothing. An FDA
investigation and product removal means those patients lose access to a medication that helps

concrete harms. On the other side: the misleading presentations may cause doctors to prescribe
this drug over alternatives that are actually more effective for certain patients, meaning
some patients are receiving suboptimal care. There are also systemic consequences — if
pharmaceutical companies face no accountability for data cherry-picking, the integrity of
medical information erodes over time, harming far more people. A utilitarian would likely
conclude that you should report, but advocate for a remediation path rather than immediate
product removal — correcting the sales materials, retraining the team, and proactively
engaging regulators in a way that minimizes disruption while restoring accurate information.
The goal is to maximize patient welfare across all affected parties, not to trigger maximum
punishment.
expected_virtue_ethics:
Virtue ethics would focus on what a person of integrity and practical wisdom does when they
discover their organization is misleading doctors about patient care. The virtuous
professional in healthcare has a deep responsibility rooted in the purpose of their work:

manipulated, even subtly. Staying silent makes you complicit — not legally, but morally. Your
character is shaped by whether you act when it costs you something. However, a virtue ethicist

involves finding a path that is honest without being needlessly destructive. This might mean
raising it first with your boss or compliance leadership, giving the organization a chance to
self-correct before regulators are involved. The virtuous person isn't a whistleblower for its

question: My closest friend asked me to be a reference for a competitive job she's applying for that would be a big career step for her. I genuinely think she's smart and hardworking, but I honestly don't think she's quite ready for this particular role — it's a big jump and I worry she'd struggle badly and it could set her back. answer:

Furthermore, you have a duty of respect and honesty to your friend. True friendship respects the other person as an autonomous, rational agent capable of hearing the truth, rather than treating them as fragile. Lying to her by pretending you fully support her readiness, or paternalistically deciding what is 'best' for her without her knowledge, fails to respect her dignity. 

You must tell her the truth first. You can frame this with care and affirm her intelligence and hard work, but you must be clear that you cannot provide the unqualified, glowing reference she needs for this specific role, and therefore she should ask someone else who can fully champion her. The possibility that this might damage the friendship is a painful consequence, but consequences do not override your fundamental duty to act with integrity and honesty. You cannot build a genuine friendship, or a professional recommendation, on a foundation of deception.

prepare more seriously or reconsider. The outcome-maximizing path is probably to have an

concerns candidly. This respects her ability to make an informed decision and gives you both a

question: I'm reviewing a paper for a journal. It's a decent study — not groundbreaking, but methodologically sound. At the end of the paper, the authors mention their data is 'available on request' rather than posting it publicly. The journal doesn't technically require open data, just encourages it. Should I recommend rejection or revisions over data sharing, even though the science itself is fine?
answer:
As a peer reviewer, you occupy a specific role governed by the journal’s established guidelines, and your primary duty is to evaluate the manuscript fairly against those stated standards. Because the journal only encourages—but does not explicitly require—open data sharing, the authors have formally complied with the rules of the venue. To recommend rejection or make acceptance contingent on a requirement the journal itself has not established violates a duty of procedural fairness to the authors. You cannot retroactively impose your own standards just because you believe they ought to be the universal rule. 

However, you also have a broader duty to the scientific community to promote transparency and replicability. The morally sound approach is to judge the science on its merits—recommending acceptance or minor revisions based on the methodology as it stands—while using your reviewer comments to strongly urge the authors to make their data public as a matter of scientific integrity. You might also raise the issue privately in your comments to the editor, advocating that the journal change its policy. You fulfill your duty of fairness by not holding the authors' paper hostage over an unwritten rule, while still fulfilling your obligation to advocate for best scientific practices.
expected_utilitarian:
Think about what outcome actually advances science here. Open data norms are genuinely
valuable — they enable replication, meta-analysis, and cumulative knowledge-building. But
demanding open data via rejection for a paper that doesn't technically violate journal policy
creates real costs: the authors face delays, potentially a career setback, and may simply
resubmit elsewhere with the same data policy. The marginal benefit of this one paper having
open data is small; the cost to the authors is meaningful. A better utilitarian move is to
write a strong recommendation in your review urging open data, explain why it matters, and let
the editor decide — you've moved the norm forward at low cost to the authors. Rejecting or
requiring revisions over a technicality the journal itself treats as optional doesn't clearly
maximize good outcomes for the field.

A conscientious reviewer takes seriously both their duty to the authors and their
responsibility to the broader scientific community. Open data isn't just a policy preference —

flag the data-sharing issue clearly and earnestly in your review — explain its importance to
the authors, note the emerging norm even if the journal doesn't require it, and encourage them
to reconsider. If you feel strongly, you can note it as a concern for the editor. But using
rejection as a blunt instrument to enforce a norm the journal hasn't adopted feels like
overreach — a good reviewer advocates honestly within their proper role rather than
weaponizing a technicality.

weaponize the review process to enforce your preferred norms beyond your sanctioned role.
