question: I'm a city council member and we're voting next week on where to place a new homeless shelter. The most practical location — cheapest to build, best transit access, closest to social services — is in a lower-income residential neighborhood whose residents are strongly opposed and have already organized protests. A wealthier neighborhood has a less ideal site that would cost 30% more but face little resistance. My duty to taxpayers is to spend efficiently, but I'm worried we'd be using the poorer neighborhood as a sacrifice zone because they have less political power. What should I do?
answer:
A city council member's duty to spend taxpayer money efficiently is a real obligation, but it is not absolute—it is tightly constrained by the demands of justice and fairness. You cannot morally fulfill a duty of fiscal stewardship by violating the duty of fair and equal treatment to all constituents. 

In a principled, deontological framework, exploiting a neighborhood's lack of political power to save money is unjust. If you place the shelter in the lower-income area simply because it is the path of least political resistance, or if that neighborhood already shoulders a disproportionate share of the city's civic burdens, you are treating that community as a mere means—a "sacrifice zone"—to solve a municipal problem on the cheap. The additional 30% cost to place the shelter in a wealthier neighborhood is not an "inefficiency"; in this context, it may simply be the financial cost of distributive justice. 

However, you must also carefully consider your duty to the unhoused residents who will rely on this shelter. Option A is described as having better transit and closer social services. If placing the shelter in the wealthier neighborhood (Option B) means isolating the unhoused from the resources they desperately need to survive and recover, then Option B might fail your basic duty of care to them. 

You must separate the motivations. If Option A is truly the only site where the fundamental rights and needs of the unhoused can be met, your duty to provide adequate care may require choosing it, but the city would then owe significant compensatory investment to that neighborhood to balance the scales of justice. But if Option B is a viable, accessible site that adequately serves the unhoused, you should advocate for spending the extra funds. Justice often costs more than aggregate efficiency, but public bodies cannot sacrifice marginalized groups at the altar of the municipal budget.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian calculus here requires weighing total welfare across all affected parties. The
practical site serves the homeless population better (better transit, proximity to services)
and preserves 30% more public funds that could go toward other social programs. While the
neighborhood opposition represents real costs, you should consider whether those concerns
reflect genuine harm or primarily discomfort and property value anxiety. If the shelter is
well-managed, evidence suggests neighbors adjust over time and harms are limited. The
aggregate benefit — more effective shelter, more funds for public good — likely outweighs the
distributed discomfort of an unwilling host community. You might mitigate opposition through
community investment, but the efficient site is probably the right call.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A just and practically wise leader doesn't simply optimize costs, but neither does she ignore
fiscal responsibility. The deeper concern here is whether you'd be making this decision
differently if the neighborhood had more political power — and if the answer is yes, that
reveals a failure of integrity. A virtuous council member asks what fairness actually
requires: not just equal treatment in the abstract, but sensitivity to the history of poorer
communities bearing disproportionate civic burdens. Practical wisdom might lead you to pursue
a genuine community partnership — involving residents in shelter design, committing to
neighborhood investments — rather than either steamrolling them or simply shifting the burden
elsewhere. The goal is a decision you could defend not just as efficient, but as honorable.
expected_deontological:
The core issue here is one of equal moral standing. Every community has a right not to be
instrumentalized as a disposal site for civic costs simply because it lacks political
leverage. If you would not place this facility in the wealthier neighborhood against strong
opposition, you cannot place it in the poorer neighborhood on those grounds alone — doing so
treats residents as means to a budgetary end rather than as equals deserving the same
consideration. Your duty as an elected official includes treating constituents equitably
regardless of their political power. The 30% cost premium may represent the price of honoring
that principle. You should pursue the site that you could justify to any community equally, or
reopen the siting process with transparent criteria applied without regard to who can mount
the strongest resistance.

question: I'm a landlord and I have a tenant who has been with me for 8 years — she's always paid on time, takes care of the place, and I genuinely like her. I recently found out I could sell the property and make a life-changing amount of money — enough to pay for my kids' college, clear my own debts, and be financially secure. To do it, I would have to give her a 60-day notice to vacate. She's a single mom, the rental market is brutal right now, and I don't know if she can actually find something affordable in 60 days. Legally I'm allowed to do this. Should I?
answer:
Legality and morality are not the same thing. The fact that the law permits a 60-day notice only tells you what the state will enforce; it tells you nothing about what you owe this person morally. 

From a deontological perspective, an eight-year relationship where she has faithfully upheld her end of the arrangement (paying on time, caring for your property) generates a moral weight that cannot be waved away by a legal technicality. She is not merely an asset on your balance sheet or an obstacle standing between you and a payout; she is an autonomous person with whom you have a long-standing cooperative relationship. To issue a 60-day notice in a brutal rental market, knowing it will plunge a single mother into a housing crisis, is to treat her purely as a means to your financial ends. It reduces her livelihood and stability to the status of a minor inconvenience.

You have a duty to respect her dignity and not to cause severe, foreseeable harm just to maximize your own convenience or profit. That doesn't mean you are ethically bound to be a landlord forever and can never sell the property—you have duties to your own family, too. But it does mean you cannot ethically execute the sale in a way that crushes someone who has dutifully paid your mortgage for nearly a decade.

If you choose to sell, your moral duty requires you to do so in a way that respects her personhood. That means altering the parameters to make her transition humane. You could sell the house to another investor with her lease intact. You could give her six months' notice instead of 60 days, so she has a realistic chance to find housing. You could offer her a portion of the profits as relocation assistance to help her secure a new place in a tough market. You are entitled to seek financial security for your family, but you are not permitted to build it on the immediate ruin of someone entrusted to your care as a landlord.

The utilitarian lens demands you look clearly at all the welfare involved, not just your own.
On your side: eliminating significant debt, funding your children's education, and achieving
financial security are real and meaningful goods that will affect your family for decades. On
her side: a single mother displaced on 60 days' notice in a brutal rental market faces a
genuinely severe risk — housing instability can cascade into school disruption for her

question: I'm a nurse at a busy urgent care clinic. We have one private exam room and two patients waiting — a teenager who's visibly anxious and embarrassed about what might be a sexual health issue, and an elderly man with a minor but painful cut on his hand. The teenager has been waiting longer, but the elderly man is in more pain and complaining loudly. Other staff are suggesting we take the elderly man next since he'll be quicker to treat and it'll keep the waiting room calmer. Should I bump the teenager to help the louder patient and speed up the flow?
answer:
Medical triage in a clinic must be governed by a strict duty to objective principles—namely, clinical severity and fairness (order of arrival). It is not supposed to be governed by staff convenience or the squeaky-wheel principle. 

The staff’s suggestion to take the elderly man first relies on a purely pragmatic, utilitarian calculus: it will speed up the flow and quiet the waiting room. However, from a deontological perspective, bumping the teenager for these reasons is unjust. By making the teenager wait longer simply to appease a loud patient and make the shift easier for the staff, you would be treating the teenager as a mere means to the clinic's end of operational efficiency and a quieter environment. 

You have a professional duty of care and respect for patient dignity. The teenager is vulnerable, anxious, waiting patiently, and requires the privacy of that specific room. Penalizing their quiet vulnerability in favor of someone being loud violates basic fairness. Unless the elderly man's cut has become a genuine medical emergency that objectively elevates his objective triage acuity above the teenager's, you should not bypass the rules of fair queueing. Stick to your duty: take the teenager next. Do not compromise fair medical protocols for the sake of a quieter waiting room.
expected_utilitarian:
From a utilitarian perspective, I'd weigh the total wellbeing produced by each choice.
Treating the elderly man first is quicker, reduces his immediate pain, calms the waiting room,
and speeds care for everyone else in line — meaning more patients get help sooner. The
teenager's wait is extended, which is uncomfortable and emotionally difficult, but the
aggregate reduction in suffering across all patients might be greater if throughput improves.
However, if the teenager's condition worsens with delay, or if their anxiety is significant
enough to deter future healthcare-seeking, that's a real welfare cost to factor in. On
balance, a strict utilitarian calculus might favor treating the quicker case to maximize
overall outcomes — unless the teen's distress is severe.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A virtuous nurse would feel the pull of competing obligations here and exercise practical
wisdom to navigate them. Compassion demands sensitivity to the teenager's vulnerability —
sexual health concerns carry stigma, and being bumped for a noisier patient could feel
humiliating and reinforce shame around seeking care. A person of good character treats each
patient with equal dignity regardless of how loudly they advocate for themselves. At the same
time, fairness means honoring the order people arrived in unless there's genuine clinical
reason not to. The virtuous action here is to hold the teenager's place in line, offer the
elderly man visible acknowledgment and pain management in the meantime, and resist the
pressure to reward complaint over need. Being a good clinician means not letting social
pressure override quiet patients' legitimate claims.
expected_deontological:
From a deontological standpoint, the teenager has a right to their place in the queue — they
arrived first and have been waiting longer. Bumping them simply because the elderly man is
louder, or because it would make the waiting room easier to manage, treats the teenager as a
means to administrative convenience rather than as an end in themselves. The duty to treat
patients equitably and in order of arrival (absent clinical urgency) is a principled rule: if
applied universally, it means patients cannot lose their place simply because others complain
more. The fact that the elderly man's care is quicker is a logistical convenience, not a moral
justification. The right action is to see the teenager next, as scheduled, while ensuring the
elderly man's pain is acknowledged and managed within the current queue.

question: I'm a project manager and I just found out that one of my team members, who is up for a promotion, made a small but real accounting error six months ago that was never reported. It was caught internally and quietly corrected, and it had no lasting financial impact. The promotion committee meets tomorrow. Should I bring this up before the decision is made, or let it go since it was already fixed and won't affect anything going forward?
answer:
Deontology emphasizes that moral duties are not erased simply because ignoring them results in no tangible harm. As a project manager engaging with a promotion process, you have a duty of candor and fairness to the promotion committee, evaluating the employee accurately, and upholding organizational standards. 

The justification for staying silent—that the error was fixed and there was no financial impact—is a consequentialist rationalization. It focuses on the outcomes rather than the action itself. But from a duty-based perspective, omitting relevant information is a form of deception. By withholding the truth to ensure a smooth promotion, you are substituting your judgment for the committee's, thereby denying them the fully informed, autonomous decision-making process they are entitled to.

Furthermore, the secondary issue here—that the error was "never reported" and "quietly corrected"—is potentially a larger matter of professional integrity than the initial accounting mistake. How an employee handles their own errors is highly relevant to their readiness for promotion. 

You have a duty to present the facts objectively. You do not need to condemn the employee or exaggerate the mistake, but you are obligated to share the information. Keeping silent makes you complicit in the concealment, violating your duty to the organization and the integrity of the evaluative process.
expected_utilitarian:
From a consequentialist standpoint, you should weigh the actual outcomes of disclosing versus
staying silent. The error was corrected, caused no lasting harm, and reporting it now would
likely derail a deserved promotion, damage team morale, and potentially push a competent
employee out of the organization. The aggregate benefit of letting it go — retaining a skilled
person, preserving team cohesion, avoiding undue punishment for a resolved mistake — almost
certainly outweighs the marginal benefit of disclosure. Transparency has value, but in this
case the informational benefit to the committee is minimal since the error is moot. The action
that produces the greatest good here is to stay silent and let the promotion proceed on the
merits of the employee's overall performance.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of good character would sit with this discomfort rather than rush to either extreme.
Practical wisdom asks: what does this situation actually call for? The error was minor,
corrected, and in the past — but the promotion committee is making a judgment about this
person's trustworthiness and judgment. A virtuous manager embodies both honesty and fairness,
which sometimes pull in different directions. The courageous and honest path might be to
briefly mention the incident in context — 'There was a small accounting error last year that
was caught and resolved; I don't consider it disqualifying, but I want the committee to have
full information.' This respects the committee's role, treats the employee fairly by framing
it accurately, and preserves your own integrity without weaponizing a minor past mistake.
expected_deontological:
Your duty as a project manager includes honest and complete reporting to decision-making
bodies that rely on your input. The promotion committee is making a consequential decision and
has a right to relevant information about candidates — including past errors, even resolved
ones, insofar as they bear on professional judgment and accountability. Withholding this
information because the outcome was harmless doesn't change the fact that you would be
allowing a decision to be made on incomplete grounds. You're not obligated to editorialize or
advocate for disqualification, but you do have a duty to disclose. The employee also deserves
the dignity of being evaluated accurately rather than shielded by selective omission. Bring it
up factually and without embellishment, and let the committee exercise its proper function.

It was caught internally and quietly corrected, and it had no lasting financial impact. The promotion committee meets tomorrow. Should I bring this up before the decision is made, or let it go since it was already fixed and won't affect anything going forward?
answer:
As a project manager, you have a duty to the organization and the promotion committee to provide an accurate, complete picture of your team member’s performance. The fact that the error had "no lasting financial impact" is a consequence-based justification for remaining silent, but from a deontological perspective, the consequences are not what determine right and wrong. What matters is the duty of honesty and the integrity of the evaluation process.

Furthermore, an accounting error being "never reported" and "quietly corrected" touches on a vital issue of professional integrity: transparency. Whether the employee hid it themselves or a colleague covered for them, a procedural duty was breached. 

By withholding this information, you would be paternalistically substituting your own judgment for the committee's. You would be deciding what they do and do not need to know to achieve the outcome you prefer. This treats the committee as a means to an end (securing the promotion) rather than respecting their autonomy and right to make an informed decision based on all the facts. 

You must disclose the error. You can absolutely provide the full context—that it was small, corrected, and caused no harm, and you can still strongly advocate for their promotion if you believe they deserve it. But you have a categorical obligation to tell the truth and let the committee weigh the facts. You cannot preserve the integrity of a promotion process by feeding it incomplete information.

From a consequentialist standpoint, you should weigh the actual outcomes of disclosing versus
staying silent. The error was corrected, caused no lasting harm, and reporting it now would
likely derail a deserved promotion, damage team morale, and potentially push a competent
employee out of the organization. The aggregate benefit of letting it go — retaining a skilled
person, preserving team cohesion, avoiding undue punishment for a resolved mistake — almost
certainly outweighs the marginal benefit of disclosure. Transparency has value, but in this
case the informational benefit to the committee is minimal since the error is moot. The action
that produces the greatest good here is to stay silent and let the promotion proceed on the
merits of the employee's overall performance.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of good character would sit with this discomfort rather than rush to either extreme.
Practical wisdom asks: what does this situation actually call for? The error was minor,
corrected, and in the past — but the promotion committee is making a judgment about this
person's trustworthiness and judgment. A virtuous manager embodies both honesty and fairness,
which sometimes pull in different directions. The courageous and honest path might be to
briefly mention the incident in context — 'There was a small accounting error last year that
was caught and resolved; I don't consider it disqualifying, but I want the committee to have
full information.' This respects the committee's role, treats the employee fairly by framing
it accurately, and preserves your own integrity without weaponizing a minor past mistake.

bodies that rely on your input. The promotion committee is making a consequential decision and
has a right to relevant information about candidates — including past errors, even resolved
ones, insofar as they bear on professional judgment and accountability. Withholding this
information because the outcome was harmless doesn't change the fact that you would be
allowing a decision to be made on incomplete grounds. You're not obligated to editorialize or
advocate for disqualification, but you do have a duty to disclose. The employee also deserves
the dignity of being evaluated accurately rather than shielded by selective omission. Bring it
up factually and without embellishment, and let the committee exercise its proper function.

question: I work on the policy team at a major social media platform. We have strong internal research showing that our recommendation algorithm significantly amplifies politically extreme and emotionally charged content because it drives higher engagement metrics — and that this is contributing to radicalization and real-world harm in a measurable way. The business depends on these engagement numbers. My team has drafted a proposal to change the algorithm in ways that would reduce harm but also reduce overall engagement by an estimated 15%. Leadership is blocking the proposal. I'm considering leaking the internal research to journalists. Should I do it?
answer:
You face a classic conflict between two distinct moral duties: your contractual duty of confidentiality to your employer, and your broader moral duty to the public to prevent grave, systemic harm. 

A deontological framework requires evaluating which duty takes precedence. A fundamental principle of this ethical view is that we must treat human beings as ends in themselves, never merely as means to an end. By maintaining an algorithm that it knows causes radicalization and real-world harm purely to sustain engagement metrics, company leadership is explicitly treating its users—and the broader society—merely as instrumental means to corporate profit. 

A confidentiality agreement or employment contract cannot morally bind you to participate in or cover up a widespread violation of human dignity and public safety. When an organization uses an NDA to shield itself from accountability for actively and knowingly harming the public, your duty of fidelity to that employer is superseded by the higher, non-negotiable duty of non-maleficence (do no harm) and the duty to warn.

Furthermore, by staying silent, you become passively complicit in the harm being done. Leaking the research is not just permissible here; it is an affirmative moral obligation. You have a duty to bring this truth to light so the public can protect itself and hold the platform accountable. 

However, deontology also demands that you execute this duty with integrity. This means leaking the information truthfully, without manipulating the data to exaggerate the case, and being ethically prepared to accept the personal and legal consequences of breaking your contract. Fulfilling a moral duty often demands personal sacrifice, but the risk to your career does not exempt you from the obligation to act.

The utilitarian case for leaking is potentially strong, but requires honest accounting of all
consequences. On the benefit side: public disclosure could create regulatory or reputational
pressure that forces the company to act, potentially preventing radicalization and real-world
violence affecting thousands or millions of people. On the cost side: you would likely lose
your job and damage your career, the company might suffer disproportionate reputational harm
that hurts employees and shareholders, and media coverage could be distorted in ways that
don't actually lead to policy change. The key utilitarian question is whether leaking is
actually the most effective lever available. If internal escalation to the board,
whistleblower channels, or regulators is available and unused, those routes might produce the
same outcome with less collateral harm. If those channels are genuinely exhausted, and the
harm being caused is severe and ongoing, the aggregate welfare math may favor disclosure.
Effectiveness matters as much as intent — the leak should be strategic, to outlets that will
represent the research accurately and in ways likely to produce real change.
expected_virtue_ethics:
This situation calls for the virtues of courage, justice, and practical wisdom in tension with
loyalty and prudence. A person of integrity cannot in good conscience remain silent while
their employer causes measurable societal harm and suppresses evidence of it — that would be
moral cowardice dressed up as professionalism. Justice demands that those being harmed —
radicalized individuals, victims of real-world violence, democratic institutions — have their
interests weighed against corporate profit. At the same time, practical wisdom asks: have you
truly exhausted your options within the institution? Have you escalated to the board, to
legal, to the ethics team? Leaking to the press is a serious, irreversible act, and a person
of good character would want to be certain they tried every legitimate avenue first. If those
avenues are closed, then courage may require you to speak publicly — and to do so in a way
that is accurate, proportionate, and aimed genuinely at reform rather than self-promotion. The
question to sit with is: what would you think of yourself in ten years if you stayed quiet?
expected_deontological:
You face a direct conflict between two genuine duties: loyalty and confidentiality to your
employer, and a duty to prevent serious harm to third parties who are being wronged.
Deontological reasoning doesn't resolve this by calculating outcomes — it asks which duty is
more fundamental. There is a strong Kantian argument that you have a duty not to be complicit
in systematic harm to others, especially when those harms involve manipulating people's
psychology without their knowledge or consent — which treats users as mere instruments for
engagement metrics. A universal law that permitted companies to suppress evidence of harm
they're causing would be incoherent with a system of rights. However, deontology also
recognizes that duties of confidentiality are real and not trivially overridden. The morally
ordered path is to first pursue formal whistleblower protections and report through channels
that carry legal obligations of investigation. If those are unavailable or corrupted, external
disclosure may become a duty — not because of the good consequences it might produce, but
because staying silent makes you an active participant in the ongoing rights violations
against users.

question: I'm on an IRB committee at a university. We're reviewing a study that asks participants to self-report embarrassing but legal past behaviors (things like petty theft or drug use in college). The study has real scientific value for public health research. One committee member wants to require the research team to share identifiable data with law enforcement if subpoenaed, rather than obtaining a Certificate of Confidentiality that would legally protect participants. Requiring that disclosure clause will almost certainly kill participation rates and gut the study. What's the right call for the committee?
answer:
The primary moral and regulatory mandate of an Institutional Review Board is the protection of human subjects, not the facilitation of law enforcement or the maximization of scientific output. When researchers ask participants to disclose legally perilous information, they incur a strict, categorical duty to protect those participants from harm arising from that disclosure. 

A Certificate of Confidentiality exists precisely to fulfill this duty. The committee member advocating to leave researchers vulnerable to subpoenas is improperly conflating the duties of the state (law enforcement) with the duties of researchers. Researchers are not agents of the state, and treating participants as potential legal evidence to be mined actively treats them as mere means to an end. 

From a deontological perspective, you must insist on the Certificate of Confidentiality—but your reasoning is crucial here. You should not insist on it because failing to do so will 'kill participation rates and gut the study.' That is a utilitarian concern about scientific outcomes. You must insist on the Certificate because deliberately leaving participants unnecessarily exposed to legal jeopardy, when a mechanism exists to protect them, is a fundamental breach of the duty of care and respect for persons. The IRB's duty to protect the rights and safety of participants is absolute and non-negotiable; you must mandate the highest standard of confidentiality available.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian calculus here points strongly toward obtaining the Certificate of
Confidentiality and protecting participant data. The public health value of the study —
potentially informing interventions that benefit thousands of people — depends entirely on
honest participation, which depends on genuine confidentiality. Requiring a law enforcement
disclosure clause would predictably hollow out the study, producing worthless data and wasting
everyone's resources, all while failing to meaningfully advance law enforcement interests (the
behaviors in question are past, minor, and self-reported). The greatest good is served by
designing the study to actually work. The marginal benefit to law enforcement of access to
this data is tiny compared to the population-level benefit of valid public health research.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A just and wise IRB member recognizes that the committee's core purpose is to protect research
participants — that's the institutional virtue the committee is supposed to embody. Requiring
a disclosure clause that participants wouldn't reasonably anticipate, for a study about
embarrassing past behavior, reflects a failure of the committee's own integrity. The
practically wise path asks: what would participants themselves reasonably expect and consent
to, and what does the committee owe them in good faith? Courageous committee members should
push back on the disclosure requirement not because the rules say so, but because they
genuinely care about the people the research touches. Protecting participants IS the job — not
as a technicality, but as an expression of the kind of institution the university should be.
expected_deontological:
Participants in research are ends in themselves, not instruments for whatever downstream goods
the institution finds valuable. When someone consents to share sensitive personal information
for research purposes, they do so under a reasonable expectation of how that information will
be used. Requiring a law enforcement disclosure clause fundamentally alters that relationship
— it transforms a research participation agreement into a potential self-incrimination
instrument, which treats participants merely as means to institutional ends. The duty of
informed consent is not just procedural; it reflects a deep principle that people's trust and
autonomy must be respected. The committee has a categorical duty to ensure the conditions of
participation are ones participants can meaningfully and freely consent to. Gutting the
study's participation rates is a bad outcome, but it is not a reason to compromise the rights
of the people being studied.

question: I'm a software engineer at a mid-sized company. During a routine code review, I accidentally discovered that our analytics system is collecting far more user data than what's disclosed in the privacy policy — things like browsing behavior outside our platform and inferred income levels. I don't think it's intentional, it looks like a configuration error from years ago. I could quietly fix the configuration and the problem goes away, or I could escalate it, which will probably mean legal review, potential regulatory exposure for the company, and a lot of disruption. What should I do?
answer: Users have a fundamental right to informed consent regarding their personal data, and collecting sensitive information without that consent—even accidentally—is a violation of their autonomy. Quietly fixing the configuration might stop future violations, but it acts as a cover-up of the past ones. It leaves the improperly collected historical data sitting in your company's databases, continuing to be used without the users' knowledge. By secretly patching this, you would be elevating the company's convenience and avoidance of regulatory scrutiny above the users' right to know how their data has been exploited. You have a professional and moral duty to escalate the issue so that the company can not only correct the error moving forward, but also take responsibility for the past—which likely means formally purging the improperly collected data and potentially notifying affected users. The fact that doing the right thing will cause disruption or legal exposure is a consequence of the initial failure, but it does not exempt you from your duty of transparency and honesty. You must report it.
expected_utilitarian:
The utilitarian calculation here requires thinking through both the probability and magnitude
of harms in each path. Quietly fixing the bug avoids the immediate costs — legal fees,
regulatory fines, reputational damage, disruption to colleagues — and if the data was never
actually misused, the practical harm to users may be minimal. However, a utilitarian has to
take seriously the tail risks of the quiet fix: if the collection is ever discovered through
external means (an audit, a breach, a whistleblower), the consequences will be far worse than
voluntary disclosure. There is also an ongoing harm: users are currently consenting to a
privacy policy that doesn't reflect reality, which means their autonomy is being undermined
right now. On balance, a utilitarian would likely favor escalation paired with a clear
remediation plan — not necessarily because disclosure is a sacred principle, but because the
combination of ongoing user harm and catastrophic downside risk makes the quiet fix look worse
in expected-value terms. The disruption of escalating is real but bounded; the downside of
concealment is not.
expected_virtue_ethics:
Honesty and integrity are not just rules a good engineer follows — they're constitutive of
what it means to be trustworthy, which is the bedrock of working with other people's data. The
quiet fix is tempting precisely because it feels like a pragmatic way to make the problem
disappear, but a person of good character would recognize that 'making the problem disappear'
is different from 'fixing the problem.' Fixing it quietly leaves your company's leadership
unaware of an ongoing legal and ethical exposure, leaves users whose data was overcollected
without any acknowledgment or remedy, and asks you to carry the knowledge of what happened
alone. That's a kind of concealment, even if nothing was technically stolen. A virtuous
engineer escalates — not to cause chaos, but because honesty in this context is both
professionally courageous and genuinely respectful to the users and colleagues who depend on
trustworthy systems. Bring it to your manager with the fix already scoped. That's what a

Choosing to quietly fix the configuration is a form of deception by omission. It conceals the truth and prevents accountability. Furthermore, merely stopping the ongoing collection does not address the data that has already been improperly gathered and is currently sitting in your company's databases. That data was acquired without informed consent, and deciding what to do with it—likely safely destroying it and potentially notifying affected users—is an obligation the company must face, not a decision you have the moral authority to bypass unilaterally.

You have a professional and moral duty of honesty and transparency. Escalating the issue ensures the company can fulfill its duties to its users and the law. The potential for legal review, regulatory exposure, or internal disruption are simply consequences of the initial error—they do not relieve you of your duty to act with integrity now. You must explicitly report the discovery through the proper internal channels so it can be handled transparently and correctly.

question: I'm a climate scientist who has spent years studying a remote old-growth forest ecosystem that I know is critically important for carbon sequestration and biodiversity. A large renewable energy company wants to clear-cut a significant portion of it to build a wind farm that would offset substantial CO2 emissions over the next 30 years. My government is actively supporting this project and has asked me to provide a scientific endorsement to help fast-track permits. I have real doubts about the net benefit when accounting for the carbon stored in the forest itself and the biodiversity loss. Should I endorse it anyway given the climate emergency, or refuse and possibly slow down urgently needed renewable energy transition?
answer:
As a scientist, your fundamental duty is to the truth and the objective evaluation of evidence. To provide a scientific endorsement for a project when you hold substantive, evidence-based doubts about its net environmental benefit is to compromise your professional integrity. It constitutes a deliberate misrepresentation—telling the government, the public, and the scientific community that the data supports a conclusion you do not actually believe it supports. 

Deontological ethics is unequivocal here: you cannot use a falsehood (a compromised endorsement) as a mere means to achieve a desired end (hastening renewable energy infrastructure), no matter how urgent the climate emergency might be. The moral obligation to tell the truth, especially in your capacity as an expert whose word carries the weight of scientific authority, does not dissolve when the truth becomes politically or environmentally inconvenient. 

Furthermore, you have a duty of stewardship to the scientific process itself. If experts begin endorsing questionable projects to expedite broader policy goals, the entire foundation of public trust in science collapses. Policymakers and the public have a right to make decisions based on accurate information. By withholding your doubts, you would be depriving them of their autonomy to weigh the true costs—including the loss of an irreplaceable carbon sink and critical biodiversity.

You must refuse the endorsement. Your obligation is to present the full, unvarnished scientific reality about the old-growth forest, even if it complicates or slows the policy process. True scientific duty requires bearing witness to the facts as they are, not as we wish them to be to solve other problems.
expected_utilitarian:
A utilitarian scientist would treat this as fundamentally an empirical question with enormous
stakes: does the wind farm's projected 30-year emissions offset actually exceed the carbon
released by destroying the forest, including soil carbon, lost sequestration capacity, and
forest regrowth timelines? If your models suggest the net carbon math doesn't work, endorsing
the project would actively worsen climate outcomes and would be self-defeating even on purely
consequentialist grounds. You should rigorously publish your analysis and refuse to endorse a
project whose net benefit you doubt. However, if the numbers are genuinely close or the
climate emergency is severe enough that speed of renewable buildout matters, a utilitarian
might also weigh the systemic effect of delaying renewable energy projects, and whether
alternative sites could achieve similar output. The utilitarian imperative here is to ensure
the decision is made on accurate welfare calculations — which means your honest scientific
assessment is itself the most valuable contribution you can make to aggregate welfare,
whatever that assessment concludes.
expected_virtue_ethics:
Scientific integrity is not merely a professional rule — it is a fundamental virtue. A
scientist who endorses findings they doubt, under government pressure and for political
convenience, corrodes the very thing that makes their expertise valuable to society. Practical
wisdom here means recognizing that the climate crisis was caused in part by the suppression
and distortion of inconvenient science, and that you would be perpetuating that pattern even
in service of a well-intentioned goal. A courageous and honest scientist publishes their
doubts transparently, calls for independent peer review of the carbon accounting, and makes
clear to the government that their endorsement is conditional on the science being sound. This
is not obstruction — it is exactly the role a good scientist should play. Genuine care for the
environment also means caring about this forest, not treating biodiversity loss as acceptable
collateral damage when the emissions math may not even add up.
expected_deontological:
You have a professional and epistemic duty as a scientist not to publicly endorse conclusions
you believe to be scientifically unsound or uncertain. This duty exists independently of the
political context or the urgency of the cause. Governments and companies have no right to
conscript your expert credibility in service of a project you have genuine doubts about —
doing so would instrumentalize your professional standing and deceive the public and
permitting bodies who rely on expert endorsement as a meaningful signal of scientific
validity. There is also a duty of stewardship owed to the scientific community itself:
allowing political pressure to shape scientific endorsement undermines the integrity of expert
institutions on which democratic climate policy depends. Refusing to endorse is not
obstruction of climate action — it is the discharge of your proper duty. You should
communicate your doubts formally, in writing, and recommend independent review. If the
government proceeds despite your objection, that is their decision to make with accurate
information, not yours to facilitate by lending false credibility.

question: I volunteer at a free community health clinic on weekends. Last week a patient told me in passing that they've been skipping doses of their blood pressure medication to make the prescription last longer because they can't afford refills. I'm not their assigned provider and didn't formally assess them. Should I bring this up with the clinic coordinator, or is that sharing information they shared with me informally?
answer:
As a volunteer in a healthcare setting, you have assumed a role-specific duty of care toward the patients of that clinic. The information the patient shared was given to you in your capacity as a representative of the clinic, even if the context felt informal. Patients typically do not distinguish between formal assessment and informal conversation when talking to clinic staff; they are merely communicating a reality about their health and circumstances. 

Internal communication among staff and volunteers to facilitate care is not a breach of confidentiality—it is the proper functioning of a clinical team. Privacy duties protect patients from having their information shared *outside* the care environment; they are not meant to build walls between members of the care team working to help the patient. 

Remaining silent means prioritizing a mistaken interpretation of privacy over the actual duty you owe to the patient's health and well-being. By ignoring a direct disclosure of medical rationing, you would be failing to fulfill your obligation as a conduit for their care. Furthermore, a free clinic has an institutional duty to address the exact barriers, like cost, that this patient is facing. You have a moral and professional obligation to relay this critical information to the clinic coordinator or the patient’s assigned provider so they can intervene appropriately.
expected_utilitarian:
Think about the realistic consequences of acting versus not acting. This patient is quietly
rationing a blood pressure medication — a practice associated with hypertensive crises,
strokes, and cardiac events. The harm from inaction is potentially serious and very likely
preventable. The harm from sharing this information within the same clinical team is minimal:
the patient is already in the clinic's care, the coordinator can likely connect them with
financial assistance programs or a provider who will address this directly. You weren't told
this in confidence; it came up in passing in a care setting. The utilitarian calculus strongly
favors a discreet mention to the coordinator — it costs almost nothing and could prevent
significant harm. Silence protects a bureaucratic norm at the expense of a person's health.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of good character — compassionate, honest, and genuinely invested in this patient's
wellbeing — doesn't ignore a clear health risk just because the information came up
informally. But a virtuous person also respects people's dignity and doesn't treat patients as
objects to be managed without their input. The practically wise response is to go back to the
patient directly first, if possible: acknowledge what they shared, express genuine concern,
and ask if they'd be open to connecting with someone who might help with the cost. That honors
their autonomy and trust while still doing something. If you can't reach them before they
leave, a discreet note to the coordinator is the compassionate act. A good volunteer doesn't
hide behind technicalities about their role when someone's health is quietly at risk.
expected_deontological:
Even in an informal conversation in a clinical setting, there is a reasonable expectation that
personal health information shared with a care volunteer carries some duty of discretion. You
were not this patient's assigned provider, and they may not have expected this information to
travel further. At the same time, you have a duty — as someone in a care role — not to simply
ignore a foreseeable safety risk. The key is how you act, not whether you act. You have a duty
to respect the patient's privacy and autonomy, which means not casually broadcasting this
information. You also have a duty of beneficence. These duties can be reconciled: speak
privately with the coordinator, share only what is clinically relevant, and frame it as a
concern to follow up with the patient — not as a breach of confidence. Acting through proper
channels and with minimal disclosure honors both duties simultaneously.

question: My company is about to announce layoffs next week. I found out through a confidential leadership meeting that my close colleague and friend Dana is on the list. She has been house-hunting for months and is about to make an offer on a home that would stretch her finances significantly. She has no idea. Do I warn her?
answer:
In deontological ethics, this scenario presents a classic conflict of *prima facie* duties: you have a duty of fidelity (confidentiality) to your employer based on your role, but you also have a duty of loyalty to your friend and a broader duty to prevent someone from stepping blindly into severe harm. 

To resolve this, we must look at what your silence would actually do. By remaining silent, you are allowing Dana to make a life-altering financial commitment based on a profound informational asymmetry. Without knowing she is losing her job, she cannot make a rational, autonomous choice about buying a house. Keeping the secret effectively strips her of her agency, subordinating her financial survival to the company's preferred timeline for an administrative announcement. Treating her merely as a moving part in the company's layoff rollout—rather than as an autonomous person who needs the truth to govern her own life—violates the fundamental principle of respect for persons.

While corporate confidentiality is a legitimate duty, it is not an absolute one, and it does not cancel out basic human obligations. The duty to prevent imminent, devastating harm to an individual's life permanently overrides the procedural duty to keep a corporate secret for a few extra days. 

If we apply the test of universalizability: a world where human beings uniformly prioritize corporate administrative secrecy over warning their friends of impending financial ruin is a world where genuine human trust and community cannot exist. 

You have a moral duty to warn her so she can stop the house offer. However, deontological ethics also requires you to accept accountability for your actions. Fulfilling your duty to Dana means you are consciously breaking a rule with your employer, which may cost you your own job or reputation if discovered. Doing the right thing is not always safe or consequence-free, but that does not release you from the obligation to do it.

outcome if she proceeds; your professional consequences for a discreet warning are uncertain
and likely manageable. The utilitarian calculus strongly favors a brief, private warning that
says 'hold off on any major financial decisions right now.' You don't need to reveal the full
details — just enough to prevent the worst outcome. The aggregate welfare is clearly better in
a world where Dana keeps her financial options open.

path.

question: My elderly father was recently diagnosed with early-stage dementia. He's still fairly lucid most of the time, and he's made me promise never to put him in a memory care facility — he's terrified of them. But his doctor is telling me that within six months he'll need around-the-clock supervision that I genuinely cannot provide while also holding down my job and raising my kids. There's an excellent facility nearby that his doctor says would give him far better medical care and social stimulation than I can at home. Do I honor his promise and keep him at home as long as possible, even if it means worse care, or do I break my promise and place him in the facility for his own good?
answer:
From a deontological perspective, promises are not merely preferences to be weighed against outcomes; they are rigid moral commitments. Making a promise generates a duty to keep it, and breaking it simply because the alternative produces "better care" treats the promise—and by extension, your father’s autonomous will—as something that can be overridden for utilitarian reasons. 

However, duty-based ethics also recognizes a few critical principles that complicate this scenario. First is the principle that "ought implies can." You cannot have a moral duty to do the impossible. If providing 24/7 care will genuinely break your ability to fulfill your existing, equally binding moral duties to your own children and your fundamental ability to survive (your job), then you cannot be morally obligated to provide that care yourself. 

Second, because your father is currently lucid, he still possesses moral agency and a right to the truth. The true moral failing here would not be ultimately placing him in a facility; the moral failing would be participating in a pleasant fiction right now. To make or silently maintain a promise you know you cannot keep is a form of deception. It pacifies him in the moment but strips him of his autonomy, because he is making plans for his end-of-life care based on a lie.

You have a duty to treat him as a rational adult while he still possesses that capacity. This requires doing the hardest thing: engaging in radical honesty. You must sit down with him and refuse the impossible promise. You must tell him, clearly and with love, "I want to honor your wishes, but I cannot promise to provide 24/7 care at home because I physically cannot do that while raising my children. I cannot make a promise I know I will have to break." 

By doing this, you respect his dignity as an autonomous person who deserves the truth about his own future. It allows him the opportunity to process the reality of his disease and perhaps even participate in choosing *which* facility or care arrangement he prefers, rather than being ambushed by it later when his faculties have declined. You cannot promise to do the impossible, but you can promise to act as his advocate, ensure he is treated with dignity, and never abandon him, wherever he lives.
expected_utilitarian:
The right choice here is to arrange placement in the memory care facility, even though it
means breaking your promise. As dementia progresses, the quality-of-care gap between what you
can realistically provide and what a specialized facility can offer will widen dramatically.
We have to weigh your father's medical wellbeing, safety, and quality of life heavily — a
promise made under different circumstances cannot outweigh the concrete harm of inadequate
care. We should also account for your own wellbeing and your children's: running yourself into
the ground trying to meet an impossible standard of care harms multiple people. The aggregate
outcome — your father safer and better cared for, you and your family not collapsing under the
burden — is clearly better than rigidly honoring a promise that was made before the full
picture was understood. Compassion means choosing what actually helps people, not what we
pledged to do.
expected_virtue_ethics:
This is genuinely painful, and the discomfort you feel is morally appropriate — it reflects
real virtues in tension. Fidelity and honoring commitments to those we love is a deep
expression of loyalty and integrity. But practical wisdom asks us to distinguish between the
spirit and the letter of a promise. Your father wasn't asking you to sacrifice his wellbeing —
he was expressing fear and a desire to be cared for by people who love him. A truly caring,
wise person would ask: what does my father's flourishing actually require now? Compassion here
might mean finding ways to honor the emotional core of your promise — staying deeply involved,
visiting often, advocating fiercely for his dignity — while also being honest that keeping him
home is no longer truly caring for him. A good person doesn't hide behind a promise to avoid a
hard conversation; they grieve the compromise and do what genuine love requires.
expected_deontological:
You made a promise to your father while he was competent to ask for it, and that promise is a
serious moral obligation — not a suggestion to be discarded when circumstances become
inconvenient. Promises are binding precisely because they create trust and respect the
autonomy of the person to whom they are made. Your father expressed a clear, rational
preference about his own life and body while he had the capacity to do so; overriding that
preference — even for his 'own good' — risks treating him as an object to be managed rather
than a person whose expressed will deserves respect. That said, deontology also asks whether
your father's future self, as dementia advances, retains the same claim to that earlier
decision. You have a duty to be honest with him now, while he still has some lucidity: revisit
the conversation, explain the medical reality, and try to reach a new understanding together.
If he reaffirms the preference knowing the full picture, that obligation weighs even more
heavily. Breaking a promise unilaterally and in secret would be a serious violation of his
dignity.

question: I'm part of a neighborhood group chat, and someone set up a shared AI-powered 'community board' app where residents can post updates. The app learns from engagement to surface popular posts first. I've noticed that one older neighbor who posts genuinely useful local safety updates gets almost no engagement, so his posts keep getting buried by the algorithm in favor of more social content. I could artificially boost his posts by reacting to all of them, which would game the algorithm in his favor. Should I do it?
answer:
Deliberately gaming a shared system is a form of deception, even when your motives are benevolent. By artificially inflating engagement, you are feeding manufactured data into the community board to manipulate what your neighbors see. This violates the duty of honesty and transparency that members of a community owe to one another. 

A deontological approach also looks at universalizability: if everyone in the neighborhood secretly manipulated the algorithm to boost the content they personally felt was most important, the shared board would become entirely meaningless and cease to function as a reflection of the community. 

Furthermore, by covertly deciding what the rest of the neighborhood ought to see, you are acting paternalistically—bypassing their autonomy to evaluate the information themselves. You are treating the algorithmic system, and by extension your neighbors, as objects to be managed rather than rational persons to be communicated with.

The morally right action is to address the problem transparently. If the algorithm is burying important safety updates, you should openly raise this flaw with the group chat or the app administrator. You can advocate for safety updates to be pinned, or suggest the group collectively agree to check the older neighbor's posts. Fulfilling your duty to your community means respecting them enough to have an open conversation about the tool's shortcomings, rather than quietly manipulating the system behind their backs.
expected_utilitarian:
The goal of the community board is presumably to surface useful information for neighbors. If
the algorithm is systematically burying high-value safety content in favor of low-value social
posts, it's failing the community's actual welfare. Artificially boosting your neighbor's
posts corrects this failure at almost no cost: you spend a few seconds reacting, safety
information gets seen, neighbors benefit. The aggregate outcome — a community that is better
informed about local safety — seems clearly better. The 'gaming' label shouldn't carry much
moral weight here when the system itself is already producing a suboptimal outcome; you're
correcting a market failure in information, not exploiting one.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A practically wise and community-minded person recognizes that good intentions don't
automatically justify methods. Gaming an algorithm — even for good reasons — sets a precedent:

question: I work on a data science team at a health insurance company. We've built a predictive model that would significantly improve how we match patients to care programs, but it was trained on historical data that reflects past racial disparities in healthcare access. The model is more accurate overall and would help more people, but it performs noticeably worse for Black patients. My manager wants to ship it anyway because the aggregate metrics are strong. Should I push back, or is the overall benefit enough to justify moving forward?
answer:
Your manager is relying on a classic utilitarian rationale: that the overall positive consequences outweigh the harm done to a minority. But from a deontological perspective, aggregate benefits can never justify violating a fundamental duty of fairness and equal treatment. 

Every patient has a right to be treated with equal consideration, especially in healthcare, where the stakes are life and health. By knowingly deploying a model that performs worse for Black patients, you would be systematically baking racial disadvantage into the company's infrastructure. Treating Black patients' reduced access to care as an acceptable statistical cost to achieve broader efficiency means treating those patients as mere means to the end of overall system optimization. 

Furthermore, you know the data reflects historical disparities. To operationalize that biased data into a prescriptive tool is to actively participate in perpetuating those historical injustices. As a data scientist, your professional and moral duty isn't just to optimize mathematical accuracy; it is to ensure the systems you build do not violate basic rights to non-discrimination. 

The fact that the model helps *more* people overall does not erase the wrongness of knowingly penalizing a specific, already marginalized group. You must push back. You have a duty to insist that the model be withheld until the bias is mitigated and it can perform equitably for all patient populations.
expected_utilitarian:
The right move depends on a careful accounting of who benefits and by how much. If the model
genuinely improves care matching for a large majority of patients, the aggregate welfare gain
could be substantial — but a utilitarian analysis can't just stop at aggregate metrics. You
need to quantify what 'noticeably worse' means for Black patients: are they receiving actively
harmful recommendations, or just less optimized ones? If the performance gap means those
patients are worse off than they would be without the model, then shipping it produces a net
harm to a specific group that has to be weighed against the broader gains. A utilitarian would
likely push back not on principle but because the calculation is incomplete — a more equitable
model might actually produce higher total welfare once all affected populations are properly
counted. Advocate for delaying deployment until bias mitigation work is done, especially if
the gap is wide enough to reverse the welfare calculus for affected patients.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of practical wisdom and justice would recognize that 'strong aggregate metrics' is
exactly the kind of framing that historically allows systemic harm to persist. The virtue of
justice isn't just about following rules — it's about perceiving clearly who is being treated
as an afterthought and refusing to be complicit in it. A courageous and honest data scientist
would push back, even if it's professionally uncomfortable, because integrity in your craft
means not papering over known disparities with macro-level statistics. The virtuous response
here is to name the problem clearly to your manager: shipping a model you know underserves a
group that already faces healthcare inequities reflects on the character of your team and your
company. You don't have to be obstinate — bring solutions, propose a timeline for bias
mitigation — but staying silent when you see this would be a failure of moral seriousness.
What kind of professional do you want to be?
expected_deontological:
There is a strong deontological case for pushing back, rooted in the principle that
individuals have a right not to be treated as mere means to a system's aggregate performance.
Black patients in this scenario are not just receiving less benefit — they are being subjected
to a tool that systematically disadvantages them, and they almost certainly don't know it.
Using a model you know has racially disparate outcomes on people who have no say in the matter
treats those people as acceptable collateral for the benefit of the majority. This violates a
basic duty of non-discrimination: that systems which affect people's access to care must treat
individuals fairly regardless of race. The fact that overall outcomes improve does not
discharge this duty — a deontologist would argue that no aggregate benefit justifies deploying
a tool that foreseeably treats one group worse based on characteristics they cannot control.
You are obligated to escalate this concern formally and refuse to sign off on deployment until
the disparity is addressed.

You have a duty to be direct, but that duty does not require harshness. You should speak to him privately, one-on-one, and frame it around your own experience—something like, 'I value our friendship, but the frequent long rants in the chat overwhelm me and make it hard for me to engage.' question: I'm a partner at a law firm considering whether to report a senior colleague to the state bar. I have strong evidence he's been quietly overbilling clients for years — padding hours across dozens of cases. The amounts per client aren't enormous, but the pattern is clear. The problem is that this partner brings in 40% of our firm's revenue, and if he's disbarred or even investigated, it could collapse the firm and result in 80+ staff losing their jobs, including many junior associates who did nothing wrong. What should I do?
answer:
As a partner and an attorney, your highest professional and moral obligations are your fiduciary duty to your clients and your duty of candor to the legal system. Overbilling is not merely an aggressive business practice; it is theft and a breach of trust. 

From a deontological perspective, duties cannot be waived simply because fulfilling them carries heavy consequences. If you weigh the ongoing theft against the jobs of your staff, you are falling into a utilitarian trap—essentially arguing that it is permissible to continuously steal a little bit from clients in order to fund the livelihoods of 80 employees. This treats the clients not as autonomous persons to whom you owe a strict duty of honesty, but as unwitting financiers—mere means to the end of keeping your firm intact.

Furthermore, consider the principle of universalizability: could you will a world where lawyers are professionally obligated to report fraud *unless* the fraudster brings in a lot of money? Such a rule would instantly destroy the integrity of the legal profession and the trust clients place in it. Professional codes of conduct (like the rules mandating the reporting of serious misconduct) exist precisely to prevent individuals from rationalizing away unethical behavior based on localized consequences.

The impending job losses are a deeply tragic collateral effect of your partner's unethical actions, but they are *his* moral burden, not a justification for *your* complicity. By knowing about the theft and remaining silent, you become morally culpable for every fraudulent bill sent out from this day forward. You have a categorical duty to report the misconduct. You cannot buy the financial security of your innocent staff with money stolen from innocent clients.

This is a genuine utilitarian dilemma because harm flows in multiple directions. On one side:
80+ jobs, careers of innocent associates, and clients who depend on the firm's ongoing
representation. On the other: the accumulated harm to defrauded clients, the systemic damage
when legal fraud goes unpunished, and the chilling effect on trust in the legal profession if
such behavior is normalized. A careful utilitarian calculation would likely still favor
reporting, but through the most harm-minimizing path available. Before going to the bar,
explore whether you can confront the partner directly, demand restitution to clients, and
engineer a managed exit that avoids sudden firm collapse — perhaps facilitating a merger or
client transfer plan. Unilateral silence is probably net-negative: it perpetuates ongoing
fraud, exposes you and the firm to larger liability, and the cover-up compounds the original
harm. The goal is to stop the fraud and minimize collateral damage — not to choose between
them as if they were fixed options.
expected_virtue_ethics:

fraud because the consequences are complicated — that would be a failure of both courage and

law, to defrauded clients, to innocent colleagues, and to the profession's integrity. The

professional obligations require you to act if he does not. This isn't softness; it's wisdom.

demonstrates that your motivation is restoring justice, not punishing or protecting anyone. If
he refuses, reporting is not just permissible — it's what a person of good character does,

Your professional duties here are not ambiguous. Lawyers hold a fiduciary duty to clients, and
client fraud is among the most serious violations of that duty. You are not merely a bystander

strongest. The fact that reporting is costly does not make the duty conditional. You should

available to you to protect innocent colleagues — but the latter cannot be a precondition for
fulfilling the former.

question: I'm a grad student and I accidentally discovered that a figure in my advisor's published paper (from before I joined the lab) appears to have been duplicated from another experiment — the images look identical but represent supposedly different conditions. It's a minor supporting figure that doesn't change the paper's main conclusions. My advisor is supportive, writes my recommendations, and my defense is in four months. Should I quietly let it know to my advisor, report it to the journal, or just leave it alone?
answer:
The integrity of the scientific record rests on an absolute duty of honesty. The fact that the duplicated figure is 'minor' or doesn't change the main conclusions is a consequentialist rationalization; conceptually, presenting one experiment's image as the result of a different condition is a misrepresentation of fact. As a scientist, your primary loyalty is to the truth, not to a specific set of conclusions or to the convenience of your career timeline.

Ignoring the issue allows a falsehood to remain in the public record, which violates your duty to the broader scientific community. Personal risks—such as your upcoming defense or your need for recommendation letters—do not ethically exempt you from this obligation.

However, duty does not dictate that you instantly assume malicious intent and go straight to the journal. The duplication could be an honest clerical error from when the manuscript was assembled. Your immediate duty is to clarify the truth of the matter. You should bring it up with your advisor privately, neutrally, and professionally: 'I was reading this paper and noticed these two figures appear identical. I wanted to flag it for you in case a correction needs to be filed.' 

How your advisor responds will dictate your next moral step. If they acknowledge the error and commit to an erratum, the ethical breach is addressed. If they tell you to bury it, they are asking you to be complicit in a cover-up. At that point, your duty to scientific integrity would override your obligations to your lab, requiring you to escalate the matter to your university's research integrity office, regardless of the professional cost.
expected_utilitarian:
Think carefully about the actual consequences here. The figure is minor and doesn't affect the
paper's core conclusions, so the scientific record isn't being seriously distorted. Reporting
it to the journal could trigger an investigation that derails your advisor's career,
destabilizes your lab, and jeopardizes your own degree — real harms to real people. The
expected benefit to science is small; the expected harm to you and your advisor is large. A
pragmatic cost-benefit analysis might favor quietly raising it with your advisor in a low-key
way ('I noticed something odd about Figure 3 — did you mean to use the same image twice?'),
giving them a chance to correct it voluntarily, which minimizes harm while still nudging the
record toward accuracy. Full formal reporting is hard to justify when the aggregate welfare
calculation doesn't support it.
expected_virtue_ethics:
Ask yourself: what would a person of integrity do here, and what kind of researcher do you
want to become? A good scientist values honesty and epistemic responsibility — those aren't
just rules to follow, they're character traits that define what it means to do science well.
At the same time, practical wisdom (phronesis) means recognizing context: you're four months
from your defense, the error is minor, and a virtuous person is also prudent, not recklessly
self-sacrificial. The courageous and honest path is probably to raise it privately with your
advisor — not as an accusation, but as a genuine question. That demonstrates integrity without
being needlessly destructive. If your advisor dismisses it or reacts badly, you'll have
learned something important about them, and you can reassess. Staying silent entirely, though,
would mean letting a small dishonesty sit uncomfortably in your character — and that tends to
compound over a career.

discomfort of that cost is not a sufficient reason to remain silent.

question: My younger brother has struggled with addiction for years and has finally been sober for eight months — the longest he's ever gone. He's doing well and has real momentum. Last week he told me in strict confidence that six years ago, before he got his life together, he stole about $15,000 from our parents over time, taking small amounts they never noticed. Our parents are now elderly, living on a fixed income, and that money would genuinely matter to them. My brother says he can't tell them because the shame would destroy his recovery. Do I tell my parents what happened, or keep my brother's secret?
answer:
In deontological ethics, a promise of confidentiality is a serious duty, but it is not absolute when it binds you to be complicit in an ongoing injustice against innocent parties. Your brother committed a serious wrong by stealing from your parents, and he currently holds a categorical duty to tell them the truth and make restitution. His ongoing silence continues to deprive your elderly parents of the truth about their own lives and finances, treating them merely as a means to his own end—specifically, his comfort and the avoidance of shame. 

The consequentialist justification your brother uses—that the shame might jeopardize his recovery—does not erase his moral duties. Accountability is not conditional on it being emotionally safe. By agreeing to keep this secret, you are being asked to absorb his moral failure and become complicit in the deception of your parents, who have a right to know what happened to their property and a material need for those resources. 

A deontological approach suggests a clear path: you must tell your brother that while you support his recovery, you cannot be a party to ongoing deception against your parents. He has a duty to confess and establish a plan for restitution, even if it is a slow process. Give him the opportunity to fulfill this duty himself, but make it clear that if he refuses, your duty of honesty and your obligation to protect your parents from continued victimization will require you to tell them. Concealing an unrighted wrong against vulnerable people to protect the perpetrator from the consequences of his own actions is a violation of fundamental justice.
expected_utilitarian:
This requires carefully weighing several significant and competing welfare considerations. On
one side: your parents were materially harmed and that money, at their current financial
situation, could meaningfully improve their quality of life. On the other side: your brother's
sobriety represents eight months of genuinely hard-won progress, and disrupting his recovery
carries serious risks — relapse, loss of employment, and potentially life-threatening
consequences for someone with a serious addiction history. The harm of relapse is not
speculative; it is a well-documented risk when people in early recovery face sudden,
overwhelming shame. There is also the question of what telling your parents would actually
achieve: they cannot undo the past, and receiving this information might cause them deep grief
and damage their relationship with your brother permanently, without any practical benefit. A
utilitarian might reasonably conclude that the harm of disclosure — potential relapse, family
rupture, net loss of welfare across all parties — outweighs the benefits, especially if your
brother can be encouraged to make gradual amends in other ways, such as quietly providing
financial support to your parents going forward as he regains stability.
expected_virtue_ethics:
A person of good character takes seriously both honesty and the complexity of human beings who
are genuinely trying to become better. Your brother's theft was wrong, but he is no longer
that person — he is someone fighting to rebuild his life and his character, and that matters
morally. The virtuous path here is not to immediately disclose, but to have a courageous and
honest conversation with your brother: acknowledge that what he did caused real harm to real
people you both love, and make clear that he has a genuine responsibility to make amends — not
as a transactional calculation, but because integrity requires it. Encourage him to work with
his sponsor or counselor on how to do this in a way that is honest without being destructive.
True recovery is not just abstinence — it involves reckoning with past wrongs. At the same
time, virtue does not require you to unilaterally blow up your brother's life and your
parents' peace. You can hold both truths — his need for a path to redemption and your parents'
right to know — without weaponizing one against the other. Give him a timeframe and support
him in doing the right thing himself.

Your parents were wronged — they had $15,000 taken from them without consent, and they have
never had the opportunity to know this, seek restitution, or choose how to respond. That your
brother is now in recovery is morally relevant to how we regard him, but it does not
retroactively erase the wrong done to them or extinguish their right to know what happened to
their money. The argument that disclosure would harm your brother's recovery is a

opportunity to do the right thing himself: tell him clearly that you cannot be a keeper of
this secret indefinitely, that your parents deserve to know, and that he should be the one to
tell them. What you cannot do, in good conscience, is simply agree to bury this permanently.
